sources.title: Why marketing isn't a science for solopreneurs: funnels are a myth, so do true work
sources.originalTitle: sorry but marketing is not a science (for solopreneurs)
sources.summary: Alex West argues that at small scale, conversion data is mostly noise and funnels are a tidy story that marketers invented. Real buying is chaotic and slow, so keep showing your product to more people and spend your time on work that makes money, not "pretend work".

principles.text: Don't track conversion rates at low traffic; small samples give noisy data that leads to bad calls.
principles.quote: you should not be tracking any conversion rates if your uh traffic is let's say uh not in the tens of thousands of millions per month.

principles.text: Funnels are a neat story; real buying is chaotic, delayed and non-linear.
principles.quote: I believe that funnels don't exist. They are made up by professional marketers that are trying to make their job a science when it is not.

principles.text: You can't force anyone to buy. Keep showing your product again and again until they decide.
principles.quote: All you can do is keep them in your orbit. Show them what you have built again and again and again until they might decide that they want to buy.

principles.text: At low numbers, trust your gut over your data, since the data is likely noise or an artifact.
principles.quote: at low numbers, it's better to work with your gut than with your mind and your data because your data is probably going to be absolute

principles.text: Avoid 'pretend work' like A/B tests on tiny traffic, refactors or business cards before revenue; it feels productive but makes no money.
principles.quote: set up an A/B test when you have 300 visitors per month this is exactly the same uh the same example or redesign landing page when the conversion is just fine.

principles.text: True work is trying to make money: launch, show it to people, follow up and send payment links.
principles.quote: You launch, you show it to people, you follow up to people and send them payment links. That is what true work is.

sources.title: Alex West on burnout, a 5X income drop and starting over: luck, product-market fit and a sabbatical
sources.originalTitle: Alex West Q&A | burnout, 5X drop in income, taking a sabbatical and more
sources.summary: Alex West explains why he went quiet for a year: constant travel, burnout and nihilism after his first million, while his agency income fell from about 500k to 100k a year. He shares how he is resetting with a sabbatical and treats finding the next product as a numbers-and-luck game.

principles.text: Work on the right idea at the right time and it feels effortless; without product-market fit it feels like a drag.
principles.quote: if you're working on something that does not have product market fit, it will feel like a drag. You know, it will feel like you're fighting against nature.

principles.text: Luck is a real factor in finding winning products, so launch many ideas and be ready to fail repeatedly.
principles.quote: I am prepared to fail 20 times again. I am prepared to build like 20 products again if need be

principles.text: An audience or past success does not make the next launch easier; luck applies at every stage.
principles.quote: just because I have an audience or like past track record does not mean that it it's going to be easier. Now luck is a real factor no matter where you are like in in your trajectory.

principles.text: Feeling lost is permanent for founders, even after milestones; accept starting from scratch as part of the life.
principles.quote: you have to be okay with starting from scratch.

principles.text: Business performance depends on your personal state; a bad headspace shows up in the numbers.
principles.quote: there are no business problems they're only personal problems and to an extent I I agree

principles.text: Creativity and new offers need a calm, low-stimulation environment; constant travel and client stress crowd out innovation.
principles.quote: I could not innovate or come up with anything new while traveling and moving house every week.

sources.title: Alex West's game plan for rebuilding a $1M business: constraints, ingredients and catching the AI wave
sources.originalTitle: building a $1M business for the second time (my gameplan)
sources.summary: Alex West explains how he is approaching his next business after Cyberleads without a fixed idea. He sets an open mind plus hard constraints: use the audience he already owns, mix his existing assets, and deliberately catch a new wave (AI employees and AI sales) instead of ignoring waves.

principles.text: Stay humble about predicting what works; early success doesn't give you a Midas touch.
principles.quote: I thought suddenly I have Midas touch. I know now. I got it, baby. I'm a winner now. I'm smart. I tried building two or three different products, bang, bang bang, slapped by the open market, and humbled.

principles.text: Experiment widely but don't fall in love with any one idea or business.
principles.quote: I want to be playful, I want to be creative, and I want to experiment a lot. And also very important, I do not want to fall in love with any idea or business.

principles.text: Open-mindedness needs constraints; set a middle way so you aren't ideating in a vacuum.
principles.quote: How open-minded? Like, am I going to build something for pet stores? Or like the newsletter industry? I don't know. There needs to be a line. I need some constraints.

principles.text: Building a marketing channel was the hardest output; reuse the one you already have instead of restarting from zero.
principles.quote: building a marketing channel, like this stupid X account that you are on now was indeed the hardest thing to do. And I absolutely do not mean from an input perspective. I mean from an output perspective.

principles.text: Inventory your ingredients (past customers, free list, cold email skill, lead database) and mix and match them into ideas.
principles.quote: Now I have a few ingredients. Like I think it is healthy to have some constraints and some ingredients. Now I can make mix and match these ingredients and create like ideas.

principles.text: Deliberately catch a wave; ignoring every wave was the wrong lesson from a business that survived them.
principles.quote: My lesson was that I should not pay attention to anything. And I that I should ignore every single wave that comes. And I just stay fixed on CyberLease.

sources.title: How Alex West launches solo products fast: launch to learn, strip the fat, validate with money
sources.originalTitle: how i launched my $1M solopreneur business (fast and easy guide)
sources.summary: Alex West explains his repeatable process for launching a solo business idea: treat each launch as a learning experiment, keep scale relative, make every MVP simpler than the last but able to charge money, and then launch in one day via warm outbound, cold outbound and one-to-many channels like Reddit, Product Hunt and social.

principles.text: Launch to learn, not to get rich in 30 days; learning comes from scars, not videos.
principles.quote: you're not launching your idea to become a millionaire in 30 days or 90 days or whatever you're launching to learn

principles.text: Treat scale as relative: the next milestone is just the next step up from where you are now.
principles.quote: if you are at zero users right now scale and success is getting one user if you are at one user now scale is getting to 10 users or customers

principles.text: Knowledge is subtractive: each launch should strip unnecessary things, so every launch is simpler than the last.
principles.quote: knowledge is subtractive not additive it's not about adding things it's about removing things

principles.text: Don't build before validating: a landing page and a buy button can test demand before any backend.
principles.quote: I could have validated this idea with a landing page and nothing at the back nothing on the back end just a a button you know like get started now or pay now

principles.text: An MVP must be able to charge money, otherwise it isn't viable.
principles.quote: minimum viable product it's not viable if it doesn't make money simple Common Sense

principles.text: Launch in one day: start with warm outbound to friends, then cold outreach to bloggers and journalists, then one-to-many channels.
principles.quote: you start with warm outbound just block a day which is launch day one day will be launch day warm outbound you DM you know text message or call any friends that might be interested

sources.title: How Alex West found his $500K/year business idea: go Channel → Market → Idea, B2B, no uniqueness
sources.originalTitle: how i accidentally found a $1M solopreneur business idea
sources.summary: Alex West explains how he went from about $200/month to roughly $500K/year by changing which ideas he picked, not how hard he worked. He argues against passion projects, uniqueness and B2C, and for entering proven markets, selling to businesses, and starting from an audience channel you already have.

principles.text: Finding a 10x better idea is easier than becoming 10x better at executing any idea.
principles.quote: it's a lot easier to find a 10 times better idea than it is to become 10 times better at executing any idea

principles.text: Don't make your business your passion; passion can distort your incentives and rarely makes a good business.
principles.quote: typically your passion is probably not going to be a good business idea

principles.text: If nobody else is doing your idea, that's a red flag; look for multiple people already making money at it.
principles.quote: if you have an idea and you look online and no one else has done it it's not a good thing it's a bad thing it's a red flag

principles.text: Don't fear competing with big companies; they are slow, so you effectively compete against a handful of motivated people.
principles.quote: when you're competing against a 50 person company you're really competing against five people and 45 Yes Men

principles.text: Sell to businesses, not consumers; businesses pay far more and don't haggle the way individuals do.
principles.quote: you can charge 5K per month to a single business they do it all the time

principles.text: Don't go idea → market → channel; start from the channel you already have, find the market it reaches, then the idea.
principles.quote: instead of me going idea Market Channel I went Channel Market idea

sources.title: Why most solopreneurs fail: the four phases from $0 to $1M/year
sources.originalTitle: Why Most Solopreneurs Fail ($0 to $1M/year)
sources.summary: Alex West maps the biggest barrier at each stage of a solo business: first dollar, hundreds to thousands, thousands to tens of thousands, and scaling toward $1M/year. Each stage has a different failure mode: impatience and fear, product obsession over distribution, refusing to delegate, then needing volume.

principles.text: Expect years, not months; most people quit before compounding starts.
principles.quote: you cannot expect to change your life in 6 months you know like it takes years

principles.text: Pick a good market: not winner-take-all, several players earning what you want, reachable via channels you already have.
principles.quote: a good Market as a market that is not a win or take all market and you see multiple people winning at the same time making the amount of money that you're aspiring to make

principles.text: Picking a 10x better idea is far easier than executing 10x better, so idea quality matters a lot.
principles.quote: it's very difficult to become a 10x executioner like to execute an idea 10 times better but it's so easy to pick a 10 times better idea

principles.text: B2B buyers pay far more readily than you expect; don't project your own reluctance to spend onto customers.
principles.quote: B2B is not that hard actually to make people pay because if someone is running a business it's actually pretty easy for them to pay

principles.text: Once a product earns hundreds per month, spend about 90% of time on distribution and keep the product simple.
principles.quote: people I think at this stage should focus 90% of their time on distribution and only maintaining the core product

principles.text: Shift from artist to athlete: stop launching new products and double down on marketing one product, even if boring.
principles.quote: at this point you have to become an athlete you know like do the same [ __ ] every day double down on your marketing focus on that one product

sources.title: When to quit your job as a solopreneur: Alex West's 10 reasons and the asymmetric-risk test
sources.originalTitle: When To Quit Your Job (for solopreneurs)
sources.summary: Alex West explains why he quit his job after Cyberleads out-earned his salary for six months, and distills a decision framework. Quit when results are consistent, you've stopped learning, you have 2+ years of runway, and the downside is capped while the upside is life-changing.

principles.text: Quit only after your business has consistently beaten your salary, not after one lucky spike.
principles.quote: my my business had made more than my salary for 6 months in a row

principles.text: Take asymmetric risks: cheap, playful bets where the downside is small and the upside is large; be conservative on ruinous ones.
principles.quote: with other risk it should be the opposite right like you should be wild you should be experimental and you should be very playful and those are risks that they won't ruin you if they go wrong

principles.text: Stack the odds before leaving: save runway while employed so a total failure still leaves years to recover.
principles.quote: I managed to set aside 50k which means that even if for some reason I was to start making 0 per month starting from tomorrow

principles.text: Embrace the wild, viral nature of social media as a channel instead of trying to make it predictable.
principles.quote: embrace the unpredictable viral nature of social media and go with it

principles.text: For software businesses, a calm mind and one correct scaled decision beat long hours; two focused hours can drive most results.
principles.quote: taking a simple correct decision and scaling it is far more important than the number of hours you put in

principles.text: Small companies' scale is an illusion: a 50-person company is really a handful of doers plus people just moving tasks along, so incumbents are beatable.
principles.quote: when you're competing with a 50% PE uh company you're essentially competing against five people and 45 Yes Men

sources.title: Channel Tier List: how a solopreneur ranks distribution channels from his own results
sources.originalTitle: Channel Tier List (for solopreneurs)
sources.summary: Alex West ranks distribution channels A to F from a decade of trying them. He recommends launching and warm outbound first, then cold outbound and social, then long-term assets like email, YouTube and podcasts. He says channels compound together, and distribution now matters more than product.

principles.text: Distribution matters more than product, and it's only getting more important as competition rises and no new channels appear.
principles.quote: you can have a mediocre okay product average and have insane distribution uh and you can become crazy rich and improve the product over time as well

principles.text: Start with warm outbound and a launch, add cold outbound, and build inbound in parallel.
principles.quote: I always recommend start with warm out rats then add cold outre and in the meantime like build your social uh and SEO and all that other stuff

principles.text: Channels compound together rather than competing: first customers give testimonials, social proof, then inbound, which also lifts cold email replies.
principles.quote: all these channels they're not mutually exclusive like I'm doing outbound now and I'm also building my inbound and they're separate no they work together

principles.text: A launch is a strategy to get your first customers and the confidence to keep going.
principles.quote: launching is a strategy you know like you can get your first 10 customers with a launch and that's how I got my first 10 customers with cyber leads I launched on product hunt

principles.text: Cold email only fits expensive offers, and works far better when you already have a brand. A $200/month offer became $22k/month, enabling cold email.
principles.quote: it only works when you are selling expensive stuff so if you're selling like a SAS product for like $50 a month I don't think it's the best fit

principles.text: Choose the platform by customer type: B2C platforms are easy to grow but convert badly; Twitter's B2B audience is harder to grow but converts far better.
principles.quote: my business is built on a 30,000 Twitter account that's it 30,000 follower Twitter account like nothing crazy but the conversions are insane

sources.title: Why solo founders can ignore competition: 4-part overlap test and the midwit copycat curve
sources.originalTitle: Why Competition Is BULLSH*T (Indie Hackers)
sources.summary: Alex West argues that for small businesses (up to ~$1M/year) in healthy markets, competition barely matters. Most customers don't know you exist, companies move slowly, true competition requires overlap on product, customer, positioning/price and channel, and copycats self-select out.

principles.text: Competition worry only applies to big-win markets; in a healthy market with many players earning your target revenue, ignore it.
principles.quote: you're in a market that is not a win or take all market and that you see many players winning at the same time making the amount of money that you want to make

principles.text: Nearly all potential customers don't know you or your competitors exist, so spend energy on traffic instead of rivals.
principles.quote: 99.9% of your potential customers do not even know that you exist yet

principles.text: A 50-person company is really about five doers, slowed by process, while a solo founder can pivot in a day.
principles.quote: you're not competing against 50 people you're competing against 45 yes men and five people that are actually doing work

principles.text: Two products only truly compete if product, target customer, positioning/pricing and acquisition channel all overlap.
principles.quote: it's only if you if all these four overlap where I I I would agree with you that you are actually competing with someone

principles.text: Often your real competitor is an intangible alternative, like a VA, doing it manually, or an Excel sheet, not another company.
principles.quote: most of the time you're not really competing against other people you're competing against intangible things

principles.text: Copycats mostly fall in the midwit curve: low-end copiers quit fast, overcomplicators won't copy, and smart copiers pick better businesses.
principles.quote: these people usually they quit it within two months okay these people are too scared to copy a product that is making 40K per month

sources.title: One vs multiple businesses: Alex West's sniper, shotgun and fractal strategy
sources.originalTitle: One vs Multiple Businesses (for indie hackers)
sources.summary: Alex West compares building many products (shotgun) with focusing on one (sniper), using his own record: 20 products in two years before finding Cyber Leads. He argues for shotgun before product-market fit, sniper after, and a "fractal" loop that runs the shotgun on distribution channels whenever growth plateaus.

principles.text: Before you have a product that can change your life, ship many small products fast; each launch closes a feedback loop.
principles.quote: pre-product Market fit so if you don't have that product that has the potential to change your life or get you to where you want to go right if you want to be a billionaire that's different

principles.text: After you find a product that works, go sniper and focus on it; spreading across new products only diluted his income.
principles.quote: when I implemented shotgun after I had cyber leads all I did was spread myself thin and make less money

principles.text: When growth plateaus, run the shotgun on distribution channels, not new products, then focus on the winner.
principles.quote: you go within the business and you you you implement the shortgun strategy in order to build new distribution channels

principles.text: Distribution deserves as much time as product; most founders spend 80-90% on product.
principles.quote: every startup should focus 50% of their time on marketing and 50% of their time on product

principles.text: Launch scrappy: polish does not matter. A landing page and a buy button were enough.
principles.quote: all I needed was a landing page and a buy button

principles.text: One product with several distribution channels is safer than several products sharing one channel.
principles.quote: the best is one product with three channels

sources.title: Alex West: Raising prices from $2K to $3K, trust in high-ticket sales, and the 10x price thought experiment
sources.originalTitle: Alex West on raising your prices and sales
sources.summary: Alex West shares weekly notes from running a ~$500K/yr, 90%-profit cold email business. He covers raising prices without losing conversions, why trust is the key lever in high-priced sales, a 10x-price thought experiment for improving a service, and keeping a boring business alongside an exciting life.

principles.text: Trust is the ultimate leverage in high-priced sales; cold prospects raise many objections.
principles.quote: having trust when you're charging a lot of money is the ultimate leverage Point like people don't care as much

principles.text: Raise prices when the service is worth it; he went $2K to $3K per month with no drop in conversions.
principles.quote: I recently raised my prices from 2K to 3K uh and I saw no change whatsoever people still converted

principles.text: Improve the service before or alongside raising prices, so you feel good about what you charge.
principles.quote: I don't want to just raise my price because I can you know I want to improve stuff before I want to feel good about what I do

principles.text: Ask what your service would look like at 10x the price, then ask why you don't do those things anyway.
principles.quote: what would my service look like if it cost 10 times more

principles.text: Marketing results lag; good months often reflect earlier hard work, so keep marketing consistently.
principles.quote: there is a lagging effect between the marketing you do and the customers you get

principles.text: Treat even a boring business with the respect of a science to become a pro and enjoy it.
principles.quote: I try to treat sending cold emails and analyzing their responses and the tracking different metrics

sources.title: Alex West on service business fundamentals: run your clients, over-communicate, and build a fail-safe
sources.originalTitle: Alex West talks service business fundamentals
sources.summary: After hiring an agency to see the other side, Alex lists four intangibles for service businesses: lead the client, show constant progress, be friendly and transparent, and design a fail-safe so lukewarm clients still leave happy. He also notes follow-ups only pay off for warm leads, not cold ones.

principles.text: Act as your client's boss: proactively tell them what to do and follow up, because they hired you for your expertise.
principles.quote: I always thought that when someone hires you he is your boss but it's not the case like you are their boss you have to tell them what to do because they came to you for your expertise

principles.text: You can't over-communicate in a service business; show progress and always state the next step, even without big results.
principles.quote: in my opinion there is no such thing as over communicating when it comes to service businesses you should always keep them updated even even if no results are happening

principles.text: A client who demands instant ROI and isn't satisfied with visible progress is probably not your dream client.
principles.quote: if your client wants instantly results instantly Roi and is not happy with just progress probably is not your dream client

principles.text: Be friendly and fully transparent about progress, good or bad, and show you care beyond the money.
principles.quote: trying to show them that I actually [ __ ] care about you uh and I don't just want your money and to churn and burn through you

principles.text: Build a fail-safe (like a money-back guarantee, transparency, goodwill) so lukewarm or bad-result clients still leave happy, since not everyone gets great results.
principles.quote: for those clients both in the lukewarm place and the negative results you want to for them to leave happy and for that thing you can have like a money back guarantee

principles.text: Follow-ups pay off with warm leads, not cold ones: stop after two or three cold emails, but follow up forever with anyone who replied.
principles.quote: the money is in the follow-ups and that is true but what they don't tell you is that it's true for warm leads not cold leads

sources.title: Alex West on copycats, audience vs building, and playful projects (Podcast #1)
sources.originalTitle: Launching my new podcast - Episode #1
sources.summary: Alex West argues one-to-one copycats are nothing to fear because they are usually beginners or very experienced operators, and that copying signals low-revenue visibility, not validation. He says you build an audience by building interesting things, and that playful, unserious projects can take off unpredictably.

principles.text: Don't fear one-to-one copycats; they tend to be complete beginners or far more experienced people who will copy bigger things.
principles.quote: One-to-one copycats, I don't think you should be afraid of. Cuz most probably either they're going to be complete beginners, or they're going to be very experienced people.

principles.text: Being copied isn't validation. Copycats target small, beatable projects, so you attract more of them at low revenue.
principles.quote: I got more copycats at 1K MRR than I got at 50. Because I think it's almost like um in the brain like oh [ __ ] 50. I There's no way I can do that. Let me copy something that is more in my league.

principles.text: Your moat is what you keep building, not what exists. Competitors can only copy what you've already shipped.
principles.quote: They can copy your product. Okay, true. They can copy your features. Yes, they can copy your design, but they can only copy what you've already built. They cannot copy what you haven't created with That's your advantage.

principles.text: Build cool things and share them to get an audience; audience-building in a vacuum is the wrong order.
principles.quote: You don't build an audience in a vacuum. You do interesting things and share them with the world in order to get an audience.

principles.text: An audience helps but doesn't guarantee success; quality of the post matters more than follower count.
principles.quote: I have 45,000 followers. And if it's [ __ ] I will get 10 likes. But if it's good, it can go viral. Like, okay, yes, it does help, but to an extent.

principles.text: You can't predict what will work, so be playful and experimental; fun projects can become real businesses.
principles.quote: You cannot predict what is going to work, and not everything has to be serious, including this stupid little podcast.

sources.title: Alex West on dropping moats, validating with outreach and ads, and not boxing yourself into labels
sources.originalTitle: Moats are dead, making it as a parent, perfectionism and outbid.lol | Alex West Podcast EP 2
sources.summary: Alex West co-hosts a weekly news chat with Dimitro of Screenshot One. He argues obsessing over moats is disguised perfectionism, that revenue-stage rules ignore each business's "genetics", and that labels like solopreneur or indie hacker should guide you without becoming dogma. He also uses outreach and ads to validate offers.

principles.text: Obsessing over moats is often perfectionism: a search for the ultimate magical business that lasts.
principles.quote: Looking back I feel like that is just another word for in a way perfectionism, right? Like you're looking for the ultimate magical business that's going to last

principles.text: Assume there is no moat and keep building, improving and staying competitive.
principles.quote: you assume there is no mode and you just keep building, keep improving, keep being competitive

principles.text: Use outreach to validate new offers and ideas quickly, not as a substitute for organic channels.
principles.quote: I use outreach mainly to validate new offers and ideas. Like at the moment now I am sending like a thousand emails a day testing new ideas.

principles.text: Revenue-stage rules ('do X until $1M') ignore that every business has different economics and ceilings.
principles.quote: Every business is unique, dude. Every business has different genetics.

principles.text: Labels can point you in a direction, but don't let them become dogma that boxes you in.
principles.quote: as time goes on you don't want this to be dogmatic and box you up

principles.text: Constraints force focus: limited time made him more productive.
principles.quote: my best work ever was when I was working a full-time job that I hated. That was my most productive year of my life.

sources.title: How Alex West built a $300k solo B2B service business (Cyber Leads) from a simple monthly list
sources.originalTitle: $300k service business - interview with Alex West
sources.summary: Alex West explains why he left flashy B2C products for a "boring" B2B funded-companies newsletter, then added a $2k/month done-for-you cold email service. He covers simplicity as a differentiator, finding one product plus one distribution channel (Twitter), and switching from artist to athlete once something works.

principles.text: Build a boring business that funds your lifestyle rather than something that sounds cool at parties.
principles.quote: everything you do do it for yourself and what is TR truly meaningful for me is to to have a great lifestyle and if that means that I have that I have to run a boring business

principles.text: Go B2B: businesses pay far more readily than consumers, so you need far fewer customers.
principles.quote: with cyber Le at 200 customers it could be like a million per year with the other business 200 customers would be 1K per month

principles.text: Go high ticket so the number of customers you need is tiny and competition stops mattering.
principles.quote: for that I charge 2K per month okay so that means to hit 1 million per year I need 40 customers from the whole damn world

principles.text: Use simplicity as a differentiator; busy buyers won't invest time decoding your product or landing page.
principles.quote: use Simplicity as a differentiator like people don't have time uh and that goes for your landing page that goes for your product

principles.text: Find one product people pay for and one repeatable distribution channel, then run it again and again.
principles.quote: the game is to have one product that people are willing to pay for and one distribution Channel you can utilize again and again and again

principles.text: Experiment broadly to find what works, then switch from artist to athlete: repeat the winner while running side experiments for the next lever.
principles.quote: you have to become like an athlete from an artist you have to become an athlete do the boring stuff do again and again the thing that took you from zero to 10 customers

sources.title: How Alex West built a $300K/yr solo business (Cyber Leads) market-first with no-code
sources.originalTitle: Ep 8 - Building $300,000/ARR solo-business using no-code | Alex West | The ChoubeySahab Podcast
sources.summary: Alex West explains how, after 19 failed products, he picked a healthy market first, launched a no-code newsletter selling lead data, and found traction by trying every channel until Twitter worked. He also argues that money is easy to measure but a poor sole metric, and that quality of life should come first.

principles.text: Pick a healthy market first, then find the idea, instead of building an idea and hunting for a market.
principles.quote: instead of going from idea to product to trying to find someone to sell it i went the other way around i went market first

principles.text: A healthy market has many players already making money, something you can build, and something you can promote.
principles.quote: number one it has many many players making millions of dollars

principles.text: Boring products make money; cool products that impress people at parties usually don't.
principles.quote: those don't make money usually that's the bad thing the boring things make money

principles.text: Start with no-code; nobody cares what a product is built with, only the value it creates.
principles.quote: no one cares like when was the last time you went on a website and you're like okay what is this built with who cares

principles.text: Launching isn't the finish line; you need a repeatable way to get customers again and again.
principles.quote: you have to find a way to get customers again and again and again and again and again every every every week every day because customers don't stay forever

principles.text: Try every acquisition channel, then drop the rest and go all in on the one that works.
principles.quote: try everything and when you find the one that works drop everything else and focus on that one thousand percent

sources.title: How Alex West got to CyberLeads after 19 failed products: build boring, double down
sources.originalTitle: [Episode #8] Bruno Talks With... Alex West • Don't give up
sources.summary: Alex West explains how 19 failed products led to CyberLeads, a lead-gen newsletter for agencies. Lessons: build boring ideas people already pay for, learn from doing, find one product plus one distribution channel and double down, and treat competition as no threat. Also covers habits over motivation and why small teams can outmove companies.

principles.text: Build boring products people already pay for, not unique world-changing ones.
principles.quote: let's build something boring let's build something that i know that people will pay for let's build something without code

sources.title: Alex West: Shotgun approach to products, owning data infrastructure, and trust as the moat
sources.originalTitle: Alex West: Building a $1M solo business while travelling the world after 19 failed products. #1
sources.summary: Alex West, a bootstrapping solo developer, talks about building many products on shared infrastructure, why he thinks trust and attention win as everything gets commoditized, and how to find and validate ideas. He also covers working in the building phase versus the marketing phase and the Peter Levels shotgun approach.

principles.text: Own reusable data infrastructure and build every product on it so you can ship new ones fast.
principles.quote: everybody should own a data pipeline because I think that the future is or the value of the next economies will or the next economy will be on data

principles.text: Test many products to find traction. Diversify only after you are wealthy, not while chasing your first big win.
principles.quote: I think diversifying is great for retaining your wealth not for making your wealth so I think when you're up and coming you should focus on one thing try to hit the [ __ ] home run

principles.text: Most success stories start with traction, which is what makes founders willing to pull their soul into a product.

principles.text: As tech is commoditized and barriers to entry fall, trust and attention are what cannot be copied.

principles.text: Identical products can win through different positioning, which attracts different customers.

sources.title: Alex West: Finding one product and one channel, channel-first market selection (500-subscriber Q&A)

sources.title: How Alex West went from 0 to $100/month in two years of shotgun building and sniper pivots
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 1: Screaming into the void ($100/month, years 1-2)
sources.summary: Alex West's candid account of his first two indie years: 15 product launches, a $200/month peak, and many mistakes. He shows why products that work without network effects beat communities and marketplaces, why small fast launches beat years of polishing, and where B2B pivots and bad-fit customers hurt.

principles.text: Kill ideas that need huge scale or network effects, and don't treat the idea as yourself.
principles.quote: It would only generate profit at large scale, given the business model. And it was in a network effects market, an all-or-nothing model, either you go viral or you die.

principles.text: Build products that deliver the same value with zero users, not communities or marketplaces that start empty.
principles.quote: The only product that was different was MultiNewTab. And it was my most successful product.

principles.text: Small, low-expectation products launched fast beat big ideas. His least-planned ideas were the most successful.
principles.quote: The 2 ideas I thought of the least, MultiNewTab and GitGardener, have been my most successful ones.

principles.text: Build and launch in public with a firm deadline. Announcing it makes quitting harder even with no audience.
principles.quote: Saying it out loud publicly made quitting harder, even when no one was listening.

principles.text: Let customer requests drive premium features. A user's question about private repos became GitGardener's first paid tier.
principles.quote: GitGardener went from $0 to $50/month in one week. All free users that upgraded.

principles.text: Validate demand before building. A viral launch with zero customers shows a landing page and buy button would have worked as well.
principles.quote: I realized that even a fake landing page with a "buy now" button could have done the same job.

sources.title: How Alex West went from $100/month to $2k/month with CyberLeads in 6 months
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 2: Breaking through the ceiling ($2,000/month, year 3)
sources.summary: Alex recounts how, after two years of failed launches, he took a day job, flipped his plan to a boring validated B2B idea, killed "pretend work," launched fast on Product Hunt, then found Twitter as a repeatable channel. Core lessons: go market-first, ship before building, focus on one product plus one channel.

principles.text: Go market-first: pick validated ideas in healthy, non-winner-take-all markets and take a slice instead of inventing unique ones.
principles.quote: These were markets that were not winner-take-all and many players were making good money with products I could build and market by myself.

principles.text: Existing competitors are validation, not a reason to skip an idea.
principles.quote: I was actually glad it already existed. That meant it was already validated for me.

principles.text: Kill pretend work with the gun-to-your-head test: what would you do to earn revenue this week?
principles.quote: You have to generate revenue online by the end of the week. If you don't, you're dead.

principles.text: Launch with a landing page and payment, then build after customers pay; paying customers' deadlines force speed.
principles.quote: I was building my parachute while falling.

principles.text: Without a repeatable distribution channel you are stuck; you need a way to get traffic as if launching every week.
principles.quote: Well, that's why you need a marketing channel and a way to utilize it. Repeatedly. At a good cost.

principles.text: Once something works, double down on one product and one channel instead of scattering your attention.
principles.quote: Less is more. Focused attention on one thing is far better than scattered attention on multiple things.

sources.title: How Alex West escaped competition with CyberLeads: niche down, raise prices, grow to $3k/month and beyond
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 3: Learning through scars ($3,000/month, year 3)
sources.summary: Alex West explains how clones and copycats threatened CyberLeads, and how he escaped them by analyzing paying customers, niching down to agencies, adding social proof, tripling prices and building one tiny feature. He also covers annual plans, focusing on marketing, and managing stress as the business grew past his salary.

principles.text: Watch what customers pay and how long they stay, rather than asking for opinions; surveys were not very useful.
principles.quote: I had been burned many times asking for peoples' opinion, so I decided to observe what they do instead.

principles.text: Sell to the segment whose number one pain point you solve; that turns a nice-to-have into a must-have.
principles.quote: you ideally want to sell a solution to someone's number one pain point. Not number two. Not number three. Strictly number one. It takes your product from "nice to have" to "must have".

principles.text: Target who wants your product, not who you think needs it; wanting predicts payment.
principles.quote: Maybe it's not about who "needs" your product, after all. Maybe it's about who "wants" your product.

principles.text: Small changes escape competition: a niche tagline, testimonials and one segment-specific feature stopped 'how are you different' questions.
principles.quote: Tweak the copy. Niche down. Maybe build a single feature. That's it.

principles.text: Niching plus social proof let him raise prices from $29 to $99 while conversions kept rising.
principles.quote: From $29/month. To $49/month. To $99/month.

principles.text: Offer annual plans when customers churn after a few months: double revenue per customer, paid upfront.
principles.quote: I make double the amount of money. I make it all upfront. And customers feel like it's a steal.

sources.title: How Alex West quit his job for CyberLeads after 19 failed products and stacked the odds first
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 4: Burning the boats ($4,000/month, year 4)
sources.summary: Alex West explains why he left his job to go full time on CyberLeads, his 20th product, after earning more than his salary six months in a row. He covers his risk framework, how he built a two-year runway first, and why he distrusts corporate complexity.

principles.text: Quit only after consistent results: beat your salary for months, even if the business is messy and imperfect.
principles.quote: CyberLeads has made more than my salary six months in a row.

principles.text: Adapt to the market you have instead of waiting for an ideal one with low churn and autopilot acquisition.
principles.quote: I have to adjust my sails to the wind. Not try to change the weather.

principles.text: Be conservative with ruinous risks and playful with risks that cap the downside but have large upside.
principles.quote: With some risks, you should be super conservative. Risks that could ruin you if they go wrong.

principles.text: Stack the odds before leaping: save a runway so failure leaves you time to recover.
principles.quote: I managed to set aside almost $50k.

principles.text: Focused hours on the right things beat long hours on the wrong things; clarity of mind matters more than more time.
principles.quote: I remember working 10 hours per day on the wrong things back in Greece, going nowhere.

principles.text: Building products early shows you can do it solo; corporate complexity can make founding seem impossible.
principles.quote: If I had joined the company before building any products of my own, maybe I would have never built products.

sources.title: How Alex West went solo: risk, programmatic SEO, and designing life ($5K/month)
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 5: Into the wild ($5,000/month, year 4)
sources.summary: Alex West recounts his first year self-employed running CyberLeads at about $5K/month take-home. He covers take-home math, diversification as insurance (two is enough), a months-long programmatic SEO bet undermined by bot data, and trading small spending for happiness and memorable time.

principles.text: Revenue is not take-home: even a lean solo business keeps only 70-75% after taxes and expenses.
principles.quote: I realize that, at the end of the day, I would be taking home 70% to 75% of my revenue, after all my expenses my expenses and taxes.

principles.text: A small, high-margin solo business can match the take-home of a larger company with co-founders and low margins.
principles.quote: Yet they call the first a side project and the second a business.

principles.text: You will make mistakes; the goal is to avoid the catastrophic, avoidable ones and survive long enough to keep growing.
principles.quote: I have accepted that I'll make mistakes. Many of them. But I have to avoid the catastrophic ones. Especially the ones I can avoid.

principles.text: Treat diversification as insurance: a second bank or channel buys time to recover the first, and two is enough.
principles.quote: If I think of diversification as insurance, I feel like having a second option is enough. A second option that will help me buy time to recover my first option. Or build a new one.

principles.text: Avoid depending on one distribution channel; build a second one before the first breaks.
principles.quote: I have started building a second distribution channel. More than 90% of my customers come from Twitter, and that scares me.

principles.text: Micro-optimizing metrics without talking to real users can mislead; verify the data is human and talk to customers.
principles.quote: Enough with the scientific nonsense. ... Back to old school. Let's talk to humans. And use common sense.

sources.title: How Alex West went from $1k to $6k/month by selling a $2k/month email service to his own customers
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 6: Breaking the frame ($6,000/month, year 4)
sources.summary: Alex West recounts a year of failed growth experiments (a database SaaS, Google SEO, upsells, affiliates, lead magnets, a podcast) before a customer question led him to sell a done-for-you email service. He closed three clients in a week, reframing scaling, service vs. software, and perfectionism.

principles.text: Ask churned customers why they leave; their cancellation reasons point to the product you should be selling.
principles.quote: they are all saying the exact same thing. That they don't have the time to setup everything and send the emails. Or they don't know how to do it.

principles.text: Judge channels by customers acquired, not effort. A year of SEO work can be pretend work next to one tweet.
principles.quote: After 12 months, 1 million impressions and tens of thousands of visitors, I got 5 customers from Google.

principles.text: Sell to your warmest audience first: long-time readers and customers who trust you buy fastest.
principles.quote: They said that they had been following me for years and were customers for a long time. They said that they trusted me.

principles.text: Free lead magnets can attract the wrong buyers. Beginners with endless questions and no budget act as a reverse filter.
principles.quote: It was a reverse filter. I was attracting beginner freelancers that were never intending to spend a single dollar.

principles.text: Test a service offer cheaply by emailing your list and quoting a high price. Instant acceptance is strong validation.
principles.quote: I dropped a crazy price of $2k/month just to see what they would say.

principles.text: Redefine scaling as just the next revenue step, not infinite scalability, and don't dismiss manual service work.
principles.quote: scaling is simply taking your revenue to the next level. Just one step.

sources.title: How Alex West went from $0 to $100k/year: shotgun-to-sniper experiments, then a simple low-tax base
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 7: Setting up my base ($8,000/month, year 5)
sources.summary: Alex West recaps five years of bootstrapping, from a failed two-year product to CyberLeads and a $2k/month productized service. He distills a shotgun-then-sniper pattern with roughly a 5% hit rate, explains why he committed fully to the one thing that worked, and shows how he chose a simple low-tax setup in Cyprus.

principles.text: Alternate between shotgun and sniper: run many cheap experiments to find a winner, then focus hard on it until it plateaus.
principles.quote: Shotgun many experiments until I find a successful product. Sniper on that product until I hit a plateau. Shotgun many experiments to find the next lever of growth.

principles.text: Assume a low hit rate (~5%) and budget for about 20 attempts per product or growth lever.
principles.quote: And I assume that my hit rate will be around 5%: It took me 20 products launches to find CyberLeads.

principles.text: Pick ideas that are already validated and start from channel and market, not from the product.
principles.quote: when I was looking for ideas I tried to go channel and market first. And I tried to pick and idea that already existed and was validated.

principles.text: Raise prices over time: each customer is worth far more at higher price points, so growth gets easier.
principles.quote: And now, again 2 years later, with my $2k/mo product, getting 4 new customers means an extra $100k/year.

principles.text: When something works, run with it instead of chasing a repeat; don't assume you have the Midas touch.
principles.quote: after getting smacked in the face by reality with a few failed launches, I decided to dedicate my full attention to CyberLeads.

principles.text: A home run doesn't need to be your best or most exciting product; a boring business that works and keeps growing is enough.
principles.quote: But it's a business that works. Is growing. And will keep on growing. Hopefully for years, or even decades. So I love it.

sources.title: How Alex West scaled CyberLeads to ~$500k/year by productizing outbound and building systems
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 8: Paying the cost ($40,000/month, year 5)
sources.summary: Alex tells the story of launching a $2k/month outbound lead-gen service on top of CyberLeads. Early campaigns failed and clients churned, then he documented, automated and simplified his way to results and a viral My First Million mention, only to end up burned out in a "second cage". Lessons cover thinking for yourself, narrowing focus, and distrusting advice that sells a product.

principles.text: Following expert playbooks failed; results only came after thinking for yourself and experimenting broadly.
principles.quote: Looking back, once again, following recipes and playbooks didn't work for me. I only started seeing results when I started thinking for myself.

principles.text: Document every step in exact detail; documentation is like programming and can be automated into a SaaS.
principles.quote: Documenting things step-by-step was exactly like programming. Just in human language and images, instead of code.

principles.text: The behind-the-scenes systems are the real business; the visible product is only the surface.
principles.quote: The real business is not the final product. It's all the behind the scenes stuff that's invisible.

principles.text: Kill complexity and narrow focus: one channel, one language, one target customer made delivery faster and clients happier.
principles.quote: Every process that stayed had to fight for it's life. It was a war against complexity. If it was just ok or good, it would be killed.

principles.text: Clients want results, not effort or leads; refunds can't repair a lost reputation, so guarantees are a weak escape rope.
principles.quote: I could refund money. But I couldn't refund my reputation.

principles.text: Be wary of advice that conveniently matches what the adviser sells; beliefs are only real when they cost you something.
principles.quote: Everyone is talking their own book. And everyone's advice somehow perfectly aligns with what they are selling.

sources.title: How Alex West built a team and stepped back to run CyberLeads as a machine ($40k/month)
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 9: Building a machine ($40,000/month, year 6)
sources.summary: Alex West recounts going from solo operator to running CyberLeads with four remote hires, and what he learned about delegation, hiring, incentives and fighting entropy. He ends with the view that business is more like jazz than science.

principles.text: Delegate daily and weekly tasks; do quarterly or one-off tasks yourself, because fast feedback loops let errors get corrected.
principles.quote: Where I found delegation to truly shine was daily and weekly tasks. The feedback loop was fast enough and frequent enough for us to correct errors, improve, perfect and not forget.

principles.text: Hire for competence, reliability and responsiveness, not for being the best in the world.
principles.quote: I was hiring her because she seemed competent enough, a good person, reliable, and she replied fast.

principles.text: Don't automate or delegate everything or too fast; do a task several times first, and keep some tasks yourself.
principles.quote: Sometimes I would perform a task once, create instructions and hand it off straight away. But sometimes it was only the 3rd or 4th time I performed a task that I realized it could be done in a completely different way and be automated, or that we don't need it.

principles.text: Ask whether you are iterating, perfecting or procrastinating; almost everything has a next-day version you can ship now.
principles.quote: I found that almost everything has a "next day version".

principles.text: Keep deliberate inefficiency as a shock absorber and set a margin floor (80%) rather than squeezing every cost.
principles.quote: This inefficiency is actually optimal. It's a shock absorber.

principles.text: Hire an operator to fight entropy and handle edge cases, and pay them a profit share plus sales calls.
principles.quote: The payment structure was simple: 10% of the profits of the service part of the business. In exchange for taking all of the sales calls and handling the edge cases in fulfillment.

sources.title: Alex West on disconnecting: boring business, exciting life, and why knowledge is subtractive
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 10: Disconnecting ($40,000/month, year 6)
sources.summary: Book 10 of Alex West's personal essay series, written at roughly $40k/month in year 6. It is mostly travel and life reflection, with a few durable lessons: run a boring business that funds a rich life, converge by experimenting then keeping little, cut information, and trust real feedback over echo chambers.

principles.text: Prefer a boring, high-earning business that takes little time over an exciting project that earns nothing and eats your life.
principles.quote: I prefer working 2 hours per day, on my boring business, make a ton of money and enjoy my life, rather than the opposite.

principles.text: You can keep working on anything indefinitely if it has a mission and shows visible progress over time.
principles.quote: As long as I can attach a mission to something, and I can keep seeing some progress over time, I can keep doing it forever.

principles.text: Experiment widely, go overboard, then keep only the one or two things that prove worth keeping.
principles.quote: I go on a cycle of experimentation, go completely overboard, and eventually keep 1 or 2 little things that are actually worth keeping. While discarding all of the rest.

principles.text: More information often hurts. Wanting the few things that matter beats consuming endless, unvetted advice.
principles.quote: I used to think that the more information I have, the better. But more and more, I have started to realize that knowledge is subtractive.

principles.text: Being okay with unfinished TODOs is a core business meta skill; work never ends and the list grows as you work.
principles.quote: One of the most important meta skills in business is being ok with not finishing your TODOs.

principles.text: Insist on real feedback from the market and reality, not echo chambers, yes men or flattering AI.
principles.quote: people that are not in contact with the elements of nature or the free market, forces that don't care about your feelings and give you real feedback.

sources.title: Alex West on hitting $1M, maps vs compasses, and what business success does and doesn't give you
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 11: Highest highs, lowest lows ($50,000/month, year 7)
sources.summary: Alex West reflects on making his first $1M in revenue after six years of bootstrapping. He argues advice is a treasure map that ages badly, so rely on external maps early and your own compass as you gain experience. He is candid that the milestone felt anticlimactic and that his business was free-falling after a $50k/month peak.

principles.text: Early in a domain rely on other people's maps; as experience grows, trust your own intuition. Consult both, like a captain.
principles.quote: I believe that the earlier you are in your journey within a specific domain or subject, the more you have to rely on external knowledge.

sources.title: Book 12: When metrics lie, a dying $20k/month business needs customer truth, not more features
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 12: Looking for answers ($20,000/month, year 7)
sources.summary: Alex West recounts CyberLeads falling from $50k to $20k/month. Tracking 30+ metrics, then three big levers, backfired past a threshold. Doing the work himself and talking to clients exposed the real problems, and a feature-heavy relaunch bloated the product and diluted its core.

principles.text: Revenue reduces to three inputs: customers signed per month, how long they stay, and what they pay.
principles.quote: It was the average number of clients we sign each month. The average number of months they stay. And the average price they pay us.

principles.text: A business plateaus when customers coming in equal customers leaving; staying in business alone does not compound.
principles.quote: Because, after a while, the number of customers coming in was equal to the amount of customers leaving.

principles.text: Pushing a metric past a threshold backfires: more booked calls, forwarded leads, higher prices and more posting all hurt.
principles.quote: Increasing the number of our booked sales calls after a certain point did not increase our closes. It actually started backfiring and we were wasting our time with unqualified leads.

principles.text: Dashboards can mislead; do the work yourself and talk to customers to find the real problems.
principles.quote: They say that numbers don't lie. But in my case they did.

principles.text: Sell what customers want, not what you think they need; they want the latest tools like AI.
principles.quote: It's not about what you think your customers "need". It's about what your customers "want".

principles.text: Adding features dilutes the core that people actually wanted; keep a simple, clear positioning.
principles.quote: The more I added to CyberLeads, the more I dilluted it's core. And the core is what people wanted.

sources.title: Alex West on CyberLeads' decline: S curves, business genetics, and Shotgun to Sniper
sources.originalTitle: How I Made $1M From My Personal Projects, Book 13: Castles in the sand ($8,000/month, year 8)
sources.summary: Alex West recounts burning out as CyberLeads declined from about $500k/year, pivoting to a $3k consulting offer, and spending a year writing his books. He distills what he learned: businesses are sequences of S curves that eventually fall, waves shape outcomes more than models, and growth comes from shotgunning products, sniping a winner, then shotgunning again for the next lever.

principles.text: Businesses are a sequence of S curves, each with its own plateau, and each eventually rises, plateaus and falls.
principles.quote: Businesses are a sequence of S curves, each one reaching a different plateau.

principles.text: Price is the easiest growth lever; new channels are hardest, retention via product is in between.
principles.quote: Building new channels is the hardest. And making people pay more is by far the easiest and most effective lever to pull.

principles.text: Find the distribution channel and market first, then the idea. Building a unique product first never worked for him.
principles.quote: What worked, and the way I found CyberLeads, was thinking of my distribution channel and market first, because those are the hardest to build in the current business environment, and then the actual idea.

principles.text: Shotgun many products until one works, then sniper on it until the plateau, then shotgun again for the next growth lever.
principles.quote: Shotgun many products until you find a successful one

principles.text: Success often comes from the business's genetics (channel, pricing, timing, brand), so don't mistake it for personal mastery.
principles.quote: I mistook my success for mastery.

principles.text: Entrepreneurship is choosing which waves to ride, adapt to, or ignore. Ignoring all waves forever is the wrong lesson.
principles.quote: I think the magic of entrepreneurship is deciding how to respond to each wave while sailing the oceans. Which waves to capitalize on. Which waves to adapt to. And which waves to completely ignore.

sources.title: Reflecting on 8 launches: lessons from building a $1M business a second time
sources.originalTitle: Reflecting
sources.summary: Alex West recaps three months after finishing his books: content experiments (human, slightly original videos win) and seven product launches that mostly flopped, echoing his first journey. Takeaways: skip months-long builds, test with landing pages, keep momentum, and put more effort into each launch.

principles.text: Human posts perform well, and a tiny dose of originality in format and hook adds virality.
principles.quote: Lesson: Videos and a tiny bit different does really well. It’s about creativity and originality.

principles.text: Pick a content format you can sustain while traveling or when not feeling like performing.
principles.quote: My realization is that I need a form of video I can always do, even when I'm not feeling like performing and I'm traveling.

principles.text: Storytelling hooks beat plain launch announcements.
principles.quote: It's basic storytelling. It's more exciting and interesting than simply just launching.

principles.text: Don't spend months building; launch a landing page and see if anyone pays.
principles.quote: Lesson: stop wasting time, launch just landing pages and figure things out if you get paid.

principles.text: Scaling starts from $0 to $1, not from your past revenue level.
principles.quote: But scaling when you are at $0 is getting to $1.

principles.text: Balance speed with intent: don't overthink, don't throw random products at the wall, and put more effort into launches.
principles.quote: but also don't throw completely random shit at the wall

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West argues that at small scale, conversion data is mostly noise and funnels are a tidy story that marketers invented. Real buying is chaotic and slow, so keep showing your product to more people and spend your time on work that makes money, not "pretend work".

chunks.heading: Funnels are a story marketers tell, not how buying works
chunks.text:
Alex West argues that "marketing is not a science" for solopreneurs, and that funnels "don't exist". He says they are made up by professional marketers trying to turn their job into a science.

- The tidy model is: sign up, fill a form, join a list, enter an email sequence, upgrade on the third follow-up. He says he has never upgraded from a drip campaign.
- He tells readers to ignore books like Peter Thiel's "Zero to One" and rely on their own direct experience of how they buy.
- He describes a more chaotic path:
  - You see a product and forget it.
  - Six months later you see it again and leave your email, then forget it again.
  - A friend mentions it, but you are moving house.
  - Months later you find it buried in the promotions tab.
  - A month after that you see it once more and buy.
- He notes that a team may have tweaked its landing page or email sequence the day before you convert, and be "100% certain" that change caused the sale. His point is that the world does not work that way.

chunks.heading: You cannot convert people, only keep them in your orbit
chunks.text:
Alex's view is that you cannot persuade or force anyone to buy something they don't want. In his words, "all you can do is keep them in your orbit."

- The tactic is simple: show what you have built to more people, again and again, until some decide to buy.
- He says changes are fine, but the core of the work is repeated exposure, not optimizing a mechanism.

chunks.heading: Don't track conversion rates at low traffic
chunks.text:
Alex agrees with a tweet that many people, especially in tech, lack basic statistics: "Conversions are down 30%" from a sample of 17 with no concept of statistical significance leads to bad calls. He admits he has made this mistake himself, gathering data and making decisions from it.

- He says you should not track conversion rates unless traffic is in the tens of thousands or millions per month.
- He goes further and says that "arguably even then maybe you shouldn't track."
- At low numbers he prefers working from gut feeling over data, because the data is probably noise.

chunks.heading: Example: dropdown data that was just mouse position
chunks.text:
While collecting emails for Cyber Leads (he was focused on SEO then), Alex used a questionnaire with dropdown questions.

- Answers B and C were always the most popular.
- He shuffled and reordered the answers, and B and C still won.
- He did this several times with the same result, whatever the question was.
- He eventually realized that when people click through a form quickly, the mouse tends to rest over B and C when the dropdown opens.
- His lesson: bad data can look meaningful, and people then extrapolate from it and let it guide their product roadmap.

chunks.heading: Pretend work vs. true work
chunks.text:
Alex says people turn to optimizing because it feels productive when they don't know what to work on. He calls this "pretend work" and admits he still does it, for example writing books that lose money.

- True work is trying to make money: launch, show it to people, follow up with them, and send payment links.
- His examples of pretend work:
  - Refactoring code or moving to AWS with zero users.
  - Setting up an A/B test with 300 visitors a month.
  - Redesigning a landing page when conversion is fine.
  - Setting up a business email, business cards or paperwork before making any money.
  - Adding a feature nobody asked for.
  - Improving site speed or setting up meta tags.
- He says "true work is about making money; pretend work is stuff like this."

chunks.heading: Entrepreneurship has no recipes
chunks.text:
Alex says this is not just a knock on marketers. He compares it to his time at a company, where people complicate their work to look professional.

- In daily standups he would just say he fixed a bug and would continue a feature.
- Colleagues who "knew the game" gave long, jargon-filled updates, for example about investigating database structures for a move to Aurora DB.
- Designers and product managers often could not follow them, and he could not either.
- He says marketers do the same by trying to make their job a science, and that entrepreneurship is not a science either: "There are no recipes."
- He doubts the scientific approach in Thiel's "Zero to One", while acknowledging he can't argue with Thiel's results (he says he has made about $1 million, versus Thiel's billions).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West explains why he went quiet for a year: constant travel, burnout and nihilism after his first million, while his agency income fell from about 500k to 100k a year. He shares how he is resetting with a sabbatical and treats finding the next product as a numbers-and-luck game.

chunks.heading: Burnout and a 5x income drop: what happened to Cyber Leads in the year after Alex's first million
chunks.text:
- Alex's business is Cyber Leads, his performance-marketing agency. His normal good month used to be around $40k, with months fluctuating between $25k and $50k. That is roughly $500k a year in revenue at about 80% margin.
- Over the last year revenue fell hard. He says his income dropped 5x, from about $500k a year to about $100k a year.
- He names two causes. The first was personal: he had burned out and was not in a good place to run the business. The second was the industry: his market changed a lot and he could not innovate or come up with new offers while traveling.
- He quotes a friend's line that he likes: "there are no business problems, they're only personal problems." He agrees with it "to an extent".
- The cycle fed itself. The business declining made his mental state worse, and his worse mental state made the business decline faster.
- He says he kept running the business day to day while it dropped, instead of stepping back to fix the underlying problem.

chunks.heading: Why constant travel killed his creativity and made the work boring
chunks.text:
- Alex had always seen himself as a chill person who handled stress by working out. He thought he was not susceptible to burnout.
- The trigger was constant travel with no organization. He recently changed 13 houses in 12 weeks, which he calls the peak of the whirlwind. He was moving through places like New York, London and Bangkok, with visas and airports along the way.
- He argues that too much stimulation makes the actual work boring. New people, cultures, languages and women every day made sitting down to write a new Cyber offer feel uninteresting. "New chapter every two weeks, new country. And then you have to sit down and come up with a new offer for cyber, like it's not going to happen."
- His fix was the opposite environment. He rented an apartment by the sea in the Mediterranean and stopped using buses and cars. After about one month in this low-stimulation setup, he says he became creative again almost immediately.
- Lesson he draws: a "controlled boring", simple, pleasant environment is what restores the drive to build. He compares it to the early days when he woke up at 7am excited to open his laptop and wrote ideas down at night so he would not forget them.

chunks.heading: Hitting the first million and losing his drive
chunks.text:
- Last summer Alex made his first million from his own projects, a week before his 30th birthday. He had chased it for many years.
- The goal "make a million from my own projects before 30" was directionally correct and moved him into productive ways of acting and thinking.
- Achieving it backfired. He compares it to "a letter bomb": he opened it and "exploded into nihilism" and lost his drive. His takeaway is that you are still the same person after the milestone.
- He says this is why he stopped posting at the same time, last summer.
- He says feeling lost is permanent for builders. You feel lost now, after a plateau, or after hitting your big milestone and wondering why you are not happy. "You have to be okay with that because this is the life you have chosen." He compares it to athletes and fighters: "the highest highs and the lowest lows."

chunks.heading: Taking a sabbatical that is the opposite of travel
chunks.text:
- Alex's sabbatical is not a trip. He deliberately stopped traveling and moved to one quiet place by the sea to regroup and reflect on what is next.
- He has stopped all client work. He is only running the newsletter part of the business, which does not make much money, and keeps one or two clients.
- He is fine taking a big pay cut. He says he could actually stop working for many years, but that is not what he wants.
- Why he left client work: running performance marketing campaigns for clients carries a heavy weight of responsibility. He tries to make every client their money back, and he absorbs the stress of clients who are stressing. He says martial arts and the gym could not clear that accumulated stress, and it left no room for creativity.
- He says he still loves Cyber, which he has tattooed on his arm, and that it changed his life. But he is no longer in love with it because of the stress of running campaigns for clients.
- He is considering moving into consulting and has some new ideas, but says he is "starting from scratch." He accepts that Cyber Leads could drop to almost zero and he would have to start over.

chunks.heading: Finding ideas and building products: luck is real, so launch many
chunks.text:
- Asked how to get started finding ideas and building products, Alex says luck is a real factor. You need to try many times.
- Product-market fit shows up as effort. Working on something without product-market fit "will feel like a drag... like you're fighting against nature." When it is the right idea, at the right time, with distribution channels you have, "it will feel effortless. It would just go by itself."
- He is prepared to fail 20 times. He says he is ready to build 20 products if needed to find another Cyber that changes his life.
- Past success does not guarantee more. He argues that having an audience and a track record does not make it easier, and says "not everything I touch turns to gold." He plans to publicly iterate through products to show that luck applies wherever you are in your trajectory.
- His advice: embrace the role of luck and launch many ideas.

chunks.heading: What Alex plans next
chunks.text:
- He wants to get back to creating: writing again, recording videos, and posting more. He says he enjoys making videos because it lets him meet many people. He picks people from the comments to have conversations with and invites DMs on Twitter.
- Goal: get back to the excitement of waking up eager to open his laptop and build something new, rather than dragging his feet.
- He plans to move into consulting and test new product ideas in public, with followers able to follow along as he iterates.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West explains how he is approaching his next business after Cyberleads without a fixed idea. He sets an open mind plus hard constraints: use the audience he already owns, mix his existing assets, and deliberately catch a new wave (AI employees and AI sales) instead of ignoring waves.

chunks.heading: Rebuilding after Cyberleads: start from what he already owns
chunks.text:
Alex's stated plan is directional, not precise. He says he does not know exactly what he will build, and he treats that as acceptable. He frames his game plan as a short list of constraints that keep an open mind from turning into a vacuum.

- Keep an open mind, be playful and creative, and run many experiments.
- Do not fall in love with any idea or business. He says doing so "wasted years of my life" and never worked out for him.
- Set limits anyway. He asks "am I going to build something for pet stores? Or like the newsletter industry?" and concludes there must be a line.
- He prefers working from concrete ingredients: "I don't like thinking in a vacuum. I cannot even write in a vacuum. You need something to play with."

chunks.heading: Don't assume you have the Midas touch
chunks.text:
Alex describes a mistake from after he first made money with Cyberleads. He thought he suddenly had "Midas touch" and tried two or three other products back to back. The open market "slapped" him and humbled him.

- His correction was to refocus on Cyberleads, show it "the love it deserves," and grow it, which he did.
- He now says he is not confident in his ability to predict what will work. He does not want to "pretend that I am smarter than I am."
- Because of this, he plans to experiment broadly rather than bet everything on one prediction.

chunks.heading: Reuse the audience and channel instead of starting from zero
chunks.text:
After eight years, Alex says building a marketing channel was the hardest thing to do, measured by output rather than input.

- He tried SEO, cold email, Reddit, LinkedIn and YouTube. He wanted ten diversified channels.
- SEO and cold email did work for him, "but not like this." He never built a second channel like his X account.
- He sees room to grow on X, since he is "still a small account."
- His focus is therefore the audience he already has. He calls starting from absolute zero (no customers, credibility, users or revenue) "the dark ages" and "the hardest part by far." He would not switch places with someone there.

chunks.heading: Mix existing assets into new product ideas
chunks.text:
Alex does not plan to abandon Cyberleads. It stays alive "in zombie mode," and he will use it to spin off new products. He walked through what "new" could mean:

- **New feature for Cyberleads:** tried, found nothing, though he admits he may have missed an opportunity.
- **New offer:** he tried several for Cyberleads and found nothing. His earlier hit came from discovering a product-as-a-service offer that took off.
- **New product for the same audience:** the one he finds interesting.

His ingredients for mixing and matching:

- A thousand-plus past paying customers who hopefully trust him.
- A free newsletter with about 5,000 agencies on the free plan.
- Cold email skills, which he used for many companies as his job.
- A database of 50,000 funded startups he can reach out to.
- His X account.

He says constraints plus ingredients beat brainstorming in a vacuum.

chunks.heading: Catch a wave, and don't ignore them
chunks.text:
Alex describes a belief he held for about five years: that he was not like people "chasing all these waves left and right," and that he was building something lasting instead. On reflection he calls that wrong.

- He was riding waves all along: building a business on the internet, building in public, solopreneurship, hiring remotely and automating with code. Back then these were taboo or extreme.
- He cites "The future is already here. It is just unevenly distributed."
- He recalls telling his parents around 2015 to 2017 that he would build a remote business, hire people he had never met and live in hotels with only Wi-Fi, since his customers were in America. They did not understand it. Now it is mainstream and he says he has "lost my edge completely."
- While running Cyberleads he ignored the NFT, crypto and AI waves, and they did not hurt him. He drew the wrong lesson: ignore everything and stay fixed on one product. Other waves later "crushed" him (he says this is covered in book 13).
- He adds that not every wave is worth catching.

chunks.heading: The wave he picked: AI employees and AI sales
chunks.text:
- The target is AI, specifically AI employees and AI sales. Sales fits because it sits near his Cyberleads universe.
