- He says it is an assumption and could be wrong, but it seems "pretty obvious" the market is heading toward AI employees. He admits he does not know what that means in detail: "I know as much as you."
- His plan is to build "10 20 products within that category" rather than one.
- He frames the whole strategy as possibly wrong, but wants to get ahead of the curve again.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West explains his repeatable process for launching a solo business idea: treat each launch as a learning experiment, keep scale relative, make every MVP simpler than the last but able to charge money, and then launch in one day via warm outbound, cold outbound and one-to-many channels like Reddit, Product Hunt and social.

chunks.heading: Launching to learn, not to get rich
chunks.text:
- Alex tells people to change the philosophy around launching: "you're not launching your idea to become a millionaire in 30 days or 90 days or whatever, you're launching to learn."
- He says you learn through "scars", not videos: close YouTube, build something, make mistakes.
- He treats scale as relative and dynamic. At zero users, success is getting one user. At one, it is ten. At ten customers, it is 20, then 30, 50, 100, 200.
- He argues against the master plan of "0 to 1,000 paying customers in 30 days", saying it "never works like that" and only about one launch in a million does.
- He ran about 20 products over two years, mostly "stupid little products" without real traction. The product that changed his life was built, launched and validated within two weeks, because earlier launches had taught him what to skip.

chunks.heading: Every launch should strip away something unnecessary
chunks.text:
- Alex holds that "knowledge is subtractive, not additive" and "progress is removing things". Every launch should be simpler than the previous one, otherwise "you're doing something wrong".
- What he learned from successive launches:
  - Launch 1: the logo doesn't matter. He spent a whole day designing it.
  - Launch 2: the perfect .com domain doesn't matter. He still got zero users despite a great domain.
  - Launch 3: pixel-perfect buttons and gradients don't matter.
- He applies the same logic to a running business: he often removes automations, product offerings or features he spent a long time on, and counts that as progress.
- His simplest product ended up being his most successful.

chunks.heading: Validate with a landing page before writing code
chunks.text:
- Alex once spent months coding a Stripe-for-crypto product, launched it, and got zero customers. He says he could have validated it with a landing page and a "get started" or "pay now" button, with nothing on the back end.
- He launched Cyber Leads, which started as a newsletter of companies that had just raised millions in funding (so they have money to pay for outsourcing), with only a landing page and a buy-now button.
- If someone bought, then on the 1st of the next month they received a list of every company that had just raised money and was looking to outsource.

chunks.heading: The MVP must be able to charge money
chunks.text:
- Alex says you can launch with just a landing page, but "you should be able to ask for money".
- His reasoning: an MVP that can't make money isn't viable. "It's not viable minimum viable product if it doesn't make money."
- The rule: make the MVP as simple as possible, yet able to charge, then launch.
- He says validation doesn't take long, but "it's simple but it's not easy".

chunks.heading: One-to-one launch tactics (warm and cold outbound)
chunks.text:
- Alex blocks a single day as launch day and keeps the process "simple, sweet, fast" because the goal is to learn fast.
- Warm outbound: DM, text or call friends who might be interested. Instead of asking "do you want to pay me?", you can ask "do you know anyone who might be interested?". They may pay themselves or refer someone.
- Cold outbound:
  - Email people who might be interested.
  - Email journalists if the product is fun enough to cover.
  - Email bloggers with a relevant post (for example a "top 10 whatever" list) and "shoot your shot".
- Example: a blog ranked for the perfect keyword for one of his small projects. He emailed the owner, who agreed it was relevant and added it. The post brought him customers "for years".

chunks.heading: One-to-many launch channels
chunks.text:
- Alex describes these as the big shots. If one works, "the others are going to be a margin of error".
- Reddit:
  - Every niche has a relevant subreddit (even pet food has a massive one).
  - It is difficult: he usually gets banned and rarely gets love from it, but a hit there is massive.
- Product Hunt:
  - Mostly suited to tech products.
  - Quite easy to pull off even without an audience.
  - He suggests launching on weekends for less competition.
- Twitter and LinkedIn:
  - Post a story, not just "here's what I built".
  - Explain why you built it, how long it took, that it's your third project and the first two failed.
  - "Make it interesting, make it relatable, make it human."
- Facebook groups: similar to Reddit and tricky. He says he has never really cracked them.
- Then launch everywhere at once and see whether you get traffic and convert it into money. If you do, the idea is validated.

chunks.heading: After validating: focus on one product
chunks.text:
- Alex's advice is to launch as many products as you can until one works, then focus entirely on that one.
- Once focused, he uses what he calls "shiny object syndrome" to find new distribution channels for that product and grow it.
- He says he covers one versus multiple businesses for solopreneurs in another video.
- He admits most viewers won't follow the advice to be scrappy, because "you have to learn by doing".
- He describes his main business as making about half a million per year, which he calls "good enough".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West explains how he went from about $200/month to roughly $500K/year by changing which ideas he picked, not how hard he worked. He argues against passion projects, uniqueness and B2C, and for entering proven markets, selling to businesses, and starting from an audience channel you already have.

chunks.heading: Ideas are underrated: finding a better idea beats executing 10x better
chunks.text:
- Alex says most people think ideas mean nothing, and he agrees only if you can't execute. His point: "it's a lot easier to find a 10 times better idea than it is to become 10 times better at executing any idea."
- His own proof: five years before this video (2024) he had the same work ethic and skills and was stuck at about $200/month. At the time of recording he was making about half a million per year.
- He says the main difference is working on the right thing, "a good idea."
- His process for finding ideas: drop romance about passion, stop needing uniqueness, enter proven markets, sell B2B, and work from channel to market to idea.

chunks.heading: Don't build your business around your passion
chunks.text:
- Alex used to want his business to be his "ultimate passion" and a natural extension of his personality. He now sees that as a product of designing his lifestyle "from a place of extreme comfort" as a university student with no stress.
- Passions tend to be poor business ideas. They often revolve around sports or B2C, which he calls a red flag.
- Passion can also scramble your incentives. His example was Epilepsy Blocker, a tool that helps people with photosensitive epilepsy browse the web safely (listed on his blog and Product Hunt).
  - He charged $5/month, but users often lived on benefits and had other disabilities, so he usually gave it away free.
  - One morning he read breaking news that a new therapy could potentially cure epilepsy. His first reaction was "why now, now that I'm building this business," and he caught himself.
- His takeaway: you can mix up your incentives so much that "you don't even recognize yourself," or even hate what you once loved. His advice is to be more coldblooded and stop trying to make the business your passion.

chunks.heading: Your idea doesn't need to be unique: look for a market where several people already make money
chunks.text:
- Alex used to treat ideas like dibs and would drop one if it was "taken." That changed when he started a full-time job and shifted his priorities.
- His rule: if you search online and nobody else is doing your idea, that is a red flag, not a good sign.
- What he wants to see is multiple people (not just one) doing the thing and making money from it. He calls that a healthy market.
- Uniqueness comes later. When he entered lead generation (about four years before the video, when it was less saturated), he was not unique. His business became unique through accumulated choices:
  - He delivered leads as a newsletter rather than a database, a twist, though he wasn't the only or first one.
  - He focused specifically on agencies.
  - He added a product and a service on top.
  - He built it on his personal brand and a personal touch, including sending presents to every customer.
- His conclusion: "I entered the market and slowly it moved into something different." About two years after entering a healthy market without trying to be unique, he had a very unique business.

chunks.heading: Don't be afraid of competition, especially big companies
chunks.text:
- Alex used to be terrified of competition, which he attributes to competing in Muay Thai and kickboxing, where one person always loses.
- He argues business has no winner and loser because winning is subjective. Example: if he makes $1M/year and someone in his market makes $10M with the same business, he isn't losing, because he doesn't want more and may be more content.
- On big companies: he used to think a 50-person company meant competing against 50 people like him. After briefly working at one, he concluded you are "really competing against five people and 45 yes men" who move slowly to avoid being fired.
  - Tasks bounce from to-do to doing to blocked to another department, and "we used to have five meetings to change the color of a button."
- He has many copycats. He isn't afraid of a big company trying to compete with him; he fears "a small five person company where they're coding all day and they're crazy motivated."

chunks.heading: Go B2B: businesses pay far more than consumers
chunks.text:
- With Epilepsy Blocker he chased people for $5/month subscriptions, they asked for discounts, and he often gave it away free. He notes that reaching $5K/month would need about 1,000 concurrent paying subscribers.
- On the flip side, "you can charge 5K per month to a single business."
- A personal example: when he started taking his lead generation business (Cyber Leads) seriously, at about $300/month, he paid roughly $25/month for something for the business and realized he'd never do that for himself. He had even unsubscribed from BetterHelp at $200/month because he wasn't using it weekly, while business subscriptions run without a second thought "cuz it's a business expense."
- The mindset difference: the same CEO who won't pay $1 to download an app as a consumer will spend $10K/month on something as a business owner.
- Exceptions where B2C works, as far as he knows: education, self-improvement, and AI. He also wonders about healthcare but says it's hard to break into as an online business person.

chunks.heading: Work from channel to market to idea, not idea to market to channel
chunks.text:
- Alex's old approach was idea, then find the market, then find the channel to reach it. He says it never worked for him, and top-down approaches are easy to mess up because of stacked assumptions.
- His rough illustration: with a generous 50% chance of being right at each step, idea times market times channel gives about 12% (and he thinks the real number is nearer 5%). He built 20 products to find the one that changed his life.
- Cyber Leads went in the reverse order: channel, market, idea.
  - Channel: a Twitter account with about 600 followers at the time.
  - Market: tech and business people, who are on Twitter.
  - Idea: then ask what those people want and find a healthy market you can reach through the channel you already have.

chunks.heading: Build a channel and personal brand, then stop thinking and build
chunks.text:
- If you don't have a channel yet, Alex says to invest in one because it "is going to pay dividends." He admits he is biased but says building a personal brand is "never the wrong advice."
- It can be LinkedIn, Twitter, a big blog with SEO as the acquisition channel, or TikTok. Learn one channel really well and ideally build a personal brand on it, then use it to market your products. He says that is what he did and what he would advise someone he loves.
- A challenge to skeptics: "If the cost for you to make a million per year is to tweet once a day would you take it or not?" He can't guarantee it but says it's a good investment.
- Once you have an idea, stop analyzing: with a roughly 5% chance of being right, "don't lose time, go go go. Start building." He says all the thinking is pontificating, and the next video covers launching and validating the idea.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West maps the biggest barrier at each stage of a solo business: first dollar, hundreds to thousands, thousands to tens of thousands, and scaling toward $1M/year. Each stage has a different failure mode: impatience and fear, product obsession over distribution, refusing to delegate, then needing volume.

chunks.heading: Why most solopreneurs fail, and the four phases from $0 to $1M/year
chunks.text: Alex (2018 solopreneur and indie hacker, building products since roughly 2016) frames this as his own opinion from experience. He splits the path into four phases, each with a different barrier. At the time of the video he was at about $43K in a month, with a goal of $83K per month (the $1M/year mark).

chunks.heading: Phase 1 ($0 to first dollar): not enough time
chunks.text:
- First-dollar online is the biggest entrepreneurial filter.
- Alex says "you cannot expect to change your life in 6 months", it takes years.
- When he started, many people were more talented than him, got instant traction and went mini viral. He was building and nothing took off: no likes, no followers.
- Nine out of ten of those faster starters have since quit. He no longer sees them.
- His point: persistence over years beats early talent or early luck.

chunks.heading: Phase 1: bad ideas and bad markets
chunks.text:
- His early ideas were social-network style ideas (for example an app to decide with friends where to go for a drink), because he was a university student and his life was social. They may be good ideas in general but they are not good business ideas.
- His definition of a good market:
  - Not winner-takes-all; multiple players win at once.
  - Those players make the amount of money you aspire to make.
  - You can use acquisition and distribution channels you already have (for example a Twitter account), and you know the ropes of that market.
- Bad ideas are unavoidable early: you have to build many products and watch some get no payment before you improve.
- On ideas: they are "everything and nothing at the same time". Nothing without execution, but he cites the Indie Hackers quote (he attributes it to Courtland) that it is very hard to execute 10x better yet easy to pick a 10x better idea.

chunks.heading: Phase 1: fear of exposure and fear of charging
chunks.text:
- Fear of failing in public: people hold back because others might see them fail. In reality "no one cares", and even the people who quit are not remembered by anyone, which he calls liberating.
- Fear of charging: it is an identity issue. People who are not businesspeople, or do not spend money themselves, assume nobody will pay.
- His moment of realization: when Cyber Leads began growing, he typed his credit card number into a new software tool for his business. He would not have paid even $10/month for his own mental health, yet paid readily for business. Conclusion: B2B is not that hard to get people to pay, because business owners pay easily.
- His pricing comfort moves up with revenue: charging $500/month felt hard before and does not now, and he expects $10K/month to feel normal in some cases later.

chunks.heading: Phase 2 (hundreds to thousands per month): focus on distribution, not product
chunks.text:
- Going from the hundreds to the thousands per month is the most life-changing leap, since it can let you make a living doing what you love.
- Common failure: with a product making roughly $200 to $500/month, people try to improve the product when they actually need more customers. If people already pay, it is probably good enough.
- His rule: spend about 90% of time on distribution and only maintain the core product.
- Keep the product as simple as possible and be proud of it, especially in a world of bloated products. Cyber Leads is "still the same damn product", simple.
- Second failure: launching new products when stuck. People end up with a portfolio of products each making $200 to $500/month, none life-changing, and collectively not enough to quit a job.
- His alternative: do not shy away from shiny object syndrome, but funnel that energy into building distribution instead of new products or features. (He covers this in more depth in his video on one versus multiple products for solopreneurs.)
- The shift: from artist to athlete.
  - Early on, you think out of the box, come up with ideas, ship an MVP.
  - At this stage, do the same thing every day, double down on marketing, focus on one product, and "be a little bit more boring".
- Reference point: at about $4K/month he was living his dream after quitting his job, and he says he would be about 80% as happy as now if still at that level.

chunks.heading: Phase 3 (thousands to tens of thousands): learn to delegate and re-explore
chunks.text:
- Barrier one: wanting to stay solo forever. He hated every boss he had, so becoming someone's boss was hard. His reflection: you either die a hero or live long enough to become the villain.
- His setup: three virtual assistants working online, paid full-time, working about two hours a day on average. No meetings except one weekly team meeting. He sees them as people he works with, not employees.
- Delegation matters because going from thousands to tens of thousands often takes volume one person cannot handle alone.
- Barrier two: you often have to go back to square one, reconsider everything with an open mind, and use shiny object syndrome to find the next growth lever.
- His lever at each level:
  - $0 to $1: exposing himself and not being afraid to fail in public.
  - Hundreds to thousands: focusing on distribution, picking one channel, going B2B instead of building a unique product. He found Cyber Leads' channel on Twitter.
  - Thousands to tens of thousands: experimenting about 20 times with Cyber Leads and new offerings, then adding a done-for-you service on top of the newsletter, followed by building a team.

chunks.heading: Phase 4 (tens of thousands toward $1M/year): volume again, via the midwit meme
chunks.text:
- At about $43K last month, he thinks the barrier now is sheer volume, after dropping everything else and focusing on one thing: "the 80/20 of the 80/20 of the 80/20", then "pouring gasoline on the fire".
- He uses the midwit (bell curve) meme to explain the stages:
  - Very early stage: volume. Launch multiple products and get in front of many people.
  - Middle stage: direction. Test several things, complicate your life a bit, and find where to point your vehicle.
  - Later stage: volume again.
- Example of too little volume: his best friend built a product for three months, posted on Reddit twice, got about 25 comments, DM'd five people and concluded no one wanted it. Total reach was about 45 people, and he expected 10 customers from that.
- Alex's comparison: across Twitter, LinkedIn, SEO and cold email he reaches roughly a million impressions a month and has fewer than 100 customers. So he says early stages need far more volume than most people try.
- He says he does not know how to get to $1M/month or $10M/month, but up to $1M/year he believes this is the roadmap.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West explains why he quit his job after Cyberleads out-earned his salary for six months, and distills a decision framework. Quit when results are consistent, you've stopped learning, you have 2+ years of runway, and the downside is capped while the upside is life-changing.

chunks.heading: Quit when the results are consistent and the downside is capped
chunks.text:
Alex quit his job at the end of 2020 (he handed in notice in December and was fired anyway). He had been building products since 2015, posted online daily since 2020 and tweeted since 2018. He frames himself as an average person with no special luck, and says these were his reasons, not the "correct" reasons for everyone.

- **Revenue beat his salary six months in a row.** CyberLeads, a newsletter of companies that just raised funding and are likely to outsource, launched on 14 Feb 2020. By quitting time it had made more than his salary for 6 months straight, even though it was only about 10 months old.
- **Revenue was wild but trending up.** He got customers mostly from Twitter, so some weeks brought none and a viral week brought 10-15. Monthly revenue swung like "1,000, then 500, then 2,000, then 1.5, then 4,000, then 2.5", but "up and to the right if you zoom out". His point: consistent growth matters more than smoothness.
- **Social media is a wild beast.** "You cannot put a saddle on a wild beast." Embrace its unpredictable viral nature instead of trying to change it.
- **The tipping point was the day his revenue passed his salary.** He posted it on Twitter, it went viral, and a commenter said he would "never be able to go back now". After that he showed up at work with more confidence and a limited-days mindset.

chunks.heading: Stack the odds: save a runway and keep the job until the bet is asymmetric
chunks.text:
Alex did not quit the moment revenue crossed his salary. He rated the risk first and then reduced it.

- He kept the job to honor his contract and to keep saving.
- He set aside 50k, which was about 2 years of runway at roughly 2K/month of personal spending.
- His worst-case reasoning: if CyberLeads dropped to zero, he had 2 years to figure things out. If he still failed, he could "always just find another job and try again" and would at least have a story and have traveled.
- Best case: "If things go well I'm free for life."
- He says the exact savings number would not have changed his decision (50k vs 60k), since the business was already growing and paying his living costs. Today the same 50k would be about one year of runway because he spends more (roughly 10-20% of income).
- He admits no amount of reasoning predicts the future: "sometimes you just have to say [expletive] it and go for it". The time is never perfectly right.

chunks.heading: Take asymmetric risks, be conservative with ruinous ones
chunks.text:
Alex draws on Nassim Taleb (he has a Black Swan tattoo) for how he sorts risk.

- **Be very careful with risks that can ruin you** if they go wrong: gambling, fighting, unprotected sex with a sex worker.
- **Be wild and playful with risks where the downside is small and the upside is large:** starting a business with zero capital, building in the open on Twitter, going to a party, moving abroad for a year.
- His own track record: he built about 20 products and one worked. Inside CyberLeads he ran about 20 experiments, most failed, one took it to the next level. He did not spend 20-40K to validate an experiment; experiments stayed cheap and playful.
- His view: take enough of these asymmetric risks and you "will be blessed with luck". The skill is checking whether each risk is asymmetric in your favor or against you. Quitting the job felt unclear until he built the runway.

chunks.heading: Warning signs the job is holding you back
chunks.text:
These were the "push" reasons in his decision.

- **You stopped learning technically.** At his engineering job he mostly built dashboards, and the only lasting lessons were business ones. He realized he loved creating, not coding. CyberLeads v1 was built with no-code tools because he was sick of programming after 8 hours a day.
- **You are an entrepreneur, not a specialist.** He found scalability meetings, legacy code and Kubernetes clusters boring, and only enjoyed competition, product direction and funding talk. His analogy: some people are like Formula 1 engineers optimizing one car component; he likes high-level business.
- **Splitting energy makes you average at both.** After 2 hours of real work on his own business before the office, his brain was fried. He was a very average employee, and when he focused on the day job, CyberLeads suffered. "Very difficult for me to do great work at both at the same time."
- **Your manager's picture of your future is small.** His manager asked where he wanted to go and proposed being "the dedicated go-to guy" for the internal dashboard. He nearly laughed, and says he would have cried without CyberLeads.
- **A big change can beat small improvements.** If you feel stuck, do the opposite of what you are doing: change city, move abroad, "burn the ships". He had moved from Greece to Italy for the job a year earlier. Small habits matter, but sometimes you need an "earthquake that shakes your foundations".

chunks.heading: What the job taught him (business lessons that transferred)
chunks.text:
- **Companies are not scary to compete with.** A 50-person company is really about 5 people and 45 "yes men" who drag tasks from todo to doing to blocked, hold meetings about them and change requirements. He says he was like that too, because pushing the company forward was not his job.
- **Change your own world first.** He worked on life-saving medical devices, a dream job for someone who wanted to change the world. He flipped that: go boring, go B2B, build something useful people pay for, make money, give to charity, and have impact that way. He is open that he wants to be rich rather than a starving artist.
- **Constraints reveal what matters.** Working two hours before his day job taught him that 80-90% of his useful work happens in the first two hours of the day, and he still works this way. When he was a student with the whole day free, he scrolled Twitter and the news, went to the gym, and got almost nothing done.

chunks.heading: Quit for clarity of mind, not for more hours
chunks.text:
- His main reason for leaving was a clear head: no meetings, deadlines or worrying about his manager's view of his performance. It was not to work 10 hours a day on CyberLeads, and he says he didn't. He worked briefly all day in 2022, but was fairly relaxed when he quit in 2021.
- For software businesses he says about 2 hours a day is enough. "Taking a simple correct decision and scaling it is far more important than the number of hours you put in." A calm clear mind outperforms a team "running around like a headless chicken".
- Caveat: service or agency-style "hustle" businesses need more time. CyberLeads was a newsletter plus a done-for-you service on top, and the service side takes more hours.

chunks.heading: Downsides of his model he accepted
chunks.text:
- **Copycats copied his product word for word,** including his founder story, because he published his numbers, strategies and lessons in his daily blog. He treats this as part of the cost of building in public and cannot do anything about it.
- **The market has high churn.** Lead generation is easy to sell at a high price but people leave quickly, which makes revenue volatile.
- **Revenue and growth were not smooth,** but the consistent upward trend was what counted for his decision.

chunks.heading: His recap: when to quit
chunks.text:
- You have consistent results (income above your salary for months).
- You are not learning anything from your day job.
- You have enough runway if things go badly.
- The worst case is not dangerous and the best case changes your life.
- You are ready for a big change and want to feel alive again.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West ranks distribution channels A to F from a decade of trying them. He recommends launching and warm outbound first, then cold outbound and social, then long-term assets like email, YouTube and podcasts. He says channels compound together, and distribution now matters more than product.

chunks.heading: Alex's channel framework: inbound, outbound, and the extras
chunks.text:
- Alex argues distribution matters more than product: "you can have the best product in the world if no one knows about it it doesn't matter." A mediocre product with strong distribution can get rich and improve over time.
- No major new channel has appeared since TikTok (2016), and competition keeps rising, so distribution gets more important every year.
- He simplifies channels into inbound, outbound and ads, plus a few extras (launches, marketplaces, affiliates, going viral).
- His basis: close to 10 years of experience, posting daily online since 2020, and tweeting since 2018.
- He urges people to test channels themselves because "anything can work and everything has worked for other people."
- He recommends the book *Traction* (co-written by the DuckDuckGo co-founder), which covers 19 channels and how to test them. There are two books called Traction, so check the author.

chunks.heading: Inbound channels: social, SEO, email list, word of mouth
chunks.text:
- **Social is underrated, and the platform depends on your customer.** B2C leans Instagram and TikTok (easy to grow, convert badly). B2B leans Twitter and LinkedIn (harder to grow, convert far better).
  - His brother grew a TikTok account to 60k followers in 3 months and could not make a single dollar from it.
  - Alex's business is built on a roughly 30,000 follower Twitter account, with many millionaires and even billionaires following him. It took two years of consistent tweeting to reach 1,000 followers.
- **Audience first, product later.** He says the channel is the most important part of the business and that many people should start with a channel: "if you build up a Twitter audience trust me you can find a product." The same goes for YouTube and podcasts, which are harder to grow but convert even better.
- **Podcast mentions can be huge.** *My First Million* mentioned his business Cyber Leads twice, once in a 5-minute segment and once in an episode on million-dollar solo businesses. He estimates they brought in around a quarter of a million dollars in revenue, counting churn, and says that shows the distribution a big show has.
- **SEO** is, in his experience, very hard to grow, slow, and low converting. He has never made it work despite many attempts, and says it should not be your first channel. Blog content lasts 2-3 years versus 2-3 days for a tweet, but the slowness balances that out.
- **Email list** is hard to grow but converts very well.
  - His free Cyber Leads newsletter has about 3,500 subscribers (at recording) against roughly 35,000 Twitter followers. He says that is 10x fewer people but roughly equal power, maybe more, especially for B2B.
  - When he needs clients, he emails the list a short offer, for example 20% off for 3 days because he wants to take on a new client, and can get two or three clients whenever he wants.
- **Word of mouth** is his number one channel now, but he doesn't take credit for it. It is outside your control beyond providing the best service and building the best product you can.

chunks.heading: Outbound channels: warm and cold
chunks.text:
- **Warm outbound** means messaging friends, family, past clients, past prospects, newsletter subscribers, Twitter followers, and anyone who already knows you. Conversion is high but reach is small (about 100 people), which makes it a great way to start.
- **Cold outbound** covers cold email, cold calling, cold DMs, and sending letters and gifts.
  - Email is the 80/20 of cold outbound: the easiest and it works pretty well.
  - He has never gotten results from cold calling.
  - Cold outbound takes more time than warm outbound but less than building social or other inbound channels.
- **Recommended sequence:** start with warm outbound, add cold outbound, and build social, SEO and the rest in parallel. Start outbound and build inbound at the same time.
- **Cold email works best when selling something expensive.** At a $50/month SaaS price he doesn't think it fits. It scales linearly rather than fast.
  - Counterexample: ConvertKit grew from about $2k MRR to $200k MRR with cold email, but its founder was already well known on Twitter, so the brand amplified the emails.
  - Without a brand it is hard to stand out in cold email.

chunks.heading: Launches, marketplaces, affiliates and going viral
chunks.text:
- **Launches** are an underused strategy. Alex got his first 10 Cyber Leads customers by launching on Product Hunt, plus Twitter and Reddit.
  - You can realistically launch only every 6-12 months, but it gives momentum and validation.
  - His point is that the scariest thing is growing something you aren't sure can work. Early customers give you the confidence to commit to building a channel.
- **Marketplaces** (GitHub, Figma, Slack, the OpenAI GPT marketplace) are a hack for acquisition when you have no audience. "It's like casting your little net on a river full of fish." The risks are competition and long-term platform dependence, so he wouldn't rely on a single platform after four years in business.
- **Affiliates:** he never made them worth it. Paying affiliates was a pain, and he killed the program twice. The one useful result was learning from ads that an affiliate ran.
- **Going viral** is very hard to pull off. His examples:
  - Harry Dry's Kanye West dating site where Taylor Swift fans were banned.
  - Peter Levels' billboard saying you don't need to go back to the office, promoting remoteok.io.
- **Ads:** he skips them because they are capital intensive. He prefers high-profit businesses with organic acquisition, and says he hasn't run ads successfully (or at all).

chunks.heading: Channels compound rather than compete
chunks.text:
- Alex stresses that channels are not mutually exclusive and feed each other.
- The loop: warm outbound gets your first customers, who give you testimonials and social proof, which build your brand and grow social, which brings more inbound.
- Cross-effects he sees:
  - People reply to his cold emails saying they know him from Twitter or *My First Million*.
  - Cold email brings people into his email list.
  - The email list becomes warm outbound.
  - Word of mouth keeps growing on top of all of it.
- Different channels peak at different times.

chunks.heading: Alex's tier list
chunks.text:
- **A tier:** YouTube and podcast (deep trust, parasocial relationship, influence at scale, the best way to build a brand), email list, and word of mouth.
- **B tier:** Twitter/LinkedIn (very short half-life, a treadmill of content), SEO (slow but long-lived), and launches.
- **C tier:** cold outbound (works quickly but doesn't scale fast, and only fits expensive offers) and marketplaces (amazing but carry platform risk).
- **D tier:** Instagram, TikTok and ads. They can work but are capital intensive or convert poorly. He sees Instagram and TikTok mainly as brand amplifiers for other channels ("I know you from TikTok").
- **F tier:** cold calling, sending presents, trying to go viral, and affiliates. He has never made these matter.

chunks.heading: Alex's own growth path and channel timeline
chunks.text:
- **First customers:** he reached about $400 MRR by launching on Product Hunt, Twitter and Reddit. That was about 10 customers at $29/month (about $290 MRR) plus roughly $100 from other products.
- **Hundreds to thousands per month:** Twitter growth took him from hundreds to thousands of dollars per month, which he calls the biggest gap, going from nothing to being able to live doing what he loves.
- **Stuck at about $4k/month,** and bored, he created a service offering priced at $2,000 per month rather than $200 (the transcript is ambiguous on the exact figure, so treat this as only a higher-priced offer). That made cold email efficient.
- **Reaching $40k/month:** cold email combined with Twitter, the email list, and word of mouth took him from $4,000 to $40,000 per month. His goal now is $1 million, and he thinks YouTube, podcasting and maybe SEO could help.
- **Timeline summary:**
  - Short term: launches, marketplaces, and warm outbound.
  - Mid term (around 3 months for cold outbound to work): cold outbound and social.
  - Long term: email list, word of mouth, SEO, YouTube and podcast, which scale highest.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West argues that for small businesses (up to ~$1M/year) in healthy markets, competition barely matters. Most customers don't know you exist, companies move slowly, true competition requires overlap on product, customer, positioning/price and channel, and copycats self-select out.

chunks.heading: Why competition is mostly irrelevant for small businesses
chunks.text:
Alex's claim is that solopreneurs and indie hackers should stop worrying about competition. He scopes it with two caveats:

- **Size:** he means small businesses, from about $1K/month up to roughly $100K/month, topping out around $500K to $1M per year. He says he has no idea how to build a billion-dollar company.
- **Healthy market:** it is not winner-take-all, and he sees many players making the amount he wants (many at $1K/month, many at $10K/month, many at $1M/year). He has a separate video on how to identify a healthy market.

Markets he found when he looked about four years ago: lead generation, cybersecurity, hiring and recruiting, and social media management, posting and automations.

If both caveats hold, he says competition shouldn't be on your mind.

chunks.heading: Your customers don't know your competitors, and probably not you
chunks.text:
- 99.9% of potential customers don't know you exist yet.
- He tells founders to check their analytics: a homepage may get around 1,000 to 10,000 visitors a month, which is "nothing" in a large market.
- Founders know every competitor; customers know none of them.
- His advice: instead of focusing on other people, spend the energy bringing more traffic to your own product.

chunks.heading: Companies are slow, so they are the least scary opposition
chunks.text:
- He used to think a 50-person company meant competing against 50 people like him.
- After working inside a company, he concluded you are competing against "45 yes men and five people that are actually doing work".
- Those five move slowly: tasks sit in to-do columns, get blocked, get passed to other departments, requirements change, and meetings multiply. Changing a button color can take five meetings.
- A solo founder can pivot 180 degrees in a day. His example: change a product's positioning in 5 minutes without getting dressed.
- Employees have their own lives and aspirations, and it isn't their company, so they don't care as much. He says he was one of them.
- He is more afraid of someone like himself competing against him than of a big company.

chunks.heading: The four-part test for whether two products really compete
chunks.text:
Alex defines competition as an overlap of four things. If any one differs, he says they aren't really competing:

1. **Product:** identical products alone aren't enough.
2. **Target customer:** the same SaaS sold to SaaS companies versus sold to agencies doesn't compete.
3. **Positioning and pricing:** the same product and customer can differ as a self-serve tool at $9/month versus a high-end, custom, onboarded, almost done-for-you offer at $999/month.
4. **Acquisition channel:** one competitor on Google and Facebook ads, another posting organically on Twitter and Reddit, are not competing.

His fishing metaphor: the market is a river. If someone fishes right next to you with the same bait and nets, tell them to go to the other side because there are plenty of fish. Fighting over the same spot is just "bashing heads", and it is rarely what actually happens.

chunks.heading: Your real competition is intangible
chunks.text:
- Most of the time you aren't competing with other companies.
- For his product Cyber Leads, he says he competes with prospects hiring a VA or doing the work themselves.
- Others are "boredom and Excel sheets".
- His conclusion: there are many ways to escape competition, and even when all four factors overlap, there is enough room for everyone.

chunks.heading: Copycats: the midwit meme
chunks.text:
Alex uses the midwit meme (a normal distribution with a dumb person on one end, a smart person on the other, and an overcomplicating average person in the middle) to sort the people who might copy you.

- **Low end:** these copycats appeared far more when he was at $1K to $4K MRR than now at $40K. They usually quit within about two months. They are too scared to copy a product making $40K/month once they see strong testimonials and his 40K Twitter followers. He says he gets almost no copycats now.
- **Middle:** these people overcomplicate things and want a unique angle, so copying is too simple for them. They usually don't copy.
- **High end:** copying is a smart strategy, and he might do it in his next business. These people tend to copy a much better business than yours.
- Even in the worst case where someone does copy you, the market is big enough for more players.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West compares building many products (shotgun) with focusing on one (sniper), using his own record: 20 products in two years before finding Cyber Leads. He argues for shotgun before product-market fit, sniper after, and a "fractal" loop that runs the shotgun on distribution channels whenever growth plateaus.

chunks.heading: Sniper vs shotgun: choosing by stage, and why Alex runs one product
chunks.text:
Alex frames the question as two strategies. The sniper strategy focuses on one product until it works. The shotgun strategy builds many products to find one that works. He refuses to give advice ("I hate giving advice") because anything can work for some people and fail for others. Citing the idea that "ask someone successful for advice and they'll give you their lottery numbers", he only shows what he did.

His background: he started in 2015, took things seriously in 2018, and has posted online since 2018 and daily since 2020. He calls himself a decent case study because he is neither super smart nor super lucky, and he spent almost 10 years getting to where he is.

chunks.heading: Shotgun strategy: build, launch, learn, repeat
chunks.text:
- **Pre-product-market fit:** Alex recommends shotgun for anyone without a product that can change their life or hit their income goal, especially if they have no paying users yet.
- **His run:** He started on 1 January 2018 as a New Year resolution. Within one year he went from never having a paying user to launching 8 products, 2 of which made money. That gave him his first dollar and first recurring revenue.
- **Total count:** Across 2018 and 2019 he built about 20 products. The 20th was Cyber Leads, found in early 2020, after roughly two years of building.
- **Why it works:** Each launch closes a feedback loop, so you reassess and go again. He says "we learn with our hands, getting burned by the fire", not with our intellect.
- **Lessons from specific launches:**
  - Launch 1: the domain he chased did not save him.
  - Launch 2: the perfectly polished button did not matter.
  - Launch 3: built in 2 weeks, deliberately scrappy, and it was his most successful launch.
- **Takeaway:** Knowledge is mostly subtractive, about what not to do: don't obsess over the name, design or backend. After 20 products he concluded all he needed was a landing page and a buy button. He knew this from day one but had to learn it empirically.

chunks.heading: Sniper strategy: too slow and too risky early on
chunks.text:
- **His attempts:** He tried it from 2015 to 2017, when he wanted to be the next Mark Zuckerberg and raise money. All he learned in two years was that he did not want to raise money or build something grandiose. He wants to bootstrap a small business and be "a humble little millionaire."
- **Second attempt:** In 2019 he fell in love with a medical-related product, made it his life mission, and lost another year. It made only about $50 MRR (he says "if I remember correctly").
- **Verdict:** Sniper is too slow and too risky for learning. He notes it depends on your goal, and his ambitions are low: change his own life, not the world.
- **Compare:** In the shotgun years he learned enough to write a book, and he did write a blog post on it on his site ("two years").

chunks.heading: When to switch: shotgun before PMF, sniper after
chunks.text:
- **Before product-market fit:** Use shotgun.
- **After finding the product:** Switch to sniper. When Alex kept shotgunning after launching Cyber Leads, he "spread himself thin and made less money" instead of growing it.
- **If you love building:** Focus on one product and express that side of yourself elsewhere. He says he has a solution for this, which leads into the fractal strategy below.

chunks.heading: The fractal strategy: shotgun inside the business to find distribution
chunks.text:
- **Pattern:** Shotgun to find a product, sniper to grow it. When you plateau, run a shotgun again, but this time inside the business to find new distribution channels instead of new products.
- **Shiny object syndrome:** Funnel that energy into distribution experiments. If a channel works, go sniper on it, then repeat at the next plateau.
- **His examples with Cyber Leads:**
  - Mid 2020: discovered Twitter, focused on it for about 1.5 years.
  - 2021: stuck at around $4K, so he shotgunned every distribution and marketing channel he could think of.
  - The next lever of growth was adding a productized service on top of the business. After that he went to half a million a year. His advice: be very open-minded and "follow the money", even though it is unromantic.
  - He says he is doing it again now, and that this video is one of those experiments.
- **Book:** He recommends *Traction* (co-written by the DuckDuckGo co-founder; he warns there is another business book with the same title). Its thesis is to spend 50% of time on marketing and 50% on product, because distribution matters more than product. It covers roughly 17-19 channels. The loop is: try all channels, focus on the one that works, grow, and rerun at the plateau.

chunks.heading: Pace and iterations: 20 tries per level, about every two years
chunks.text:
- **His anecdotal pattern (not a law):**
  - 20 products to find Cyber Leads.
  - 20 experiments within Cyber Leads to find the next lever of growth.
  - Another 20 iterations to remove himself from fulfillment.
  - Each level took about 2 years.
- **Pace varies:** Others can go faster or slower. What matters is to keep going, avoid burnout, and hold reasonable expectations.
- **Iterations over hours:** Paraphrasing Naval, it's "not the 10,000 hours that lead to mastery but the 10,000 iterations."
- **No sunk-cost entitlement:** "The universe doesn't owe you anything." Launching again and again does not mean you will hit. You must improve with every iteration. He admits he once felt something was bound to happen, which he calls a sunk cost fallacy.

chunks.heading: Is one product risky? Timeless or timely markets, and channels over products
chunks.text:
- **When one product is safe:** If the product is either timeless or timely.
  - Timeless: something that does not change with time. Cyber Leads has run for 4 years, nearly 5, and he expects it to last 5-20 more.
  - Timely: a market like generative AI. Go full speed, maybe exit.
  - The risky middle: not timeless, not timely, and dependent on a platform (for example a marketplace plugin that the marketplace later builds in as a core feature).
- **Why he thinks Cyber Leads is timeless:** People will always want to make more money; agencies (companies paid to get things done) will always exist; email is a very "Lindy" technology; and the VC-backed market will still exist. He admits he could be wrong.
- **His goal:** He needs only one home run and does not care about doing it again.
- **Genetics of a business:** You can't pick your parents, but you can pick your business's genetics. Good genetics let you focus on one product.

chunks.heading: Statistics: one product with three channels beats three products on one channel
chunks.text:
- **Thought experiment (from Nassim Taleb):** Compare three setups: (a) one product with three distribution channels, (b) three products on the same channel (e.g. all built on one Twitter personal brand, or all programmatic SEO), (c) three products with one different channel each. He argues (a) is best.
- **His own case:** After Elon bought Twitter, Alex worried because about 80% of his customers had come from Twitter. Word of mouth is now his number two source, but he excludes it because he can't control it. His three solid channels are Twitter, LinkedIn and cold email, plus a tiny bit of SEO he doesn't count.
- **Illustrative numbers:** Assume a 10% chance each of Twitter, LinkedIn and cold email failing within 5 years. The chance all three fail is multiplicative, about 0.1%. He sees this as safe enough because a bootstrapped business with about 90% margins, low overhead and cash in the bank only needs one channel to survive ("like cockroaches").
- **Why not three products on one channel:** If that single channel dies, all three businesses die, and you've spread yourself thin for the same safety. This is his stated reason for running one product, not several.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West shares weekly notes from running a ~$500K/yr, 90%-profit cold email business. He covers raising prices without losing conversions, why trust is the key lever in high-priced sales, a 10x-price thought experiment for improving a service, and keeping a boring business alongside an exciting life.

chunks.heading: Pricing only works when trust and service quality back it up
chunks.text:
Alex raised his lead-generation service (Cyber Leads) from $2K to $3K per month and saw no drop in conversions. His business sends cold emails and tracks the results, at about $500K per year with roughly 90% profit. On pricing, he says:

- He has "raised my prices from 29 per month to three thousand", a 100x increase, mostly by adding service as he went.
- He is all for raising prices, but not "just because I can". He wants to improve the service first so he "feels good" about the price he charges.
- Bro advice says "you went too low" if nobody objects. He doesn't chase that; the price has to feel justified by the quality of the service, the conversations clients can have and the deals they can close.

chunks.heading: The "10x your price" thought experiment
chunks.text:
Alex uses a question borrowed from Airbnb's founder (he is unsure of the name; the "seven star hotel experience" idea): what would a seven-star experience look like?

- His version: "What would my service look like if it cost 10 times more?" For him, that means picturing Cyber Leads at $30K per month.
- Step 1: write down everything that premium service would include.
- Step 2: ask why you don't already do those things.
- Step 3: either improve the service, raise the price, or both.

chunks.heading: Selling at $3K/month to a cold prospect is mostly about trust
chunks.text:
He took his first sales call for a $3K/month deal with a prospect who found him only through Google. They had not seen his Twitter, blog or podcast interviews.

- He realized he is "spoiled": most callers already know him, so there is a "parasocial relationship" doing the selling.
- The cold prospect raised many objections: "why should we trust you", "how are you different to everyone else", "what can you guarantee us", "how do we know this actually works and you're not going to run off with the money".
- His conclusion: when you charge a lot, trust is "the ultimate leverage point". He applies the same rule when hiring: he cares less whether his VA is the smartest person and more about whether he can trust them and whether they are competent.
- Building an audience beforehand is a major advantage in high-ticket sales.

chunks.heading: Marketing results lag, so keep working in good times
chunks.text:
- There is a lag between marketing effort and customers. Funnels make people think of a clean path, but he sees consistent marketing over months or years producing results.
- A month where he is "killing it" is usually the result of hard work from earlier, stressful months.
- When things are smooth and he works less, that sets up the next downturn. Other causes include breaking changes, a new competitor, surgery or lost motivation.
- His rule: "aim for peace, but be prepared for war". Every business has problems ("there's [expletive] in every garden"), and peers he admires go through the same.
- At the time of recording, he had done little marketing lately because he was sorting out back-end work. Revenue was still around $500K per year, and his goal was $1M per year within about three months.

chunks.heading: Treat a boring business like a science
chunks.text:
- He calls his business "very boring": "I'm sending emails". But he treats sending cold emails, analyzing responses, tracking metrics and helping clients close multi-million dollar deals "as if I am building rocket ships".
- Benefits: it makes the work more enjoyable, and treating it with respect makes you a pro who can see the underlying science.
- Applies even to something dull that you have done daily for five years.

chunks.heading: Guarding against shiny object syndrome and the "new rat race"
chunks.text:
- He is naturally good at focusing on one thing but still gets shiny object syndrome, usually because he wants something to be excited about (crypto, AI and so on).
- His reminder: the goal of the business is "not to be fancy, it's just to make money".
- Current motto: "boring business, exciting life". Do something boring, make money, and set goals for your personal life rather than only business goals.
- He doesn't want to be one-dimensional, "just a business guy" with five businesses.
- He swings between wanting to build businesses into his 80s and wanting to get off the grid. He warns that escaping the 9-to-5 can turn into a "new rat race" of building a business and chasing millionaire status, and that goals like $1M per year can be arbitrary when you already have enough money.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: After hiring an agency to see the other side, Alex lists four intangibles for service businesses: lead the client, show constant progress, be friendly and transparent, and design a fail-safe so lukewarm clients still leave happy. He also notes follow-ups only pay off for warm leads, not cold ones.

chunks.heading: Hiring an agency on purpose to learn the client side
chunks.text: Alex, who runs a roughly $500k/year agency business and is aiming for $1M/year while traveling and working 2-4 hours a day, hired an agency deliberately to see his own industry from the buyer's seat. He had run an agency but never hired one. The experience produced a list of "intangibles" for running a service business, beyond the obvious need for leads and fulfillment. He kept notes daily and published them in a daily blog.

chunks.heading: Alex's four service business fundamentals
chunks.text:
He lists these as the top intangibles after being a client himself:

1. Be proactive and push your client as if you were their boss.
2. Show progress and update them constantly.
3. Be friendly and transparent.
4. Have a strong fail-safe strategy.

chunks.heading: Lead the client: "you are their boss"
chunks.text:
- Alex hired a video editor (short-form clips for social media). The premise of a done-for-you service is that it takes work off the client's plate, and "the last thing I want is extra work to do."
- He was sometimes late on deliverables. What helped was the editor following up and keeping him accountable.
- His old belief was that the person who hires you is your boss. He now says the reverse: clients come for your expertise, so you tell them what to do.
- He implemented this with his own clients and reports "amazing results"; they appreciate it.
- Most founders are busy, so chasing them for inputs and deadlines is part of the service.

chunks.heading: Communicate progress constantly, even when results are small
chunks.text:
- Alex's view: "there is no such thing as over communicating" in a service business.
- Update clients even when results haven't arrived. Example updates: "we sent 50 emails, got no replies, but I tweaked this and that," or "we got two subscribers last week, this week three" (a 50% increase that is really one subscriber).
- Visible progress is enough for many clients.
- He argues that a client who demands instant results and instant ROI, and won't accept progress, is probably not your dream client.
- Always state the next step. Every email reply should say "the next step is X," and the client must be clear on it.
- As a client, he was happy with even a tiny bit of progress plus transparency.

chunks.heading: Be friendly and transparent: both sides feel awkward
chunks.text:
- Alex used to feel awkward being the person hired, as if the company were his boss and he had to navigate being paid by them.
- He realized the relationship is just as intricate from the client's side: they want to feel as comfortable as you do, because "we're all human at the end of the day."
- Tactics: vibe with clients, show you care about them and not just their money, and don't "churn and burn" them.
- Be transparent about progress whether it goes right or wrong. If results are bad, he says he is the first to tell the client he's unhappy with them and to try to make it up to them.

chunks.heading: Fail-safe strategy: send unhappy and lukewarm clients away happy
chunks.text:
- Alex uses an MMA analogy: confidence in striking really comes from good defense, ground game and takedown defense. With strong defense you're not afraid to "let your hands fly."
- In a service business, defense means keeping clients happy even when you don't deliver results.
- Results can't be delivered for everyone: "if you could do that you're literally printing money for people." Agency testimonials come from a percentage of clients. Most clients get lukewarm results, a smaller share get good results, and another small share get bad results.
- Lukewarm and negative clients should still leave happy. Tools he names: a money-back guarantee, friendliness and transparency throughout, making it up to them, and leaving on goodwill.
- Payoff: clients with lukewarm results (some calls but no huge client closed, one client closed but still leaving) or even no results left happily and referred new clients to him. He calls service businesses "just so different to any type of business."

chunks.heading: Follow-ups: forever for warm leads, not for cold ones
chunks.text:
- Observation from running hundreds of cold email campaigns: "the money is in the follow-ups" is true for warm leads, not cold leads.
- Cold leads typically reply to the first email. If they haven't replied after two or three emails, further follow-ups are just annoying and spamming.
- Once someone replies and is interested, or jumps on a call, the philosophy is to follow up forever. He says this has closed people years later.

chunks.heading: Time horizon and delayed gratification
chunks.text:
- Alex thinks delayed gratification is over-praised as a virtue and the reality is more nuanced.
- He rejects both extremes: "live as if it's the last day of your life" and living for your deathbed.
- His middle-ground heuristic: live as if you'll die in 20 years. At 28, he assumes he'll die at about 50 and asks what he would do and what his goals would be.
- He notes he lives a lot in the future and loves setting and chasing goals, which gives him mission, focus and happiness. After a sales call with a 45-year-old pillow agency owner from Boston who also talked about what he wants by age 50, he concluded the future-focus never goes away: exciting, but also frustrating that it never changes.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West argues one-to-one copycats are nothing to fear because they are usually beginners or very experienced operators, and that copying signals low-revenue visibility, not validation. He says you build an audience by building interesting things, and that playful, unserious projects can take off unpredictably.

chunks.heading: Copycats: how Alex thinks about being cloned
chunks.text:
- A friend cried because someone copied his project "one to one." Alex says it has happened to him many times, and it hurt at first.
- Alex was copied while at his full-time job, as Cyberly's was nearing his salary and the chance to quit. Competitors:
  - stole his lists and resold them at 1/10 of the price
  - leaked the lists free on Reddit
  - cloned him one-to-one
  - emailed his customers
  - ran ads against his name
- He used to spy on copycats. He no longer does, because "you get used to it very, very quickly."
- None of the people who copied him stayed in business long term. He is unsure why.
- His tentative theory is that one-to-one copying acts as a filter attracting two types:
  - complete beginners, whom you shouldn't fear
  - far more experienced people, who will more likely copy something more lucrative than your side project
- He places himself in the experienced group as he looks to build a new business. He plans to copy again, but not one-to-one.
- Practical takeaway: don't fear one-to-one copycats.

chunks.heading: Why people copy you (it isn't flattery)
chunks.text:
- Alex rejects "imitation is the highest form of flattery" and "nobody copies a loser." He says people copy losers all the time, and he takes being copied as annoying, not as a compliment.
- Being copied doesn't prove a good product, niche or distribution strategy. At best it might suggest you're making some money.
- Many people copy $1K/month projects instead of $100K/month ones.
- He got more copycats at 1K MRR than at 50K MRR. His reasoning: "oh [ __ ] 50, there's no way I can do that. Let me copy something that is more in my league."
- People copy you because they think they can also do what you have.

chunks.heading: Where the defensible value is
chunks.text:
- Copiers can take your product, features and design.
- They can only copy what you've already built. They cannot copy what you haven't created yet.
- That is your advantage: "Wake up tomorrow and do it again."
- He says the value is not in the code.
- A story he critiques: a founder who researched the market and took inspiration from existing apps, then found a niche within a niche. Alex's view is that he shouldn't be surprised when his product, which AI could build, got cloned.

chunks.heading: Audience building vs building cool things
chunks.text:
- Alex thinks many people over-focus on building an audience, assuming that with one everything becomes trivial.
- He agrees with Mark Lou's red pill / blue pill post, where the blue pill is "I need to build an audience" and the red pill is "Build cool shit."
- His view: you don't build an audience in a vacuum. You do interesting things and share them with the world.
- That is how he built his own audience. He built for years before reaching a thousand followers and was far more prolific then than now (he calls himself a "lazy [ __ ]" compared to five years ago).
- The two aren't mutually exclusive: you build cool things in order to build an audience.
- An audience helps, "but not as much as you think."
- Caveat: this is his experience and may differ for others.

chunks.heading: An audience doesn't guarantee a hit
chunks.text:
- Alex has about 45,000 followers. If a post is bad, he gets about 10 likes. If it's good, it can go viral.
- Jonathan, the creator of outbid.lol, has about 20K followers. 20K followers doesn't mean everything he posts takes off.
- An audience helps to an extent, but it doesn't mean anything you build will take off.

chunks.heading: Playful experiments and the outbid.lol case
chunks.text:
- outbid.lol is a site where you pay to be at the top. It starts at $1 for the number one spot, then someone bids $5 and takes it, and so on.
- It got so much traffic that companies bid around $1,000 to be on top, expecting to earn it back from the traffic.
- Jonathan made more than $100,000 in a couple of days.
- Variations of this idea have existed for decades, but this one took off for reasons nobody could predict.
- Alex's lessons:
  - You cannot predict what is going to work.
  - Not everything has to be serious. Many serious companies started as jokes, and he cites Facebook starting as a fun project.
  - He likes it for reminding him of the early internet, when many things were for fun.
  - He found Cyber Leads the same way and did not expect it to take off.
- He wants to be "playful and experimental," including with his new podcast, even though he doesn't see it making money directly or indirectly.

chunks.heading: Turning viral attention into a business
chunks.text:
- Alex says Jonathan shouldn't be written off, because he hasn't yet found a way to harness the attention.
- Idea he floats: a service helping companies build viral products, or run a launch, for $5-10K. It could be "the most boring" offer and still make crazy money quickly.
- It may not be easy, but a viral joke project can become a business through a spin-off.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West co-hosts a weekly news chat with Dimitro of Screenshot One. He argues obsessing over moats is disguised perfectionism, that revenue-stage rules ignore each business's "genetics", and that labels like solopreneur or indie hacker should guide you without becoming dogma. He also uses outreach and ads to validate offers.

chunks.heading: Moats are mostly irrelevant below the unicorn tier
chunks.text:
- Alex says he used to be obsessed with moats while running Cyber Leads, because he wanted a business that would last decades.
- Looking back, he sees that obsession as "another word for perfectionism": looking for an ultimate, magical business that lasts.
- For his second business he thinks about moats "zero". He treats "assume there are no moats" as the useful heuristic.
- He might guess that community or personal brand could be moats, but thinks founders spend "way too much energy" on moats, and customers care less than founders assume.
- His working model: you cannot build a moat and then "just chill". In a free, dynamic market you must keep adapting, improving and staying competitive.
- He cites an exchange: the Snapchat CEO said software has no moat, so Snap is moving into hardware. Elon Musk replied that constant innovation is the moat. Alex agrees with Elon's framing.

chunks.heading: Stability-seeking and the 1M-in-3-months vs 200k-a-year choice
chunks.text:
- Alex paraphrases Daniel Vassallo: many entrepreneurs try to replicate a salary or a job, something stable.
- Five years ago he would have picked a business making 200k a year for 5 years over one making 1 million in 3 months and then disappearing from bad luck. He now thinks the logical answer is to take the 1 million in 3 months and move on to the next thing.
- He says he wanted that stability and peace of mind "to sleep like a baby". He now sees chasing it as a trap, not a strategy.

chunks.heading: Labels and identity: "indie hacker", "solopreneur", "nomad"
chunks.text:
- Alex says labels help at the start by pointing you in a direction. His 2018 profile at age 23 described him as a nomad, and he had just discovered indie hacking and wanted to be one of those people.
- The danger is letting a label become dogmatic and box you in. He had to break out of several self-imposed boxes:
  - **Solopreneur box:** he refused to hire anyone because it seemed cool and he wanted to make 1 million a year alone. He asked himself whether looking cool to others mattered more than lifestyle, then hired a few people, worked two hours a day and traveled.
  - **Passive income box:** he had a subscription business, the indie hacker dream, then got a chance to build a service on top of it. Services are not passive, and he had to break that identity to take it.
- Each time he broke out of an abstract box, it "freed" him.
- His analogy: being an athlete means you don't smoke, you run and exercise, but you still have a glass of wine at your sister's wedding. Keep identities, just not dogmatically.
- He agrees with the idea of being like water. Use identities as tools, consciously, and notice when one is making you suffer.
- He says he is currently trying to break out of another box again and may discuss it in a future episode.

chunks.heading: Why a bidding or "sponsor my laptop" website is a good thing
chunks.text:
- Alex likes the wave of joke projects such as bidding websites, "sponsor my laptop" and ads on someone's baby. They remind him of the early internet, where "not everything has to be serious" and some things can be for fun.
- He sees building for fun as the spirit of building on the internet.
- He links this to constraint: his best work ever came when he had a full-time job he hated. He had only two hours a day and made them count, and calls it his most productive year.
- His view is that pressure, the "fire", produces your best ideas, more than having money in the bank and lying around.

chunks.heading: Pressure from family can sharpen, not limit, a founder
chunks.text:
- Alex answers a tweet claiming nobody makes it as an indie hacker while married with young kids. His answer is "yes and no".
- Upside: ultimate motivation. At 18 he thought "I cannot be a loser" for his 10-year-old brother to look up to. Friends who became fathers told him they felt the same.
- Downside: for him, locking in to build a new business is easier with all the time in the world and no distractions. Single life can also be distracting.
- He says the quality of the home environment matters, and that a partner can influence you a lot.
- He frames kids as "tiny little humans that never asked to be born", and says that responsibility can spark things in you that you would never have lying around with money in the bank.

chunks.heading: Stage-based advice like "no paid ads until $5-10M" ignores business "genetics"
chunks.text:
- Alex uses ads and outreach mainly to validate new offers and ideas, not as a substitute for organic or social. He currently sends about a thousand outreach emails a day to test new ideas.
- He agrees with the narrow risk in the tweet: a business fully dependent on ads faces rising ad costs as competition grows, "a ticking bomb". He rejects the blanket rule.
- His objection to "0 to 1M do this, 1 to 3M do that" advice: it depends on the genetics of the business. Variables he lists: LTV, acquisition channels, retention and churn, and the market.
- Weightlifting analogy:
  - Benchmarks like repping 100 kg on bench press depend on bodyweight. His brother is 60 kg, he is 85 kg and his best friend is 105 kg.
  - His friend hit the benchmark in his first 3 months at age 16, while it took Alex years, and his brother may never reach it.
  - Businesses are the same.
- Example: Cyber Leads went straight to half a million a year without him doing much, then hit its business "genetics" ceiling.
- He admits he was once stuck at about half a million and followed the "0 to 1M, stick with one thing" videos, which kept him doing what he already had. He says he was "so dumb" to listen.
- Churn: in his experience you cannot influence it much in a high-churn market. You may be top quartile but you "revert to the mean" and won't be a different animal.

chunks.heading: Writing style: protreptic over didactic
chunks.text:
- Alex says many people love didactic writing, being told what to do and how. He planned his books that way, but changed course.
- He chose protreptic writing instead: give interesting thoughts and let readers derive their own lessons. He accepts that he lost readers who wanted step-by-step instruction.
- He says he thinks people need to figure things out themselves, not be told "post on X three times a day and don't do anything until you reach 10K a month".
- On X, the medium shapes the message. It is punchy, attention-driven and absolute, so he would never write "you will not make it and will suffer" in a book, where he would see both sides.
- His approach: write books to say things completely, and treat X as the short, punchy channel.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West explains why he left flashy B2C products for a "boring" B2B funded-companies newsletter, then added a $2k/month done-for-you cold email service. He covers simplicity as a differentiator, finding one product plus one distribution channel (Twitter), and switching from artist to athlete once something works.

chunks.heading: Boring business vs. cool business
chunks.text:
- Alex built about 20 "cool" products (e.g. a tool for people with epilepsy) that sounded great at parties and earned $100-$200/month. He then had to take a full-time job.
- He flipped his priorities: "change my life mostly rather than the world." His reasoning is that nobody cares about you beyond a "wow" that is forgotten in five seconds, so build for your own lifestyle.
- He is "so happy to be running a simple, quote unquote boring business" and warns against shiny object syndrome.
- Cyber Leads (cyber leads) is his business: a monthly list of companies that raised funding in the past month and are likely to outsource a service (design, cybersecurity, etc.), with decision-maker emails. He hit about $300k annual revenue as a solo founder.
- His biggest earner is a done-for-you service on top of the list. He sends the cold emails and books meetings on the customer's behalf, because many people don't know how to use cold email properly.
- He is not taking new service customers at the moment (waitlist).
- Being featured on the My First Million podcast brought newsletter subscribers and service leads, "but nothing insane."

chunks.heading: Simplicity as a differentiator
chunks.text:
- The newsletter is almost exactly what it was two and a half years ago. He swings between "feeling like an idiot and a genius because it's so simple."
- Competing databases and platforms hold outdated or wrong data, lack decision makers, and make users log in and build their own queries.
- His edge: "use simplicity as a differentiator." People don't have time to learn your product or decode a clever landing page.
- Data quality is manual: he cross-checks every funded company by hand so there are no mistakes.
- The "likely to outsource" label combines statistics with manual judgment:
  - A 50-person company with one or zero designers, or one that has used agencies before, fits a design studio.
  - A company storing medical information whose website says "trust" five times fits a cybersecurity agency.
- He criticizes early-stage startups with five people who copy Enterprise-style landing pages where "you don't understand anything." Enterprise sales teams can get away with that because they run live demos.
- Gumroad is his positive example: the same product for close to 10 years (excluding last year's rebrand). "Adding things is very easy but keeping things simple and being focused and grounded... is difficult."

chunks.heading: B2B vs. B2C, and why high ticket helps
chunks.text:
- He moved to B2B because most solo founders who made it were doing B2B.
- He noticed his own behavior: in business he will pay $1,000/month without thinking if it might save 10 hours or make $10,000. People balk at a 99-cent app for personal use.
- Contrast in his own numbers:
  - In B2C he struggled to sell $5/month subscriptions with churn. Reaching $1K/month needed 200 customers.
  - With Cyber Leads, 200 customers "could be like a million per year."
- Exception: B2C education sells well because people spend heavily on education.
- The done-for-you service costs $2K/month, so $1M/year needs 40 customers worldwide. With numbers that small, he says there is no point worrying about competition.

chunks.heading: Copycats and competition
chunks.text:
- He does not worry about copycats at all. People did similar things before him and will after. "There's enough room for everyone as long as they don't overlap."
- Overlap would mean the same product, wording, target customer and acquisition channel, which he calls "plain stupidity" in a space as large as the internet.
- He notes that 99% of people quit, as he quit his own 19 products, so most copycats fade.
- Early on he wrongly believed an idea had to be unique and dropped ideas that were already taken.
- Going high ticket makes the customer count needed so small that competitors matter less. For the newsletter he worried slightly more about price erosion (everyone selling at $10/month instead of $100-$200).
- Affiliate program: it sat on his homepage "just in case" and only started taking off after the My First Million mention.

chunks.heading: Finding the first customers and one distribution channel
chunks.text:
- He launched on Product Hunt at $29/month and got roughly 5-10 customers. Then came the "Finding Nemo" moment: "okay, now what?"
- His principle: have one product people will pay for and one distribution channel you can use "again and again and again." Product Hunt is not repeatable daily.
- He tested LinkedIn cold outreach, sponsored blog posts, Quora, Reddit, Twitter, SEO and his own network.
- Twitter worked: a tweet he posted with no intention of going viral brought five customers.
- Traffic today: Twitter is the all-time revenue leader; lately word of mouth is picking up even more, which surprises him. He notes word of mouth may partly be Twitter indirectly. Twitter works well if your niche is tech or business.
- His pattern: about 20 products to find one that took off, many channels to find Twitter, and about 20 experiments inside Cyber Leads (e.g. turning it into a database, building an agency network) before finding the done-for-you service.

chunks.heading: Artist to athlete, and one project vs. many
chunks.text:
- Early on, be an artist: try new things, stay open-minded, find a smart way to get customers. Once something works, "become an athlete": do the boring thing that took you from 0 to 10 customers repeatedly. He has done that for about two years.
- Keep experimenting inside the business, find the next lever, and then repeat that. He expects to run the done-for-you service for the next few years.
- On one project vs. many: both approaches have worked for different people.
  - 2018: he built 13-14 products in a year and went from zero to about $100/month, later about $500/month.
  - 2019: he fell in love with one sexy product and stuck with it for a whole year, and it went nowhere. He admits he can't know if sticking longer would have worked.
- His conclusion: you need early traction to justify sticking with something, and trying many things is how you get that early traction. Then stick with it for a long time, even without a hockey-stick trajectory.

chunks.heading: Mindset and lifestyle
chunks.text:
