- His book recommendations are the Stoics (Epictetus, Seneca, Marcus Aurelius): practical philosophy that counters an internet that feels like a "positive sum game"-style comparison trap.
- His own weakness is anxiety, not shiny object syndrome or perfectionism. His goal is to run a tech business, competing with the whole world, while staying as calm as possible. He reminds himself of this when he sees lead-generation companies making $100 million a year.
- Travel: he did one month per place (Sicily, London, Cyprus, Greece, Paris and others) and found it unsustainable. You don't make friends or see the city while working. He now plans at least two to three months per place.
- He works from home or a neighborhood coffee shop, not coworking spaces.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West explains how, after 19 failed products, he picked a healthy market first, launched a no-code newsletter selling lead data, and found traction by trying every channel until Twitter worked. He also argues that money is easy to measure but a poor sole metric, and that quality of life should come first.

chunks.heading: Starting without money, then choosing markets first
chunks.text:
- Alex studied computer science and joined a startup accelerator, where he saw many founders talking about raising money while none were making a dollar. That felt backwards to him: "businesses run on profits and not on valuations."
- Videos from Peter Levels and DHH convinced him he didn't need to be a billionaire and could be "a humble little millionaire." He has worked on this full-time-in-mind since 1 January 2018.
- He built 19 products (17 at one earlier point he recalls) that never got past roughly $100 per month, which wasn't enough to live on in Greece. They were "cool" products, the kind you can mention at a party, but he says cool products usually don't make money and boring ones do.
- Working a first real 9-to-5 (leaving in the dark, returning in the dark, in winter) pushed him to pick something boring that makes money. His logic: change your own world first, then worry about the rest of the world.

chunks.heading: Market-first idea selection (the three-part filter)
chunks.text:
Instead of going idea, then product, then hunting for buyers, Alex went market first: pick healthy markets and look for ideas inside them. A healthy market has three traits:

1. **Many players all making money.** Not one big incumbent (his example of a bad market is trying to build a search engine). The earnings can be small; even $2k per month per player is fine.
2. **Something you can actually build.**
3. **Something you can promote.** It's not just about building; it's about getting customers "again and again and again."

He had two such markets in mind, cyber security and lead generation. On cybersecurity subreddits (around early 2020) he saw a post asking for lists of companies that had raised money, with many commenters begging for the data. Looking closer, he found many sellers of the same data in different packaging: a platform with exports, a business-intelligence tool for recently funded startups, a report, a newsletter. They sold to journalists, companies and sales teams.

chunks.heading: Launching with no code
chunks.text:
- He had a full-time job and was falling out of love with coding, so he picked the format needing no code: a newsletter, which he could launch in a day without building anything.
- That became Cyber Leads, a solo business now at about $300k per year (over $30k per month at the time of the interview; he mentions roughly $3.5k MRR the previous year).
- He argues everyone should start with no code, even if they can program: "we're not building rockets, we're building websites." Nobody visiting a site asks what it was built with.
- His analogy: arguing about programming languages and frameworks is "painters arguing about brushes." What matters is making something people value.
- He moved to code about two years later, once full-time, only because some features couldn't be done with no-code tools. Making money is "a nice problem to have" after validating with no code.

chunks.heading: Finding a channel after launch: try everything, then go all-in
chunks.text:
- Most founders have a short time horizon: build, launch on one platform, expect virality. Alex says that's wrong because you need customers repeatedly, every week; you can't relaunch on Product Hunt daily.
- After launching on Product Hunt he had a "now what?" moment. He got a few customers (going from the $100-200 range to about $200 per month in a day), then churn pulled him down toward $100 and below $80.
- He tried LinkedIn, cold email, Reddit, Quora, reaching out to YouTube influencers, Twitter and more. He followed the book *Traction* by Gabriel Weinberg and JJ Mares, whose advice he summarizes as: try everything, and when one thing works, drop the rest and focus on it "one thousand percent."
- A tweet went viral with no existing following and brought about 10 customers. He recognized that he couldn't go viral daily but Twitter was a place to "fish for customers."
- He dropped the other channels and focused on Twitter: writing blog posts, tweeting, selling the business through sharing the journey. A post later hit Hacker News and went viral, adding traction.
- He admits "it's not really good advice" to hope for virality; the transferable lesson is that you never know what will work, so test broadly and then commit.

chunks.heading: Writing every day as a business habit
chunks.text:
- Alex started a daily writing practice at the end of 2019, after failing with his products and fearing he'd forget everything he'd learned. He wrote down the lessons from the products he'd built and compared it to "cleaning your room, but for your mind."
- He began with daily, weekly and monthly entries; now he does daily and monthly, skipping sometimes.
- Benefits he names: mental clarity, and a record he can reread years later to see what he was thinking.
- He keeps it going while learning stress management, communication and writing, which he sees as byproducts of building the business.

chunks.heading: Money, quality of life and "enough"
chunks.text:
- His goal moved over time: first $500 per month (equal to his salary in Greece), then $800, now chasing $1M per year. He admits "i'm not proud of this," and calls it the hamster-wheel pattern of "when I have that I'll be happy."
- His definition of financial freedom: "living as if money does not exist," meaning not thinking about bills, rent or supermarket prices. He says he was already living that way the previous year, when he earned much less.
- He now sees the game as a vehicle for self-improvement rather than money: managing stress, working out, communicating, writing.
- He warns about optimizing the one quantifiable metric: "money is so quantifiable... it's a number," whereas quality of life and happiness are hard to measure, which is why people fixate on revenue.
- Taking on more work raised his income about six times versus the prior year but lowered his quality of life. He may downscale and says more is not always better.
- He agrees with Daniel Vassallo's approach (as relayed in the conversation): work toward a cushion, then take the risk, and once the business is established be selective about customers and be willing to leave money on the table to protect peace.
- Comparison trap: "money Twitter" and "money YouTube" show anomalies who were lucky or talented, giving a distorted view of reality. A visit to friends in Athens earning around $500 per month (what he made four years earlier) humbled him: even $1,000-$2,000 per month doing your own thing is success.
- Rapid-fire preferences: marketing over product ("thousand percent"), beaches over mountains, writing, curation over creation ("I don't believe in uniqueness"), books over podcasts.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West explains how 19 failed products led to CyberLeads, a lead-gen newsletter for agencies. Lessons: build boring ideas people already pay for, learn from doing, find one product plus one distribution channel and double down, and treat competition as no threat. Also covers habits over motivation and why small teams can outmove companies.

chunks.heading: Alex's journey: 19 failed products before the 20th worked
chunks.text:
Alex built 19 products that didn't take off before his 20th, CyberLeads (getcyberlist.com), went well. CyberLeads is a monthly newsletter that sends digital agencies high-quality leads, sold on a monthly subscription. He had about two and a half years in the maker community by this point, and the product took off only in the last six months. He still held a full-time software engineering job while building it.

- **2018:** he took a "shotgun" approach. He launched about 15 products from zero experience and reached 200 dollars MRR.
- **2019:** he took a "sniper" approach. He locked onto one idea, an epilepsy-blocker Chrome extension, and spent about two months coding it. He cold-called charities and TV networks and met a CTO at a Greek telecom, and none of it paid off.
- **The extension today:** it ended up free. Real-time analysis of GIF pixels was computationally expensive, so he had planned to charge, but people with photosensitive epilepsy often live on benefits, and he disliked charging them 10 dollars a month. The project still led to the job that moved him abroad.
- **2019-2020:** he sat between 50 and 150 dollars MRR for about two years "no matter how many products I build."
- **Then:** he took a job in Milan, wrote "two years of indie hacking" (a blog post listing every product with its numbers), and went back to the shotgun approach. He had studied the Indie Hackers archive and noticed the makers he looked up to "had traction from the beginning." He quotes Taleb: "don't tell me what you think, show me your portfolio."

chunks.heading: Picking boring ideas and validating with a landing page
chunks.text:
- **Switch:** Alex stopped chasing "unique ambitious" products meant to change the world. He argues that wanting to improve humanity is mostly ego, and that you can "build something boring and give money to charity."
- **New rule:** build something he knows people will pay for, and build it without code. He fell out of love with programming and realized he loved "creating something out of nothing," not the code.
- **How CyberLeads started:** he found a Reddit post listing recently funded startups. Googling showed about 10 companies selling the same information to different buyers: journalists, sales teams, job seekers, and business-intelligence users. They delivered it as a database, newsletter, or report, and all were making money. That was validation.
- **Why a newsletter:** it "reduces friction" and he could launch it without a product.
- **MVP:** a landing page plus a Gumroad subscription, with no Stripe checkout coded. He launched on Product Hunt and got 10 paying customers.
- **What failure taught him:**
  - A .com domain doesn't matter for validation.
  - A professional logo won't make or break you.
  - Extra features don't either.
- **Reddit idea hunting:** he tried the "idea hunting on Reddit" method from a blog post. It produced ideas and some launches, with no great results.
- **On experience:** he says 2018 Alex would have noticed this opportunity and dismissed it as "taken" (his phrase: "it's a [expletive] bus seat"). He compares spotting ideas to a chess master's pattern recognition and says it comes only from repeated launches.

chunks.heading: Competition, copycats and niching down
chunks.text:
- **Bus-seat mindset:** an idea being taken isn't a reason to skip it. "Mate, you're against yourself and that's it." The internet is big enough for everyone.
- **Fishing analogy:** two people fishing the same river is fine if they target different fish. The problem is "bashing heads" with the same product, same audience, same channels and same approach.
- **Energy-drink example:** two identical drinks aren't competing if one is positioned on taste and the other on gym performance. Products then diverge as features are added.
- **Pivot in one day:** he started with general B2B sales leads. Going through customers, he saw that agency CEOs were his favorites: easy to work with, same language, and one closed deal repays the subscription 100 to 1,000 times. He pivoted to agencies in a day.
- **Features per niche:** he added agency-specific features such as forecasting which design or engineering agencies will need help, and non-profits that need agencies.
- **Copycats:** he is open about numbers and strategy. People have copied his blog, run ads against his name, and stolen and resold his data. He believes "they cannot stop you because the internet is so big."
- **Big players:** a big company has 50 people, but you really compete against about five. The other 45 are bored and "log into Jira" and do tasks. A hacker moves faster, while a company "needs meetings, plural, to change the color of one button."

chunks.heading: Distribution: the tweet that turned it around
chunks.text:
- **After launch:** with 10 customers and no growth, he tried Quora, Reddit, Hacker News and cold emails. Twitter began as a side effect while building an audience.
- **The tweet:** he tweeted about his first 50 dollars from a customer. He almost didn't post it; he only wanted to tweet once a day, and posted just before watching a film with his girlfriend. The next morning "it's chaos" and he gained roughly another 10 customers.
- **Lesson:** "now I have my product and my distribution channel." He says "that's the most important thing that no one talks about," and he doesn't want to only have product-market fit: "Facebook, you have it now. What you need is the distribution channel."
- **Moving from creative to athlete:** once product and channel exist, "you have to become an athlete," putting in the work on things you know produce results.
- **Role model:** Jordan O'Connor's blog documents going from zero to 30,000 dollars a month with one product and one distribution channel. That convinced Alex to "double down" and not chase SEO and blog posts.
- **Traction book:** he read *Traction* (19 channels, the Bullseye framework). He dabbled with everything, then doubled down on Twitter when the tweet went viral.
- **Second product:** he launched another product on Product Hunt that "went nowhere," and he regretted splitting his energy.
- **Marketing style:** instead of "use promo code X for 10% off," his marketing is "Hey, I'm Alex, I'm trying to gain my freedom and I'm not selling anything to anyone." He says "the best marketing is no marketing, no one wants to be sold anything."

chunks.heading: Work habits and mindset
chunks.text:
- **Constraints help:** with no job he did "pretend work" all day. After starting a full-time job, two hours in the morning produced more than a whole day before.
- **Mornings:** he used to wake at 11 or 12. After work he was too drained to be creative, so he switched his side-project block to mornings. Finding an idea and distribution channels is the hardest part and needs the most energy.
- **Habits over motivation:** *Atomic Habits* changed his view. "Motivation is super overrated," and discipline is overrated too. You want one or two things that are like brushing your teeth, which "you don't even think about."
- **Daily blog:** it helps him see that "pretend work" like market research or redesigning a landing page is not real work. His filter is "what are the two things you can do today that will move your business forward."
- **Doubling down:** he stays with CyberLeads and Twitter, "nothing super creative," and waits. He says inputs are yours but outcomes aren't: "you cannot make someone take his credit card out."
- **Ideas vs execution:** he rejects "ideas are nothing, execution is everything." He quotes Courtland Allen: a ten-times-better idea is easy to find, a ten-times-better executor is hard.
- **Uncertainty:** "when in doubt, do the exact opposite of what you've been doing." For him that meant taking a job, which he dreaded, and moving abroad.
- **Learn by doing:** "people learn from doing and not from learning." He cites Bruce Lee: "keep what works, discard what does not work, try new things, rinse and repeat."

chunks.heading: Money, freedom and staying grounded
chunks.text:
- **Numbers:** a few years earlier he earned about 500 dollars a month full time in Greece. By this interview, CyberLeads had brought in 4k in net revenue in a month, and one annual subscriber paid in a morning about what a month's engineering salary used to pay.
- **Why he doesn't upgrade:** he has run it for only about six months, so "I don't feel like I'm standing on solid ground." He says "I like money because of what it gives you: security, freedom, time-wise, location-wise." He doesn't like things and hasn't bought anything since.
- **Gratitude:** he reminds himself daily that "I'm living my dream." The question "what's next" is one he hates, because it stops you admitting you have what you want.
- **Closing advice:** "Don't give up." If you quit after two tries you "don't want it bad enough." You "only need one product."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West, a bootstrapping solo developer, talks about building many products on shared infrastructure, why he thinks trust and attention win as everything gets commoditized, and how to find and validate ideas. He also covers working in the building phase versus the marketing phase and the Peter Levels shotgun approach.

chunks.heading: Building a solo business through many failed products: the shotgun approach, validating before building, and the "progression" from build-first to market-first
chunks.text:
Alex describes his own arc as a progression from building first, to marketing first, to earning before building:
- **Product 1:** two years before he showed it to a single person. He perfected every button, played with the copy, built a server, a mobile app and business cards. He calls it "every mistake in the book".
- **Cyberlies (2 years later):** launched without building anything and reached $100 per month.
- **Service on top of Cyberlies (another 2 years later):** he was making $100K per year before he started building anything.
- His heuristic: "consider that you have built your dream product. Now what?" Do that part first (marketing, finding customers), before building the product.
- "Real work begins when the to-do list ends." Finishing the MVP is when the real work starts.
- The path ran from building, then marketing, then earning, to marketing, then earning, then building.

chunks.heading: Failing forward: how a cyber security idea turned into a lead-generation business
chunks.text:
- Alex set out to build a heavily technical product in the cyber security market.
- To validate it, he scraped GitHub by hand for cyber security consultants and reached out to them. He got on calls with 10 people and received strong feedback.
- That was the first time he thought: "if someone provided me with leads every month, specifically what I wanted, I would pay 50 bucks for a month". That insight pointed him toward the lead generation market.
- His conclusion: "You fail forwards, that is the way you progress." His ideas got better with every failure, and the progression went from two years building a product to making $100K per year without building anything first.
- A reader asked what to do if they cannot find any B2B ideas. Alex replied: start building your b2c ideas, and while building them B2B ideas come organically, because by then you are already a business.
- He has advocated B2B and higher prices as generic advice (with exceptions).

chunks.heading: Shotgun approach: many projects to find traction, then focus (diversify only once rich)
chunks.text:
- Alex has "always advocated for a shotgun approach": throw many things at the wall and focus solely on the one that sticks.
- He thinks most success stories start with a bang, meaning traction. With traction you are willing to "pull your soul into it".
- Focusing on a failing project out of belief has worked for some people, but he sees it as the exception.
- He distinguishes finding wealth from keeping it. "Diversifying is great for retaining your wealth, not for making your wealth."
- When you are up and coming, focus on one thing and try to hit the home run. "You've hit the ball, it's up in the air, start running. Don't think, oh let me diversify."
- He has seen people making less than $1K per month talk about diversifying revenue streams, and he doesn't think that's the way to go.
- Diversify once you are already where you want to be and just want to secure your lifestyle. Rule of thumb he gives: if you want to be a billionaire, don't start diversifying at another million per year. If you want to make 50K per year, you can diversify once you hit that.
- The remark about "19 failed products" in the title is not elaborated in this conversation; the only concrete numbers he gives are the progression above and the five years he says it took him.

chunks.heading: You don't have to be your own first user, and impostor syndrome is a wall to walk through
chunks.text:
- Alex says "be your own first customer" is "one of those myths that really makes people not do something".
- When he started Cyberlies he did not run an agency and did not do cold outbound or cold emails at the time. He sold email contacts to agencies.
- Later he started an agency charging people $2K per month and felt impostor syndrome again. His view: "The impostor syndrome is a wall you have to bomb and walk through."
- When he started the service he "had no idea". He read a few books, tried techniques, bought a few courses and experimented, and got "amazing results".
- His advice: "You can learn anything." Find something you enjoy that you think is a good business, go deep and learn.

chunks.heading: Why it takes years: obsession, not part-time effort
chunks.text:
- Alex says a reader DM'd asking to be his assistant or mentee because he is "exactly where I want to be in six months". He replied that he is not the person to look at, because it took him five years.
- He describes those as five years of "it's the only thing I'm thinking about" (in the shower, on a walk, on a run, on an airplane, on a train, sleeping), not five years on and off or part-time.
- "It has some benefits no one can argue against": freedom of time, freedom of movement, location independence, financial independence, doing what you want with who you want. "Everyone wants that, but do you want it enough?" Are you willing to sacrifice five years or more?
- He feels "extremely lucky" and thinks luck is a huge part of it.
- He cites his own drivers as ego and proving he can do it, and not wanting to work for someone else.
- On stress: working for someone else gave him constant, flat stress (daily stand-ups, a meeting at 12, Friday one-on-ones, a task that has to be done by Friday, performance reviews every two weeks). Working for himself the stress is different, not higher or lower. After he quit, his Fitbit showed his heart rate dropped about 10 beats per minute.
- He separates passions from revenue: he loves running his business but won't try to make a podcast a revenue activity.

chunks.heading: Where the economy is heading: commoditization, shrinking firms, trust and attention
chunks.text:
- Humans have a terrible track record of predicting the future, but he points to trends. He quotes Naval: the optimal size of the firm is shrinking.
- Alex says the work in his business (Cyberlies) that would once have taken about 20 people is done by him solo plus one assistant, because he automated it.
- Everything is being commoditized. Starting a software business needed capital 20 years ago (local servers). Now servers cost around $5 per month, and you can build a full Airbnb clone with no code in a weekend.
- Barriers to entry will keep dropping everywhere. "The only thing that cannot be commoditized is trust and attention." Ads are a race where prices go up as more people join.
- He expects businesses to be fronted by influencer-like faces, such as Joe Rogan-style personalities, even in B2B, with companies behind them making millions on maybe five contractors.
- Positioning example: if you hacked Red Bull's recipe and made an identical drink, you couldn't beat them head on, but you could position it differently (for example "Beast Mode" energy drink for people hitting a gym personal best) and get different customers. As everything commoditizes, trust matters more and more; brand marks like the Nike tick are worth billions.
- Alex compares small solo companies to small fish eating scraps from a shark's teeth: he competes with ZoomInfo, a public billion-dollar company, and they "don't give a [expletive] about me". The scraps are enough to make "a few million per year", which is nothing for them. He expects the middle class of business to disappear, leaving huge corporations and individual brands with companies behind them.
- He defines "small" as making up to $10M per year.

chunks.heading: Financial goals and the work-until-lunch lifestyle
chunks.text:
- His financial goal is "living as if money doesn't exist": at the supermarket he doesn't look at prices, and he buys things unless they're wildly disproportionate.
- His day-to-day goal used to be a fully automated business. He now thinks that is "so overrated". His new goal is to work until lunch, about four hours per day.
- He cites old newspaper articles predicting that automation would stop humans working by 2000; today there is more automation and more work than ever. He ties it to an innate need to build and improve things ("I find a stick, I want to collect that stick").
- His forecast: the work you don't want to do will shrink a lot, and the rest of the time you'll still be doing things, but things you enjoy. His rule: "the rest, delegate, eliminate or automate."
- He also reads the architecture/computer-science story as: "everything comes down to our fear of death", the urge to build things that outlast you. Computer science is to computers what astronomy is to a telescope: "the computer is the telescope, computer science is the stars".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West explains how he found Cyber Leads after about 20 products: pick the acquisition channel first, then a non-winner-take-all market, then the idea. He covers launching for first users, running 20 experiments inside one product, adding a done-for-you service, and shifting from artist to athlete.

chunks.heading: Picking a market before an idea (Channel, then Market, then Idea)
chunks.text:
Alex reached his 20th product, Cyber Leads, by reversing the usual order. Up to 2020 he went idea, then market, then acquisition channel. The reverse worked better.

- **Channel first.** He asked where he already hangs out and can reach. That was Twitter (about 600 followers then) and Product Hunt, mostly tech.
- **Market second.** He wanted B2B after being burned "chasing people for $5 a month invoices" and haggling over discounts.
- **Idea third.** Action beats theorizing: "action is way more important than pontificating and theorizing."
- His test for a good market:
  1. Not winner-take-all (a search engine is, since "it's very difficult to overthrow the king").
  2. Buildable solo, with a low barrier to entry.
  3. Something he enjoys and knows, with multiple players visibly making millions.
- He found three such markets: cybersecurity, lead generation (Cyber Leads) and recruiting.
- He credits Justin from Transistor FM, on an Indie Hackers podcast, for the market-first idea. He says the market you're in often matters more than effort. His blog post "Two Years of Building Products" reviews 15 products to show this.

chunks.heading: Early traction: launch everywhere, then find one channel
chunks.text:
- Scale is relative: "if you're at zero users, scaling means getting your first user."
- Launch everywhere: Twitter, Reddit, friends and family, warm inbound and outbound.
- His Product Hunt launch gave him 10 B2B customers. It was the first time he saw a business email sign up.
- Launches don't repeat: "if we could launch on Product Hunt every day we would all be rich." After launch you have to build a channel.
- The hardest stretch was the months between launching and finding his channel. Revenue was falling and he feared failure number 20.
- Twitter then took off, along with a blog post that went viral on Hacker News. That got him his first 100 customers and moved him from hundreds to thousands of dollars a month. He then doubled down on building in the open.
- His rule: "one product and one channel, that's it."

chunks.heading: Staying simple and doing things by hand
chunks.text:
- Cyber Leads is still essentially a newsletter and has not been bloated with features or integrations. He admires Trello and Bear for staying simple.
- He started on no-code, sent the newsletter and welcome emails manually, and over-engineered nothing.
- The business now makes about half a million a year and runs on a $7/month Heroku plan.
- Automation came later. Today clients pay, fill in a questionnaire, book a kickoff call, and tasks are created daily via Slack, Trello and Notion automations.
- Early on, don't plan for 10K or 100K a month: "go from zero to one user, that's a scale; one to ten, that's a scale." Setting up foundations for a 10x year is "procrastination."

chunks.heading: Time and prioritization
chunks.text:
- Working a day job, he found about 80% of his real work happened before lunch, whether he worked 2 or 10 hours. That stayed true at $400, $4,000 and now.
- His mental model, from his "2.5 years" blog post: sit down for two hours as if someone with a gun to your head says you need a customer by the end of the week. Do what you'd do then, every day.
- Quitting his job on January 7, 2021 did not speed things up: "it takes the same amount of time to boil" no matter how many cooks. He was stuck around $4K/month for a year.

chunks.heading: The pivot to a done-for-you service (about $4K to $6K/month in a day)
chunks.text:
- After a year at about $4K/month he ran 20 experiments inside Cyber Leads instead of selling or starting a new product. He points to the book Traction, co-written by DuckDuckGo's founder. He says you need "a really open mind" because you can't know what will work.
- A blog reader who had run a SaaS at roughly $1-2M ARR got on a Zoom coffee. He asked why people churn.
- Alex's cancellation form kept giving the same two reasons: they didn't know how to reach out and book meetings, or didn't have time. The reader replied: "why don't you do it for them?"
- Alex's first reaction was no: he wanted a lifestyle business, not clients or meetings. But after two years of making lists he knew what worked.
- In his next monthly list he offered to email prospects and book meetings for people, personally, for $2K/month.
  - 10 people said yes immediately.
  - One signed the next day.
  - Revenue went from $4K to $6K (about +50%) in a day.
- He says he was "terrified of that decision" but it was the right one and gave him the life he wanted. He wrote about it in "Four Years of Building Products" on alexwest.com.

chunks.heading: Customer feedback: watch payment, not opinions
chunks.text:
- "I don't care what people think or tell me, I care what they pay for."
- He doesn't ask what to build. He makes an offer ("it costs 2K per month, are you in or out") and keeps what enough people pay for.
- He rarely iterates on the main product and keeps it simple by default.

chunks.heading: Idea generation, failure and motivation
chunks.text:
- Early ideas are bad. As a student his were all B2C marketplaces because that was his life (e.g. an app to find coffee in your city).
- The fix is to start building, launching and failing fast. "Idea is like a muscle": he ended up with a list of ideas, with Cyber Leads at number 20 and seven more below it.
- Don't chase uniqueness. Cyber Leads entered a crowded market and became unique later: it now serves agencies and productized services by finding clients that just raised millions in funding. He says wanting a unique product was a crutch that cost him "many entrepreneurial years."
- Expect up to roughly 20 products, but not by launching random ones. Review what went right and wrong after each.
- "Artist to athlete": at first be the artist, trying ideas and channels to find one product and one channel. Then be the athlete and "do the same thing every single day."
- The hardest part is the beginning, when nothing works. It gets easy once a product grows past your salary and you have savings.
- It took him about 2 years and 20 tries. Others have done it faster.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West's candid account of his first two indie years: 15 product launches, a $200/month peak, and many mistakes. He shows why products that work without network effects beat communities and marketplaces, why small fast launches beat years of polishing, and where B2B pivots and bad-fit customers hurt.

chunks.heading: Alex's goal was $500/month from personal projects, and he started by building the wrong thing for two years
chunks.text:
- Alex began building at 20 after a 3-hour conversation with a funded founder. He spent two years on "City Vibes", a nightlife app where bars and clubs uploaded real-time photos so people could pick where to go out.
- He made the classic mistakes: kept the idea secret, perfected it for 2 years before showing anyone, and left marketing for last. It died within weeks of launch.
- At a startup accelerator he saw that everyone talked about raising money and no one was making money. He decided he did not need to be a billionaire and would be "ok being a millionaire".
- City Vibes needed funding and only made profit at large scale, in a network-effects market where "either you go viral or you die". He killed it and slept well: "I was not my idea."
- Watching talks by DHH and Pieter Levels, he took away that the goal is to sell and make a profit, ideally from day one. That led him to "Indies" on Twitter, people building tiny independent businesses.
- He set a goal of $500/month from projects or a remote job, enough to live in a place like Thailand.

chunks.heading: Year 1 "shotgun" strategy: ship fast, low expectations, and what the first launches taught him
chunks.text:
- Strategy: build many products, launch fast, and "throw virtual spaghetti to the wall until something sticks", then double down.
- Jan, MMAmatchups (fighter matchup voting site): built in 2 weeks, Reddit banned him for self-promotion, journalists did not reply, 300 visitors and 30 signups. Traffic died the day he stopped posting. Abandoned.
- Feb, MultiNewTab (browser extension): he had 1 week to build it instead of the 3 he thought he needed, and suspects 3 weeks would have taken 3 weeks. It hit 67 Product Hunt upvotes and 100+ installs, which he only saw 10 days later when the Chrome dashboard refreshed.
- Mar, TalentShare (platform for companies to share top candidates they could not hire): he collected emails, but no founder or hiring manager would share applicants. He could not launch an empty platform, since "an empty platform is not a product".
- Apr, RemoteJuniorClub (community with leaderboard, chat and a scraped junior remote job board): 8 people joined, but communities collapse if you do not push them, and he disliked chatting online.
- Pattern he noticed in May: 3 of his 4 products were communities or marketplaces, which are worthless without users (City Vibes, TalentShare, RemoteJuniorClub). The exception, MultiNewTab, "offered the same value, regardless of users" and was his most successful.

chunks.heading: May: building in public and Product Hunt launches that worked
chunks.text:
- After four duds, he picked the easiest idea from his list: GitGardener, automated daily GitHub commits to keep your contribution graph green. It was not a business idea, but it worked regardless of user count.
- He had zero followers but tweeted publicly that he would build it in one week. Saying it out loud made quitting harder "even when no one was listening".
- GitGardener launched on a Sunday on Product Hunt: number 3 product of the day, 4,000 visitors, 400 signups, about 100 Twitter followers. Reddit bashed it and he did not care.
- The following week he built MakerFeed (a site to find and follow makers building on Twitter), tweeting each step, and hit number 1 on Product Hunt with 350+ upvotes. Followers went from 100 to 200.
- His lesson: "The 2 ideas I thought of the least, MultiNewTab and GitGardener, have been my most successful ones." The big ideas (City Vibes, TalentShare, RemoteJuniorClub) went nowhere.
- Formula that worked: "Low expectations. Fast feedback loop. Building in the open." He committed to building and launching 1 product a week and sharing the behind-the-scenes.
- He did not try to monetize MakerFeed because he could not imagine people paying for it.

chunks.heading: Making the first dollar: a user request turned into a paid tier
chunks.text:
- A Twitter user asked if GitGardener could work with private repositories, so the green graph shows without exposing the automated commits.
- Alex built it as a premium feature at $5/month. No one paid in the first 24 hours, so he forgot about it, then GitGardener went from $0 to $50/month in a week, all from free users upgrading.
- A GitHub engineer encouraged him to apply to the GitHub Marketplace. He expected GitHub staff to hate a hack, but they found it funny. He was not accepted.
- Later, GitHub was acquired by Microsoft and made private repos free, which widened the audience for his private-repo plan. With an extra $10/month tier and doubled prices, GitGardener reached $130/month.
- He aimed for more website visitors because he got one paying customer per 300 visitors.

chunks.heading: Telemonetize: two months of building, a viral launch, and the wrong customers
chunks.text:
- Idea: connect a Telegram channel plus Stripe, get an automatic dashboard and landing page, and have members added or removed automatically as they subscribe or cancel.
- It took two months of full-time coding and was "way too complex": Telegram bots, payments, a website builder, webhooks and automations were each full projects.
- The launch went "viral" with hundreds of thousands of impressions, front page on Product Hunt with 300+ upvotes and a 300-like tweet. It reached the wrong people: zero customers and zero free trials after a week.
- His takeaway: "even a fake landing page with a 'buy now' button could have done the same job."
- Crypto channels told him they would subscribe if he supported crypto payments. He built his own crypto payment gateway and they never subscribed.
- Trial users were mostly scammers, betting gurus, someone selling prostitutes, an apparent arms dealer, and an amateur porn performer. They were needy, rude, stingy, used burner cards and asked for extra trial time.
- He ended with 1 customer at $29/month (later 2 customers, $58/month), then killed it as "serving scammers".
- Peer validation helped: Pieter Levels called his turnaround from seeing demand to building what people need "10/10".

chunks.heading: Epilepsy Blocker: a hard build, the wrong audience, and a B2B detour
chunks.text:
- Idea came from a NYT article about a journalist sent to hospital by a flashing GIF. He found no existing solution and built a browser extension that scans pages and hides content that could trigger photosensitive seizures, using linear algebra, histograms, Python and optimized C, plus scientific papers and broadcast telecom guidelines.
- He added a $10/month price only because his server crashed under even one user. It got 1 paying customer on day one from a Reddit post that was removed within 2 hours, after which he was banned.
- A tweet with 600+ likes and 100,000 views brought designers and engineers at big tech companies, not customers. Facebook groups also gave zero customers. "Vanity metrics" and "the wrong audience, again."
- Selling to individuals hurt: many people with epilepsy have other conditions or rely on benefits, $10/month was too much, and he kept giving it away free. A blunt "not interested" reply hurt more than he expected. He stopped "chasing $10 checks" and tried B2B.
- Setting a north star metric per product: GitGardener got more visitors, Telemonetize got retention through user conversations, and Epilepsy Blocker got visibility plus a B2B version.

chunks.heading: Going B2B: non-profits, clinics and TV channels
chunks.text:
- An MIT startup founder in the epilepsy space found Epilepsy Blocker and offered Alex a job (offices in Boston, Seoul and Milan, work with MIT, Johns Hopkins and NASA). He accepted to start at the end of the year as a "Plan B" while still hoping to hit his goal first.
- Non-profits would not promote a for-profit product. Neurology clinics and doctors were friendly but nothing came of it, and they told him innovation of this kind was hard in Greece.
- TV route: a new Greek law would require warnings before dangerous content, starting Sept 1. He called the ministry, reached the responsible lawyer and confirmed it was real. He was surprised at "how easy you can reach and contact people at the top with a little persistence and an open mind".
- He got a CTO meeting via his accelerator coach, who called an ex-CTO, who then called the current CTO in front of him. He wanted to close the deal before building, and noted industry pricing of about $350 to analyze one video file.
- The CTO laughed: the law had been discussed for 5 years and would not take effect for another 5. Years later he still has not seen the warnings on TV.
- After an anonymous user said "You just do anything for money", he made Epilepsy Blocker free, killed Telemonetize and shelved GitGardener.

chunks.heading: Second-half spiral and what he learned from researching markets
chunks.text:
- Doubting himself ("If you start thinking, you lose", a lesson from Muay Thai) left him swinging between the shotgun and sniper strategies with no conviction.
- He went back to fast launches that produced $0: Orthios (chatbot uptime monitoring), LocalTweetTime, IndieChannels (a distribution channels directory with 500+ upvotes, "but that doesn't mean anything, this isn't a business"), Epilepsy Blocker for Designers, DuckDuckGoSometimes, and Splash Search.
- Splash Search got about 250-300 installs and was copied into Unsplash's own product, indirectly reaching millions, but it earned nothing. Designer version: he asked on Reddit first, got lots of feedback, built it in 2 weeks, got hundreds of downloads, but no one paid.
- Market research: he cold emailed cybersecurity professionals asking for advice, not pitching, and offered to pay. About one Zoom call a day, all friendly, no one took money. He learned pain points but "can see the tree. But I can't see the forest."
- Accessibility market was the opposite: few replies, one asked for $150/hour, others would not help a for-profit product. His conclusion: pick a good market.
- He admits he is good at building and bad at marketing, and that he kept making the same mistakes.

chunks.heading: Two-year results and key numbers
chunks.text:
- Year 1: $55/month, 8 products launched, 2 profitable. First 6 months "felt like a dream", last 6 "like a slug".
- Year 2: peaked at $198 to $200/month (GitGardener $130, Telemonetize $58, Epilepsy Blocker $10), then fell to $100/month after shutting products down. 7 products launched, 1 profitable. No paycheck from a company in two years.
- Later in his life, per his preface: he became self employed at 25, hit a $1M net worth at 27, made his first million at 29, and scaled down at 30 after burning out. He states plainly this is "not a playbook" and that luck is a real factor.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex recounts how, after two years of failed launches, he took a day job, flipped his plan to a boring validated B2B idea, killed "pretend work," launched fast on Product Hunt, then found Twitter as a repeatable channel. Core lessons: go market-first, ship before building, focus on one product plus one channel.

chunks.heading: From zero to $2,000/month: the sequence that worked (and the two years of "pretend work" before it)
chunks.text:
Alex's core claim is that CyberLeads took "two weeks of true work" to reach $290/month. That came after two years of pretend work that built the skills to do those two weeks well. He lists those skills as: recognizing a good idea, recognizing a good distribution channel, killing perfectionism, launching fast, and knowing which idea suits his skills and resources.

- Month 0: no idea. He launched in February, on Valentine's Day, with ten paying customers at $29/month, which was $290/month.
- The first list shipped March 1st.
- April 21st: a tweet went viral and distribution kicked in.
- 4 months old: $1.5k/month.
- 6 months old: $2k/month.

His takeaway: things get easier once you find the product/channel/system combination, and you only need to find it once.

chunks.heading: Plan: non-unique, B2B, no-code, expensive
chunks.text:
After a month at a day job, Alex rebuilt his strategy. His final plan was: "build a non romantic, non unique, B2B product, build it without writing code, charge a lot of money for it, and whatever happens, give 10% of its profits to charities."

- He stopped chasing unique, world-improving ideas. Epilepsy Blocker's market was small: about 1% of people have epilepsy and only about 5% of those have photosensitive epilepsy.
- He noticed his incentives were warping. He caught himself hoping a cure wouldn't be found. His conclusion was that a business should fund his passions, not be them.
- For two years, every customer he had was an individual paying about $10/month. Meanwhile his employer spent hundreds of dollars a day on salad bowls for lunch, so he moved to B2B.
- He fell out of love with coding after eight hours a day and realized he loved creating, which can be done without code.
- He targets "humble" $5k to $25k/month solo businesses in large B2B markets where many players can coexist.

chunks.heading: Why competing with companies isn't scary
chunks.text:
From working inside a company, Alex drew four lessons:

- **People:** a 50-person company is really "5 motivated people and 45 yes-men". Employees care about their own lives first, and he promised never to expect hires to care like a founder.
- **Speed:** employees try to minimize work: tickets, handoffs, meetings, QA, regulatory review. "You can pivot 180 degrees in one day. Large companies have to hold meetings to change the color of a single button."
- **Budgets:** companies spend freely on small things, which makes them better customers than individuals.
- **Ugliness:** a life-saving product brings refunds, bug reports and fear of downtime. "You have more responsibility. And when you charge money to cover your costs, they hate you even more."

chunks.heading: Finding the idea: market first, already validated
chunks.text:
Alex stopped inventing solutions and went idea hunting in markets that were healthy and not winner-take-all. He picked cyber security, recruiting and lead generation, and he favored audiences he could reach on Twitter and Product Hunt (tech people and startups).

- **Cyberflake** (pen-tester collaboration tool): too technical, wrong market for him.
- **Scrapcat** (uptime monitor for scrapers): landing page and Reddit mockup got no real interest.
- **Cyberhound** (developers to reach out to): no response from a landing page, Twitter, Reddit or cold emails.
- **Birdleads** (Twitter keyword alerts): skipped because it required code.

CyberLeads came from a Reddit post listing recently funded startups. He found at least 10 businesses already selling this information as a service, database, list, newsletter or intelligence platform, to investors, salespeople, journalists, job seekers and tech followers. For the first time he treated an existing competitor as validation instead of "bus seats" ("Oops. This is taken!"). His own day job helped him see why funded startups buy: they have money and scaling problems.

chunks.heading: Launch with no product: sell first, build the list after
chunks.text:
Alex chose a monthly newsletter format because it lowers signup friction and needs no code. The offer was company, funding and contact data for hundreds of newly funded startups, delivered on the 1st of each month.

- He built the site in a no-code tool and launched on Product Hunt, which none of the competitors had used.
- He had no list yet. He built the first one after launch, in two weeks, waking at 04:00 to work until 09:00, then working again 19:00 to 22:00. "I was building my parachute while falling."
- He says he would never have worked that hard without paying customers waiting, and that building the list first would have taken months and changed the product.
- Even mockups, soft launches, Reddit posts and cold emails had started to feel like pretend work. His rule: "Just launch already."
- The monthly list still takes 50 to 100 hours to compile, even with automation.
- He later narrowed positioning to agencies.

chunks.heading: Finding the distribution channel
chunks.text:
After launch he had no repeatable acquisition. He tried Facebook Groups, LinkedIn, Reddit, cold outreach, Hacker News, direct sales and Twitter for almost two months while revenue fell back to $100/month. The lead-gen market has high churn: buyers blast a cold email template, get no results and cancel, so "you have to keep rowing".

- He had a habit of tweeting daily. On April 21st, with about 600 followers, he tweeted "Got my first $50/mo customer!" and went to bed. It reached about 100,000 impressions and 2,000 likes, and brought 10 paying customers.
- The next week he posted a monthly update that someone shared to the top of Hacker News. It brought another 10 customers.
- He was not promoting or selling: "I was sharing my personal journey, lessons and milestones." His view: "The best marketing is no marketing. No one wants to be sold anything."

chunks.heading: Focus, the failed detour, and artist-to-athlete
chunks.text:
In March he spent nearly the whole month on a second product, a monthly list of actively investing investors for startups raising money. It got zero customers despite more effort than CyberLeads, and he took it as a lesson in humility: "You have a gift in your hands... Double down and show it the attention it deserves."

- After the viral week he resisted using other channels and new products and focused only on CyberLeads and Twitter: "Less is more."
- Before the system exists you must be an artist: creative, trying different things daily. After it exists you must be an athlete: disciplined, doing the same things every day.
- His routine became 2 hours of marketing in the morning and 2 hours on the lists in the evening.

chunks.heading: Work habits and filters against "pretend work"
chunks.text:
- **Mornings:** evening sessions failed because the gym and day job used up his creative capacity. He moved to 05:00 to 08:00 work, then the gym until 09:00, then the office by 10:00. The limit helped: "These constraints set me free."
- **Pretend work:** restructuring code with zero users, A/B tests at 300 visitors/month, redesigning a page that converts fine, business cards and email, features no one requested, speeding up the site.
- **True work:** emailing 10 potential customers for feedback, posting in FB groups, Twitter and Reddit, a landing page with signup and a soft launch, asking local businesses for feedback and payment, launching on Product Hunt.
- **Gun test:** "You have to generate revenue online by the end of the week. If you don't, you're dead." Today he asks the same about CyberLeads growing by month end.
- **Lessons from five launches:** the .com domain, the logo, extra features and upvotes from the wrong audience didn't matter, and faster launching is better. All he needed was a landing page and a payment button.
- **Habit tracker:** he marks daily habits green or red in a notebook.

chunks.heading: Shotgun vs sniper
chunks.text:
Alex reviewed hundreds of business podcast episodes by observing what founders did rather than what they said. The pattern: they built stuff, launched without overthinking, got some traction, then kept going.

- His first year: 12 products and almost $200/month.
- His second year: only Epilepsy Blocker, which didn't work.
- His conclusion: the answer is in the middle. Persistence is needed, but you need initial traction to know it's worth it.
- On ideas, he quotes: "It's very difficult to become a 10 times better executioner of ideas, but it's easy to have a 10 times better idea." The right idea is one you can build, run and get in front of customers repeatedly at a good cost.
- He is clear that luck mattered, and that imitators who copied his steps quit within weeks. His line: "If you show up every day for two years, one day you'll get lucky."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West explains how clones and copycats threatened CyberLeads, and how he escaped them by analyzing paying customers, niching down to agencies, adding social proof, tripling prices and building one tiny feature. He also covers annual plans, focusing on marketing, and managing stress as the business grew past his salary.

chunks.heading: Pricing and positioning: niche down, raise prices, and let conversions rise
chunks.text:
Alex launched CyberLeads (a hand-compiled monthly list of fast-growing startups) with a generic pitch: "Find fast growing startups to do business with." He cast a wide net on purpose, because he didn't know who would subscribe and didn't want to assume. He notes you "can catch bigger fish with a speargun" (higher prices, easier conversions), but it's also easier to miss, so he advises starting generic and niching down later.

When competitors and "how are you different to X/Y/Z?" questions appeared, he niched down and raised prices:
- He changed the homepage tagline from "Find fast growing startups to do business with" to "Find new clients for your digital agency."
- He added testimonials from agencies that closed deals ($50k, $25k, $10k) and redesigned the landing page. His customers had collectively made more than he had from CyberLeads.
- Prices went from $29/month to $49/month to $99/month. "Conversions kept going up at the same time."
- After this, questions like "how are you different, and why are you more expensive?" dropped to zero.

He adds that there are no universal rules: staying generic or being the cheapest could be right in some cases. "The only rule is that there are no rules. It's about trying and seeing for yourself." Worst case, you revert.

chunks.heading: Choosing a niche from customer behavior, not surveys
chunks.text:
After a few months, his customers were a mix of SaaS companies, freelancers, consultants, agencies, journalists, investors and solopreneurs. He found surveys not very useful ("I had been burned many times asking for peoples' opinion") and observed behavior instead: who pays the most and stays the longest.

Agencies won every category:
- Largest customer segment
- Willing to pay the most
- Stayed the longest
- Best results (one closed a $50k deal)
- Busy founders who never bothered him

He connected this to a podcast idea: sell to someone's number one pain point, not number two or three, which moves a product from "nice to have" to "must have" and makes paying easy. A poll showed finding new clients is agencies' number one pain point; SaaS companies and others didn't share it.

He had hoped freelancers and consultants would win, since one client could transform their lives, but they didn't want it enough to pay agency prices. Lesson from past projects: people with epilepsy wouldn't pay $10/month for Epilepsy Blocker even though he felt they needed it, while people found and paid $10/month for GitGardener on their own. "Maybe it's not about who 'needs' your product, after all. Maybe it's about who 'wants' your product."

chunks.heading: One small niche feature beats big differentiation
chunks.text:
Months after the tagline change and price increases, the only differences from competitors were homepage copy and testimonials. Then he added a single feature for agencies: an extra column in the monthly list called "Likely to outsource to agencies" with values like "Design", "Development", "Marketing". He filled it in manually, one startup at a time, and made it obvious on the homepage. People loved it.

His takeaway on competition:
- You don't need to be crazy different at first. Tweak the copy, niche down, maybe build one feature.
- Most customers weren't comparing him to competitors; many didn't know they existed. His real competition was "their time, boredom and a spreadsheet."
- Competitors copied his site word for word, resold his lists at a third of the price, gave similar lists away free, ran ads against his name and leaked lists on Reddit. He still grew.
- His rule: "When competing, ignore everyone and focus only on yourself." He later muted copycats instead of spying on them.
- He argues sharing everything (including revenue) creates copycats, but the internet is usually big enough for another player and sharing grows you faster.

chunks.heading: Boutique positioning: turning weaknesses into strengths
chunks.text:
In week one, at $300/month, a prospect asked for a phone call before committing to the $29/month plan. Alex was nervous because the lists were compiled by hand with no team, AI or systems. He recalled a talk saying to run an online business like a boutique, not a supermarket: few customers, high prices, exceptional service. He flipped it and owned it, pitching: exclusive, brand new leads, verified and handpicked one by one by a human, not outdated robot-collected lists thousands of companies spam.

The prospect said it sounded "too good to be true for $29/month" and subscribed. Alex's realization: low price can signal low quality, and to be a boutique he needed boutique prices.

He reframed his perceived weaknesses:
- A simple newsletter is better for some people than a bloated platform, and takes 10 seconds to set up.
- Not being a big company means leads are exclusive and convert better.
- Hand collection means leads are up to date and manually verified, "something no other platform can promise."
- Being a one-person team is a superpower for connecting with customers, especially other founders. "Don't pretend to be a company."

chunks.heading: Revenue focus: annual plans and a lifetime deal
chunks.text:
Alex realized monthly recurring revenue was "a mirage": subscribers stay a few months, then cancel, unlike a salary. So he focused on revenue per customer.

His math: customers paid $49 or $99/month and stayed 2-4 months, so about $150 per customer on average. He added an annual plan at $299/year, which roughly doubles revenue per customer, collects it upfront, and feels like a steal to buyers. It was very popular.

Results: he passed his salary (about $2k/month at his day job), reaching around $3k/month from CyberLeads on top of $2k/month from the job.

Black Friday affiliate deal:
- A Twitter friend, Dru, was preparing deals for his community of 30,000+ founders. Alex pitched featuring CyberLeads and he agreed.
- Worried a discount would be "off brand" for an exclusive, expensive product, he offered a single $1k payment for lifetime access to the lists: still expensive, still a good deal.
- Dru took 30%.
- Result: more than 10 lifetime customers across November and December, over $10k revenue, and double his salary in profit in both months. Once he woke up to 2 lifetime customers overnight.

chunks.heading: Marketing focus, one channel, one or two metrics
chunks.text:
Alex observed that competitors didn't quit because of a bad product but because of bad marketing, and he decided to put his limited time there:
- "No pretend work. No new features. No new marketing channels." Just post on Twitter, focus on revenue, ignore other metrics ("athlete mode").
- Twitter was volatile but consistent: some days zero traffic, other days viral with thousands of visitors and many customers.

His related principles:
- Prioritize marketing over product: most startups die from lack of traction, not lack of product-market fit.
- Stick to one distribution channel; better to be great at one than average everywhere.
- Track one or two metrics rather than turning all the screws a little.
- Eliminate "pretend work": two hours on the right things beats twelve on the wrong ones.
- Volatile systems that consistently work beat stable systems that are dead.
- Don't be a perfectionist when building; it won't matter to users.
- After finding success, double down on what you have instead of launching new things.
- Share ideas early; people won't steal them and feedback improves them.
- Niching lets you be the best in a segment and take advantage of power laws.
- Exposure beats prediction: "It has been easier to become ten times luckier by increasing my exposure to the world and shots on target, than it has been to become ten times better at understanding and predicting the world."

chunks.heading: Handling the pressure of fast growth
chunks.text:
Going viral brought severe anxiety at first. Alex got personally attacked on Hacker News for running a lead generation business (and for GitGardener), and refreshed the thread all night. Days later the crowd had moved on to attacking another company. His conclusion: "I may be the hero of my own movie, but in everyone else's I am nothing but an extra." That freed him to fail publicly and double down.

His coping habits:
- Control inputs, not outcomes: he cites Epictetus's Enchiridion (some things are up to you, others aren't). He can't make someone subscribe or a competitor quit, but can focus on inputs.
- Daily exercise (especially running) as a deliberate dose of stress that makes the rest of life feel easier.
- Comfort zones expand: the first viral moment cost him sleep, but after three in a row he "slept like a baby." Podcast interviews went from a one-hour pre-run to a friendly chat.
- Reframe fear as excitement, a trick from fighting: the pre-fight heart racing and dry mouth feel like excitement once warmed up, so say "I'm so excited" like you mean it.
- Nuance only comes from real-world trials, not books or practice. He learned this in fighting: after moving from a technique-only gym to a hard-sparring one, beginners with real-world reps beat him. Progress is slow, then arrives in breakthroughs.

He ends the book about to quit his job and go full time on CyberLeads, estimating the market could support $1M/year and that "I am the actual ceiling of my business."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West explains why he left his job to go full time on CyberLeads, his 20th product, after earning more than his salary six months in a row. He covers his risk framework, how he built a two-year runway first, and why he distrusts corporate complexity.

chunks.heading: Quitting the day job at $4,000/month: why Alex left, with $50k runway and CyberLeads outearning his salary
chunks.text:
- **Where he stood.** CyberLeads was Alex's 20th product; the first 19 failed. After about a year of CyberLeads, it had paid more than his salary six months in a row, some months double.
- **Journey recap.** Year 1: 10+ products, up to $100/month. Year 2: focused on one product, up to $200/month, not enough, so he took a full-time job. Year 3: launched CyberLeads while employed and passed his salary. Year 4: quit.
- **Core framing.** He had a cool job (MIT startup, NASA work, life-saving medical devices, good pay) and says "it was just another job."

chunks.heading: Decision rule: quit when the numbers are consistent, not when the business is ideal
chunks.text:
- Alex lists what he dislikes about CyberLeads:
  - Twitter is the main channel, which is unstable.
  - High-churn market; customers don't stick around.
  - Revenue is wild and fluctuates, unlike a salary.
  - Growth is not smooth.
  - People compete with him constantly.
- His ideal is predictable systems, very low churn and Google-driven customers on autopilot, but "we don't live in a perfect world. I have to adjust my sails to the wind. Not try to change the weather."
- He says "I cannot argue with the numbers and the facts": the business had grown consistently despite being messy.
- On timing: he predicted that when the time is right, leaving "won't even be a dilemma anymore," and that is how it felt. Staying another year to save an extra $10-20k "will change nothing. It will probably just keep me back." Sometimes you "say 'fuck it' and go for it."

chunks.heading: Risk framework: be conservative with ruinous risks, wild with capped-downside risks
chunks.text:
- Alex took this idea from a book. Two categories of risk:
  - **Ruinous risks** (large loan from criminals, robbing a bank, all your money on a new crypto coin): be super conservative. Take enough and you pay for it.
  - **Capped-downside, big-upside risks** (starting a business with zero capital, moving countries, a new hobby, going to a party, tweeting): be wild, experimental, playful. Take enough and you get "blessed with luck."
- His tweeting example: best case you get customers, an audience and friends; worst case "there is none!"
- He asks which category quitting falls into, then answers by engineering the downside (next section).

chunks.heading: Stacking the odds: runway math before quitting
chunks.text:
- He did not leave the moment he could. He stayed to honor his contract and keep saving.
- Savings of almost $50k:
  - $10k from his Greek grandfather
  - $10k from the day job
  - $30k from CyberLeads
- That equals about 2 years of runway even if revenue dropped to $0 the next day.
- Outcomes he weighed:
  - Success: freedom, scaling CyberLeads, travel, more savings.
  - CyberLeads goes to zero: two years to figure things out.
  - Fail completely: find another job and try again, "with a cool story to tell."
- His verdict: "That's a good bet. I'll take it."

chunks.heading: Why a day job stops being worth it once the side project works
chunks.text:
- **Dream jobs don't exist.** He feared the job would be so good he'd forget his side projects; it turned out to be just another job.
- **He fell out of love with engineering.** He realized he loved creating, not coding, and software was just his tool. Eight hours a day of code made him sick of it, which is why much of CyberLeads is built without code. He enjoyed product talk (competition, positioning, features to add or remove, funding, pivots) over scalability, legacy code and sharding.
- **The learning curve flattened in 2-3 months.** What he took away was intangible:
  - Companies are slow, so competing with them isn't scary.
  - Priorities flipped: change your own world first (make money, escape the rat race), then worry about changing others'.
  - You don't need to work all day; he worked about two hours a day and made them count.
- **He was spinning his wheels.** Focusing on the job slowed CyberLeads' growth, and focusing on CyberLeads dipped his job performance. "It was impossible to do great work, at both, at the same time."
- **The "can't unsee it" moment.** When CyberLeads revenue passed his salary he posted it online, the post blew up and revenue grew further. A commenter told him: "You'll never be able to go back now. It's one of those things that once you see it, you can never unsee it again." After that, every meeting and review felt different. When his manager suggested he become "the respected, go-to guy for the 'X company dashboard'," he saw the contrast clearly.

chunks.heading: Quitting for clarity of mind, not for more hours
chunks.text:
- His main reason was to stop thinking about irrelevant things (meetings, sprint deadlines, what his manager thinks).
- He does not plan to work ten hours a day on CyberLeads. He recalls working 10 hours a day on the wrong things in Greece and going nowhere, versus 2 hours a day on the right things in his job year, which changed his life.
- "I don't want more time. I want clarity of mind to make sure that I'm rowing in the right direction."
- He also wanted a big change, like moving from Greece to Italy a year earlier. Small habits matter, but "sometimes you are not looking for a small incremental change, but for a big earthquake that will shake your foundations," and that is when you have the best chance of exponential growth. He compares it to conquistadors burning their ships.

chunks.heading: The exit: how the notice period went and the lessons from it
chunks.text:
- **Notice.** He gave 1 month's notice (4 weeks left) by not renewing his contract at the start of the new year. Legally he could have given none, but wanted a clear conscience.
- **After notice.** Meetings felt meaningless. He used them to work on CyberLeads or to write; the book itself was written during those meetings. His daily updates shrank back to one sentence, while teammates gave jargon-heavy updates. His take: the complexity is by design, to justify salaries and positions and look like "a genius at work."
- **The dark side.** Had he joined a company before building products of his own, everything (engineers, designers, marketers, salespeople, a CTO, CEO, CFO, funding) might have seemed too complicated to start. He says that is a trap for first-time builders.
- **The firing.** His manager refused to extend him 3 more months, and then the company fired him 1 day before his last day, citing bad performance in his final 2 weeks. His accountant warned that being fired could cost him tax benefits for his new business.
- **The money.** Salary cuts from the pandemic were to be repaid at the start of the new year. The company did not want to pay him that money (about $1,500) as he left, and offered to avoid firing him only if he signed away the money. He accepted, reasoning it was "just a speeding ticket" and "not every fight is worth fighting."
- **Outcome.** A few months later the company paid him the owed amount without explanation. His guess: fear of being called out on Twitter, a change of mind, or an accident.

chunks.heading: What came next
chunks.text:
- To-do list after quitting: incorporate the business, move to a different city, design a new lifestyle.
- He had no idea if CyberLeads would keep growing or how he would handle "the weight of having zero constraints," but says he had "never been more excited."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West recounts his first year self-employed running CyberLeads at about $5K/month take-home. He covers take-home math, diversification as insurance (two is enough), a months-long programmatic SEO bet undermined by bot data, and trading small spending for happiness and memorable time.

chunks.heading: Freedom from his job was the happiest day, but stress changed shape rather than shrinking
chunks.text:
- Alex quit his job at 25 and calls the last day "one of the happiest days of my life". He promised himself he would never work in an office again: "I don't care about material success. Or becoming a millionaire. All I want is to be free."
- He rejects the idea that employment means less stress and self-employment more. In his experience the stress is different: employed stress is chronic, predictable and constant (meetings, deadlines, reviews). Self-employed stress is acute and swings wildly, for example when a new competitor appears, then weeks of cruising.
- He argues the swings make him feel more alert and alive, like wild lions versus zoo lions, which are bored and waiting to be fed.
- He says having already built projects and earned revenue before leaving a job kept him from believing that a business needs a full team of designers, marketers, developers, advisors and investors.
- After going full time, his resting heart rate dropped by 5 beats per minute within a few weeks.

chunks.heading: Founder take-home is what matters, not revenue
chunks.text:
- When registering as self-employed in Italy, Alex learned that income tax is one of many taxes: social contributions, regional taxes, corporate taxes, VAT and capital gains. Even with a 90% income tax exemption as an expat, a paper simulation left him taking home 70% to 75% of revenue, with zero employees and almost no expenses.
- He turned this into a viral post: a $10K/month solo business at 90% margin means the founder takes home $9K per month. A $1M/year business with two co-founders and a 25% margin means about $10K per month each. "Yet they call the first a side project and the second a business."
- Critics said the second can scale, be sold, or work without the founder, but "they couldn't argue with the math."
- His simulations of million-dollar Western companies with co-founders and employees showed take-home of $5k to $10k per month is considered great, often as salary, with the rest reinvested.
- He concluded he was already successful at 25, taking home about $5k per month, with an alarm-free, self-scheduled life.

chunks.heading: Lessons from nearly losing his money: avoid catastrophic mistakes
chunks.text:
- Alex moved more than $40k of his roughly $50k into one bank account in a single transfer. The bank flagged it, demanded proof, gave no usable customer support, rejected his paperwork twice without explanation, and froze the account. Forum posts described people losing access for months. He sent corrected paperwork a third time and it was approved about 11 at night.
- He says he knew not to keep all his money in one account or send it in one go, just as he knew to launch fast and charge from day one but only did so after 2 years and 19 failed attempts. "It seems like I learn mostly by making mistakes."
- His fixes:
  - Split money across multiple bank accounts in multiple countries, and move money in several smaller transactions.
  - Rewrite CyberLeads in code, because his no-code tools kept breaking and going out of business.
  - Move from a merchant of record to a payment provider, accepting the invoicing and accounting work, because he had seen people lose accounts and subscribers.
  - Build a second distribution channel, since over 90% of customers came from Twitter.
- His principle: accept that mistakes are inevitable but avoid the catastrophic, avoidable ones. He quotes a film line: the biggest fish in the river gets there "By not getting caught."

chunks.heading: Diversification: two is enough
chunks.text:
- Alex treats diversification as insurance, to survive long enough to recover or build a replacement, not as a goal of having many options.
- His math: if each of two independent channels has a 10% chance of failing, the chance both fail is 10% x 10% = 1%.
- He says this "theoretical 99% safety is good enough for me" and anything beyond is paranoia. Target: two bank accounts and two marketing channels.
- He applies the same logic to banks, businesses and any other risk. (He jokes about "two girlfriends" too.)

chunks.heading: Building programmatic SEO as a second channel to replace daily posting
chunks.text:
- Six months after going full time, CyberLeads revenue was up only $1k/month, despite all the extra time.
- He disliked having to post on Twitter every day and wanted a channel not dependent on daily motivation. He framed the progression as hunting with a spear (direct sales), fishing with a net (Twitter), planting seeds (SEO).
- The strategy: use code and automation to create pages for the 25,000 funded startups in his database, such as contact information, founder information and tech stack pages for each company. Searchers land on the page, see the data but with the email hidden, and must sign up and pay to unlock it. He notes most competitors do this.
- Problems he hit:
  - Near-identical pages were treated as duplicates, so he added unique info per company.
  - Much of the early traffic was bots from a few locations.
  - Pages ranked but got no clicks until he changed titles.
  - Titles too similar to competitors failed to stand out, while distinct titles missed the right keywords.
- He ran a data-driven phase: 25 title variations (one per 1,000 companies), then split tests on showing or hiding data points, mobile layout, buttons, testimonials, FAQs, metadata, navbars versus dropdowns, popups versus buttons, company pages versus list pages, pricing and CTAs.

chunks.heading: When data-driven optimization misleads: bots, bad data and talking to humans
chunks.text:
- Session recordings showed that most of his "users" were bots, so months of split-test decisions were based on bot clicks. A test of two identical pages still produced a clear winner.
- While correcting a data point, he found that competitor databases all had the same mistake. They pull from the same sources and repackage them, whatever proprietary process they claim. "Maybe the giants are blind too," so he questioned copying their marketing.
- He admitted he would not pay for his own company pages: "This sucks, it's clickbait, and it's annoying." His reset: "Back to old school. Let's talk to humans. And use common sense."
- Tactics: collect emails, send surveys, add a chat box so visitors can message him directly.
- Real-world problems:
  - Most collected emails were garbage, so he built a custom email validator.
  - Survey dropdowns were skewed: options B and C were always most popular regardless of shuffling. He will only use text fields from now on.
  - Chat messages came from people who thought he was the company's support (for example the Amazon contact page), founders threatening to sue unless their data was removed (he removed all founder pages), and people wanting their phone or address updated.
- Result: about a month later he got 3 paying customers from Google company pages, confirmed by asking them, roughly matching Twitter's traffic. Google needs no daily effort, unlike Twitter. He says early customers always feel like flukes, as Twitter once did, and that "having patience and expecting non linear results is key."

chunks.heading: Spending on quality of life: the $500 versus $1,000 housing decision
chunks.text:
- In Palermo, Alex first tried to "be a cockroach": spend as little as possible and take the cheapest Airbnb, a tiny dark studio. He hated it and was depressed, which made him question whether his income depends on his mental state now that he has no fixed salary.
- His reasoning: a $1,000/month house versus a $500/month one is double in percentage terms but only $500 in absolute terms, or 3 CyberLeads subscribers. The question is whether a better house makes him productive and happy enough to make up those 3 subscribers.
- He decided yes and rented the apartment he loved, near a clean beach in a safe area. He stopped checking grocery prices, started taking trips and days off, and stopped feeling guilty about taxis. He calls it the wisest move he made, while noting he would be writing the opposite had it gone badly.
- The motivation was his grandfather, who worked 50 years at a London printing plant and died of lung cancer under a year after retiring: "Worked from the age of 15. For a retirement that never came." Alex no longer postpones happiness.

chunks.heading: Designing a timeless life: trade-offs, memory and the Athens test
chunks.text:
- Time accelerates when life is routine. Alex says a routine in a nice place feels enjoyable in the moment but short in hindsight, and that new experiences and travel (for example a 2-day hike up Olympus, a 5-day Sicily road trip) create lasting memories. Doing so means breaking his flow, which he finds painful because he loves his work.
