- He found he can do anything but not everything: when he focused on training, his Italian stalled; on dating and trips, training and diet slipped; on everything at once, he ignored CyberLeads. His projects that year included a marathon the year before, a triathlon, Brazilian Jiu Jitsu, learning Italian via the 1,000 most common words, and a diet toward a six pack.
- He argues that things tied to our biology are timeless, since technology and society change faster than biology, like gold jewelry that looks new after 3,000 years while stone and bronze decayed.
- His thought experiment: in ancient Athens, would you swap with a wealthy elite with carts, gold, slaves and dynasty plans, or with a healthy, free trader with a strong family, friends, travel, deep conversations and art? Alex envies the trader.
- His heuristic: live a life that would be enviable in ancient Rome, modern New York and futuristic Shanghai.
- His conclusion: his business growth was modest, but his quality of life grew enormously, "And maybe that's enough."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West recounts a year of failed growth experiments (a database SaaS, Google SEO, upsells, affiliates, lead magnets, a podcast) before a customer question led him to sell a done-for-you email service. He closed three clients in a week, reframing scaling, service vs. software, and perfectionism.

chunks.heading: Replacing the "second channel" idea with a service-first model at $6k/month (year 4)
chunks.text:
Alex had spent a year treating Google as the safe second channel for CyberLeads and got almost nothing from it. By the end of year 4 he reached about $6,000/month, with most of the jump coming from a service he sold in a week.

He argues the lever he needed was hiding in his own customer data. His cancellation form kept saying the same thing: customers had no time to set up and send the outreach emails.

chunks.heading: Why the Google and database bets failed
chunks.text:
- Alex spent roughly 12 months on Google. Result: "1 million impressions and tens of thousands of visitors" and only 5 customers.
- He notes that "sometimes I get 5 customers from one good tweet."
- Since quitting his job he had grown only about $1k/month. He thinks the same growth was reachable with "10 minutes per day to schedule a tweet."
- He calls the Google work "pretend work" and says his perfectionism disguised it as responsible risk reduction ("eliminating my final single point of failure").
- He also tried turning CyberLeads into a database SaaS. It took a month to build and ran for 2 weeks. The one customer who showed up wanted the newsletter's startup funding updates, hit a bug, and demanded a refund. Alex killed the database and concluded: "I'm so lucky to be running a newsletter."

chunks.heading: The shotgun approach: low-expectation experiments
chunks.text:
Alex ran many experiments fast, with no attachment to any of them. Results:

- **Upsells:** A customer dashboard, older lists for purchase, annual-plan upgrades, custom lists (location, industry, funding stage) and a retention flow with bundles and discounts. No one bought lists or upgraded. Custom lists produced 1 sale in months. The cancellation flow didn't work either.
- **Affiliates:** Self-signup program with a 50/50 split. More than 100 partners signed up, only 4 brought customers, and only 1 brought more than 3. The emails, questions and manual monthly commission payouts were painful, so he killed it.
- **Lead magnets:** Free lists on Reddit and Twitter. Hundreds accessed them, almost no one bought. He calls it "a reverse filter" that attracted beginner freelancers with "a million questions, feedback and critiques. But no money."
- **Podcast:** Interviewing agency founders was easy to book but he disliked scheduling and prep and felt "like a radio host."
- **Going broad again:** He tested dropping the agency niche to triple his audience. Conversions "dropped to the floor," which confirmed the niche. He was relieved.

chunks.heading: Customer conversations turn up the lever
chunks.text:
- Asking customers how they find clients showed that most agencies get clients through referrals, including from other agencies that partner and pay each other commissions.
- Alex now makes intros between agencies in his network as part of the subscription, and is waiting to see if it works.
- The real find came from a call with Vic, a reader who had bootstrapped a software company to over $1M/year. Vic asked why customers unsubscribe, then asked: "Then why don't you send the emails for them?"
- Vic said he was paying a company $2k/month to send emails for his startup.
- Alex's first reaction was that he only wanted scalable work that doesn't trade time for money. The idea stuck anyway.

chunks.heading: Testing the service offer cheaply
chunks.text:
- Alex emailed his customers offering either a referral to an agency or sending the emails for them.
- 8 people replied. Usually a similar experiment gets about 1 reply "if I was lucky."
- One prospect wanted him specifically, citing years of following him, long customer tenure, email conversations, and a welcome gift he had sent. They trusted him.
- He quoted "a crazy price of $2k/month just to see what they would say." They accepted instantly.
- He closed two more clients at $1,500/month.
- Start dates were set for January (this was November), because clients didn't want to launch new marketing at year end.
- Pre-call, he rehearsed and paced. He treated impostor syndrome "like a compass": it meant he was pushing his limits.

chunks.heading: Redefining scale and software vs. service
chunks.text:
- It took 4 years to reach $5k/month with software products and about 1 week to reach $5k/month with the service.
- He had believed scaling meant laying foundations for future explosion and infinite customers. Now he defines it as "simply taking your revenue to the next level. Just one step": if you're at zero, make $1; at $1, reach $100/month; and so on.
- He doesn't need infinite scale because "$1M/year has always been and will be end game."
- He had thought he must pick a lane, product or service. He now sees the "messy hybrid model" as possibly the answer.
- He also concedes he'd been working all day on his "passive income" business anyway, so trading time for money wasn't much worse.
- He doubled the business with a few manual emails and calls.

chunks.heading: Decision rule for a move that goes against his instincts
chunks.text:
- Alex worried about running a service business, hiring, and being a boss (he disliked every boss he had). He asked everyone he trusts, and all gave the same answer: "Alex, just follow the fucking money."
- His framework was to imagine both outcomes. If it works, money worries are gone. Worst case: he hates the lifestyle, delivers no results, feels embarrassed, refunds everyone and goes back to the newsletter.
- Because there was a clear way out, he says he ran out of excuses.
- His personal rule, quoted from years earlier: "When in doubt, do the exact opposite of what you're doing."
- He still feared turning a perfect lifestyle business into "a monster."

chunks.heading: Perfectionism and reframing
chunks.text:
- Alex says perfectionism keeps reappearing in disguise, including as "responsible" strategy.
- A friend whose father had died once asked whether Alex's complicated relationship with his father might be "just perfect." Alex's takeaway: he sometimes complains about things that could already be perfect.
- Late in the year he planned to relocate the business to Cyprus, after earlier moves to Italy and Sicily timed around tax deadlines.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West recaps five years of bootstrapping, from a failed two-year product to CyberLeads and a $2k/month productized service. He distills a shotgun-then-sniper pattern with roughly a 5% hit rate, explains why he committed fully to the one thing that worked, and shows how he chose a simple low-tax setup in Cyprus.

chunks.heading: Alex's growth pattern: shotgun, then sniper
chunks.text:
Alex describes his five-year path as a repeating loop:

- Shotgun many experiments until a successful product appears.
- Sniper on that product until it plateaus.
- Shotgun again to find the next lever of growth.
- Sniper on that lever until it plateaus, and repeat.

He assumes a hit rate of around 5%:

- It took 20 product launches to find CyberLeads.
- It took 20 experiments within CyberLeads to find Twitter as a channel.
- It took 20 experiments within CyberLeads to find the productized service.

When looking for the CyberLeads idea, he went channel and market first, and picked an idea that already existed and was validated. He adds: "there are no recipes", this is what worked for him and others must find their own way.

chunks.heading: Alex's five-year trajectory: alternating stuck years and breakthrough years
chunks.text:
Alex recaps his path as success and failure in alternating years:

- Year 1 (university): spent a year building City Vibes and learned to code.
- Year 2: spent 12 months perfecting City Vibes before getting a first user. It made $0.
- Year 3: after discovering bootstrapping, built and launched many products fast. Made his first dollar and reached $100/month across 3 profitable products.
- Year 4: spent a full year trying to grow his favorite of those 3 products with every tactic, then gave up, took a full-time job and started from scratch.
- Year 5: launched products fast again and found CyberLeads. Launched with a landing page built over a weekend, hit $300/month, then $2k/month, and quit his job.
- Year 6: tried to grow CyberLeads with SEO and failed. Just before year end he launched a new offer with a single email to his email list and instantly reached $100k/year.
- Next: run the productized service and maybe reach $250k/year with CyberLeads.

He notices progress comes in roughly 2-year blocks, stuck one year and fast growth the next.

chunks.heading: Speed and price compounded together
chunks.text:
Alex shows that both his launch speed and his prices rose in 2-year steps:

- Speed: a product built over 2 years made $0. Two years later a product built and launched in 1 week made his first dollar. Two years after that, a landing page got to $300/month. Two years after that, an email launched a new offer that hit $100k/year.
- Price: with a free product, 4 new customers meant an extra $0/yr. With a $5/mo product, 4 customers meant an extra $240/year. With a $100/mo product, 4 customers meant roughly $5k/year. With a $2k/mo product, 4 customers means an extra $100k/year.

Takeaway: higher price points make each customer worth far more, so he needs far fewer sales to move revenue.

chunks.heading: Commit to the home run instead of chasing a second one
chunks.text:
After CyberLeads worked, Alex first imagined running multiple similar products at once, assuming a "Midas touch". A few failed launches ended that idea, and he dedicated his full attention to CyberLeads.

His baseball analogy: 19 swings missed, the 20th (CyberLeads) sent the ball high in the air. Instead of running, he got cocky and sat waiting to hit another perfect one. He snapped out of it and started running.

His views:

- He does not care whether success was luck or skill, or whether he could repeat it.
- He is fine being a "one trick pony" and running the same business for decades, with nothing to prove to others or himself.
- A home run is not the best possible outcome. CyberLeads is, in his words, the most boring product he has built, but it works, is growing, and should keep growing for years.
- His goals are simple: make a lot of money, save a lot, have time, and live well.

chunks.heading: Choosing where to base the company: simple beats clever
chunks.text:
Alex left Italy despite a 90% tax exemption:

- The exemption covered only one tax among many.
- Language barrier and bureaucracy were costly, for example Italian documents to sign and thousands of euros due by Monday.
- He would still pay almost half his money in taxes.
- He was legally required to stay 6 months a year.

How he compared setups:

- He read books, spoke to accountants and paid consultants.
- Most recommended multi-country structures, holding companies and flying in and out of countries.
- He ignored individual tax rates and benefits. His only metric was how much money ends up in his pocket at the end of the year at $100k, $250k and $500k profit, across options like self-employed, company, and taking everything out as dividends.
- He noticed experts pushed complicated setups that happened to be part of their expensive services. Setups promising zero percent tax turned out far more expensive and riskier.
- He had already been tricked once by the Italy exemption, so he chose caution.

His conclusion: all he needed was a simple business in a low-tax country.

chunks.heading: Why Alex chose Cyprus, and his final setup
chunks.text:
Cyprus did not sound clever or sophisticated, but it won in every category:

- Language: English and Greek are spoken, and he speaks Greek fluently, so he can tell an accountant, lawyer or landlord "No, this is what I want. I know how things are done here."
- EU membership means no visa hassle, and it is close to family in the UK and Greece.
- Tax: on $100,000 profit he keeps $85,000, versus about $50,000 in Italy. It is low enough that he does not need to chase zero.
- Lifestyle: safe, sunny, friendly people.
- Mobility: he only has to stay on the island 2 months a year.

Investing is equally simple: one year of cash in the bank, the rest in index funds (US market, S&P 500), and a little in crypto.

His final setup:

- Business and tax residence in Cyprus.
- Customers mostly in the US, EU and UK.
- Banks in Italy, Greece, Lithuania and Belgium.
- Broker in the Netherlands.
- Lives all over the world.

His next goal is building the new version of CyberLeads to move from thousands to tens of thousands of dollars per month.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex tells the story of launching a $2k/month outbound lead-gen service on top of CyberLeads. Early campaigns failed and clients churned, then he documented, automated and simplified his way to results and a viral My First Million mention, only to end up burned out in a "second cage". Lessons cover thinking for yourself, narrowing focus, and distrusting advice that sells a product.

chunks.heading: Selling a productized outbound service: first-client reality and how results actually came
chunks.text:
**The setup (year 5).** Alex launched a productized service on top of CyberLeads: he sends cold emails (and LinkedIn messages) on behalf of clients to help them close deals.
- Pricing: $2k/month, 3-month initial period.
- He signed 5 clients, then 10, because "I can't say no. I will figure this out."
- Early lessons: setup that should take 30 minutes per client turned into a full day. He picked the wrong tool for some clients and only found out after setting up everyone, wasting 2 weeks and hundreds of dollars.
- He works 3am to 8am sleep cycles at this stage.
- Taking risks on behalf of clients is a different kind of stress than selling a newsletter.

**What the first campaigns produced.**
- He followed books and guides on outbound to the letter. The first replies were all negative, sarcastic or rude.
- Failures: a client's friend got emailed and mocked him, one campaign went out with no subject line, someone threatened to sue a client, LinkedIn warned it would ban clients' accounts, and another client's emails were blacklisted.
- Zero positive replies for the first month, even though clients had paid thousands.
- Conclusion: "Following the experts was not working for me. So I decided to do the opposite and think for myself."

**The shotgun approach for clients.** Alex tested many variables and doubled down on whatever worked:
- Channels: LinkedIn, email, and combined flows.
- Openers: generic compliment, AI-generated specific compliment, or straight to the point.
- Subject lines: long, short, clickbait.
- Calls to action: ask for a call, or offer something free.
- Proof: a case study, name-dropping big clients, founder credibility, or nothing.
- Angles: save money, save time, make money.
- Targets: funded startups only vs. hotels, ecommerce and enterprise.
- Tone: long professional emails vs. very short LinkedIn messages joking about the weather.
- Also tested: send days and times, founder vs. CTO vs. marketing officer, and number of follow-ups.

**Why copying a winning campaign did not work.** The first positive reply came for one client, David (software engineering services), from a startup that had recently raised millions. The next morning brought a second, so David had two leads from startups that had raised $15M collectively.
- Alex copied David's campaign text to all other clients. After a week and thousands of emails, only negative replies; only David kept getting positives.
- He then tailored each campaign to the client's individual strengths: strong LinkedIn presence meant LinkedIn; strong brand meant name-dropping clients; a Fintech case study meant a Fintech campaign; a client in London or New York meant reaching out to local founders to suggest a friendly coffee.
- Around 3 clients were getting replies after this. It was a lot of work and "nothing about it felt scalable, productized or right."

**Results were random, and clients cared only about deals.**
- Around month 3, none had closed a deal. He lost 4 clients in 2 weeks, about $100k/year in ARR.
- "They didn't care about my effort. They didn't care about leads either. They wanted deals."
- Then one difficult client reported 2 closed deals worth roughly $120k each, and another client closed one weeks later. Alex considered both flukes: a random LinkedIn "casual coffee" campaign and a campaign that looked like all the others won, while campaigns he was excited about went nowhere. David kept getting leads but had not closed anyone.

chunks.heading: Refunds, guarantees and why they were not a real escape
chunks.text:
**The refund policy.** Alex charged $2k/month for 3 months. If the client was unhappy at the end, he would:
- refund one month in cash,
- give access to his database and newsletter for 1 year,
- keep running campaigns for 3 more months.

He called it "a full money back guarantee, but structured in a smart way."

**Where it failed.**
- Some clients demanded a full refund and threatened chargebacks.
- Others did not want "ping pong with their money." They had goals and were losing time and opportunities regardless of a refund.
- In the early failures he fully refunded clients and offered 3 free months of campaigns to try to turn things around. They took it well, but he lost hundreds of dollars per account.
- One client told him he would have referred Alex to all his agency-owner friends but would now tell them to stay away. Alex: "I could refund money. But I couldn't refund my reputation."

**Risk he did not foresee.** A client's outreach named JPMorgan as a customer, which broke an NDA, and the client's largest customer demanded it stop. The client had a panic attack and cancelled. Lesson: name-dropping clients in outreach carries real risk to the client.

chunks.heading: Turning a custom service into a system: document, automate, then cut
chunks.text:
**Step 1: document everything.** Alex wrote down every task "word for word, comma for comma, click for click," with screenshots, arrows and text. The client process covered:
- onboarding questionnaire sent to the client,
- a gift for the client, varying by country and which store supports it,
- a dedicated to-do board and a dedicated folder per client for meeting notes, info and campaigns,
- setting up LinkedIn and email accounts and gathering leads,
- writing campaigns from best practices and his own best performers,
- reviewing and launching with the client,
- monitoring inboxes daily and forwarding leads,
- a weekly report.

**Step 2: automate.** He realized documenting step by step "was exactly like programming. Just in human language," so he translated it into code. Onboarding time dropped from 45 days for the first client to 10 days for the latest. Campaigns ran on autopilot. Still manual: monitoring inboxes, weekly reports and writing campaigns.

**Step 3: kill complexity.** Every process "had to fight for its life"; if it was just ok or good, it was killed.
- Omnichannel LinkedIn plus email went to email only.
- Weekly client meetings went to zero meetings.
- Any language went to English only.
- Any target customer went to funded startups only.
- 10+ niche campaigns became one "monster campaign" to his whole database.

Result: an easier life, faster process, same or better results, room to take on more clients. Clients were happier because he told them exactly what would be done, when and how, without too many options.

**His framing.** "The real business is not the final product. It's all the behind the scenes stuff that's invisible." His CyberLeads landing page had not changed in months, but behind the scenes the business was unrecognizable. He compares it to a restaurant's kitchen or warehouses and delivery drivers.

chunks.heading: Narrow focus creates expertise and results
chunks.text:
By focusing only on funded startups, email only, and seeing the same agency offers repeatedly, Alex found nuances he would not have found otherwise:
- which angles work best depending on when the startup last raised,
- which angle works best by funding stage,
- predicting when a startup will raise again and reaching out before everyone else.

Campaigns were still very custom and results felt random, but quality improved. One morning every client had received a lead that week, and these were high-quality leads (startups with millions in revenue that had raised millions). Comparing notes, he learned this was considered good: some clients had previously worked with another agency and got 0 qualified leads in 6 months. More clients started closing deals, and his landing page filled with testimonials from clients who had collectively made millions.

chunks.heading: Why playbooks mislead: everyone is "talking their own book"
chunks.text:
Alex argues that recipes and guides failed him, and results came only once he thought for himself. Most guides he followed were "marketing in disguise."
- Competitors' Google articles all plugged their own product or affiliate links.
- The person telling him to build a personal brand sold personal brand building as a service.
- The person telling him to surround himself with successful people ran a founder community.
- The person saying Google is the best channel sold a course on it.

"Everyone is talking their own book. And everyone's advice somehow perfectly aligns with what they are selling."

He applies this to himself. He was a privacy advocate until CyberLeads succeeded selling business data, then told himself he was helping small business owners get past gatekeepers. After Epilepsy Blocker failed, he told himself he preferred "a boring business with an exciting life." His takeaway: "it's a million times easier to change your beliefs and the advice you give, than change your actions and your business. Words are flexible. Actions are not."

His heuristic for testing beliefs:
- A belief that benefits him: be suspicious of it.
- A neutral belief: treat as cosmetic, "just words."
- A belief that costs him and he still holds it: real.

chunks.heading: Scaling pains: automation fragility, marketing vs. fulfillment, and no pipeline
chunks.text:
**Automations break constantly.** His automations imitate a human clicking around websites, so any site change breaks them. Custom client requests (e.g., direct bank transfers, report formats) break them too, as do Google updates to email registration and configuration. Maintaining automations and handling edge cases was "almost as much work as doing it manually."

**The marketing/fulfillment cycle.**
- With many clients, he stops marketing to focus on results.
- When clients leave, he rushes back to marketing, but has no pipeline, so revenue dips until marketing takes effect.
- He "pulls punches on both" and does a half-hearted job at each.

**Public revenue posts get awkward.** Posting revenue and behind-the-scenes updates was "cute at $100/month," but at this scale it can make people feel bad and make clients think he is boasting instead of getting them results. Posting the ugly side got no engagement.

**Distribution spike.** "My First Million" mentioned him and CyberLeads after finding him on Twitter. Effects:
- about 10 new newsletter subscribers per day, plus multiple calls booked for the service,
- over the next month the newsletter doubled to $20k/month and the service made over $20k/month,
- combined, CyberLeads reached around $500k/year.

He could not take more clients and wanted it to stop.

**Income did not fix the job.** He felt he had created a "second cage": hated Mondays (weekly reports, questions), carried his laptop 24/7, and said that at a normal salary he would quit. His answer was to decide to hire people and build a team.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West recounts going from solo operator to running CyberLeads with four remote hires, and what he learned about delegation, hiring, incentives and fighting entropy. He ends with the view that business is more like jazz than science.

chunks.heading: Starting the service on the side, and why he never wanted a team
chunks.text:
- Alex ran CyberLeads, a lead-generation service for clients, mostly solo at first. He never wanted to hire and become someone's boss, partly because he disliked every boss he ever had.
- He admits being solo felt "cool": a $1M solo business was rare, a $1M business with a team was normal.
- His first attempt was to build a "tribe" from girlfriend, best friend, childhood friends and siblings: "No suits. No politics. Just us." It went badly. His girlfriend was insulted by being paid, he and his sister disagreed on everything, and his best friend moved slowly.
- He describes the problem as dancing on "the thin lines between friends, colleagues, bosses and employees", and concluded the surface was too slippery.
- Lesson: he stopped hiring close loved ones and became "cold and strategic" instead. Later he reversed the guilt, deciding employees don't owe him anything and he should create an environment they don't want to leave.

chunks.heading: How he hired his first three people
chunks.text:
- **Where:** he surveyed regions by role: South Africa for sales, Colombia and Brazil for US timezones, Egypt for finance, Eastern Europe for engineering, the Philippines for virtual assistants, India/Pakistan/Sri Lanka for cheapest. He chose the Philippines because his first delegations were simple.
- **Hire 1 (Nneka, virtual assistant):** messaged people on a hiring platform, one replied within 10 minutes, call the next morning, hired in about 12 hours. Her timezone was ahead of his, so tasks were done by the time he woke up.
- **Hire 2 (Joel, client management):** interviewed several, chose the final two, picked the one with relevant experience and an extremely warm personality.
- **Hire 3 (Rayvin, campaign copywriting):** posted a job with a small writing exercise. Of 100 submissions, 5 stood out, interviewed those, one clear winner. He needed no training: "I only needed to say things once."
- **Insight:** he hired Nneka not because she was the best in the world but because she was competent enough, a good person, reliable and replied fast. He applies the same to himself: to win clients he doesn't need to be the world's best at email marketing, just competent, reliable, trustworthy, caring and top of mind.
- **Pay it forward:** he shared the top applicants he couldn't hire with fellow business owners, as the CTO of Product Hunt had done for him.
- **Business is not a science, hiring included:** Nneka was hired on luck (the only person interviewed for the role), Joel mostly on character then trained, Rayvin mostly on skills, Jonathan via personal network. All worked out.

chunks.heading: What to delegate, automate, eliminate or keep
chunks.text:
Before hiring he had three options for a task: eliminate, automate, or do it himself. Delegating became the fourth. His lessons (the "Goldilocks zone"):

- **Not everything that can be automated should be.** Some automations got complicated and broke constantly; a human was more reliable. Better: automate the first 90% and let a human finalize.
- **Not everything that can be strictly defined should be.** Over-strict instructions froze quality on tasks meant to keep improving, like writing client campaigns.
- **Don't delegate as fast as possible.** Only on the 3rd or 4th time doing a task did he sometimes realize it could be done completely differently, automated, or dropped.
- **Some things shouldn't be delegated.** Reviewing client and business numbers weekly by hand sparked ideas and fired him up. "The point is for you to lift the weights, not send a robot or employee to do it for you."
- **Delegate daily and weekly tasks, not quarterly, yearly or one-off ones.** The feedback loop is fast enough to correct and improve. Delegating personal errands (gifts, travel booking) failed: weird gifts, flying to the wrong city, booking a hostel he couldn't stay in. Personal stuff interferes with work.
- **Write text and image instructions, not video.** Documents can be edited and searched; videos can't.
- **Invisible automation compounds.** When a lead-forwarding automation broke, Nneka needed 1 hour to forward 3 leads manually; he took hours himself. He fixed it immediately: "invisible work from the past, paying dividends today."

chunks.heading: Instruction levels and management style
chunks.text:
Instructions get more abstract the higher the role:

- **Tech automations:** extremely dumb and specific ("left click on the button that says 'Next'"); break if the button text changes.
- **Virtual assistant (Nneka):** equally explicit, but trusted to notice changes and update the screenshot and text.
- **Client management (Joel):** heuristics, examples and best practices for drafting reports and email replies. Even nuanced tasks can be broken into steps, just more abstract. Training took many hours of calls over months.
- **Copywriting (Rayvin):** "write good campaigns that generate leads" based on best practices and past successful campaigns.
- **Operator (Jonathan):** "run the day to day with the team, handle edge cases, take the sales calls and close clients."

Management style per person differs: Nneka works from a TODO list, Joel remembers things himself and prefers calls, Rayvin likes reminders and texting. Incentives differ too: Nneka prefers a higher stable salary, Joel chases bonuses, Rayvin wasn't moved even by a $1k bonus per closed client deal. "Everyone is different."

chunks.heading: Org design, pay and keeping the team happy
chunks.text:
- **Pay structure:** base salary plus a monthly bonus per active paying client. He thanks great work with bonuses, even small ones.
- **Cold and pragmatic after "running a cult":** he caught himself designing travel budgets, gym memberships and retreats for his team, then realized he was forcing his own ideals (traveling, working 2 hours a day) on people with different lives. Nneka had just bought a car, Joel was opening a gym and raising kids.
- **Communication:** zero meetings, text only, tracked only whether tasks were completed. Employees could take on extra clients if it didn't interfere. He referred them to business owner friends.
- **Daily client report:** a report he reads in 10 seconds each morning showing next task, time with the client, performance numbers, closed deals, blockers, and emails with drafted replies. It replaced the stress of opening his inbox and wondering what he forgot.
- **Structure experiments:** (1) contractors execute tasks, he handles edge cases; (2) contractors handle their own edge cases; (3) hybrid, contractors do explicit tasks and an operator handles all edge cases. None is better, all have tradeoffs.
- **First all-hands meeting** felt corporate and he cringed at saying "aligned". He later said that stripping out corporate rituals is why he quit his job.

chunks.heading: Fixing the bottleneck: himself
chunks.text:
- Even after delegating, he procrastinated on the creative, important tasks (crafting, reviewing and tweaking campaigns). A 10-minute campaign tweak took a week, he ignored Joel's reminders, and a client was lost because he was late launching campaigns. His fix was to hire Rayvin and remove himself.
- **Self-check while working:** "Am I iterating? Perfecting? Or procrastinating right now?"
  - Procrastinating: working on unimportant tasks, e.g. improving accounting processes while client campaigns got no results.
  - Perfecting: building a week-long automation instead of writing a quick instruction doc for an employee in a few hours.
  - Iterating: his most productive days, working on the most important tasks in a somewhat efficient, inelegant way.
- **"Next day version":** almost everything has a version you can launch or hand off tomorrow.
- **Context switching** between systems, marketing, client fires and sales was killing him; separating roles fixed it.

chunks.heading: Client experience lessons from being a client
chunks.text:
After hiring an agency himself, Alex noticed:

- He didn't need them to be the best, only trustworthy and visibly caring and trying.
- He wanted them to act like a co-founder or boss: say exactly what they need, by when, remind him if late, drag him on a call, push back on bad ideas.
- A short message with a new idea for the future made him feel safer than a good or bad week of results.
- Soft skills beat tech: copying a London bartender who remade a late cocktail from scratch, apologized and asked for feedback, he raised client satisfaction more with intangibles like this than with technical innovation or performance work.

chunks.heading: Hiring an operator and building "a machine"
chunks.text:
- Dealing with daily fires took about 1 hour each morning, but the adrenaline dump killed his energy for the rest of the day.
- He hired Jonathan, a friend who previously ran a similar agency, as operator and closer. Pay: 10% of the profits of the service part of the business, for taking all sales calls and handling edge cases in fulfillment. Jonathan was better at sales calls than Alex: native English speaker, likeable extrovert who loved calls.
- **Entropy fighter:** order is one state, chaos is infinite states, so you constantly intervene. "It feels like a garden that starts turning into a jungle as soon as I turn my head... I need a full time gardener."
- **Machine tuning:** with Jonathan they eliminated unneeded weight, reduced drag by automating, and improved the "cockpit" with tools useful to everyone.
- **Allowing inefficiencies:** he could cut costs by thousands per month (one contractor, cheaper tools, full-time work), but savings would be less than 2 paying clients. Inefficiency is a shock absorber against someone getting sick or quitting, and chill is sustainable. His rule: stay above 80% margins and don't stress.
- **Numbers at that stage:** over $40k/month revenue, about 80% margins, most client campaigns hitting minimum benchmarks. Revenue didn't grow with the new structure and margins dropped, yet he felt he had a "real business."
- **Day-to-day:** he moved full time to marketing and systems, a weekly meeting with Jonathan reviewing every number, a morning client report glance, and only Friday sales calls previously.

chunks.heading: Sales, marketing and results are not a science
chunks.text:
- **Sales:** some buyers are allergic to bullshit, others want to be lied to. A prospect asked him to guarantee a six-figure deal like the testimonials; he answered that if he could 110% guarantee $250,000 in 3 months he'd charge $60k, not $6k, and pointed to the money-back guarantee. He lost the deal.
- **Marketing:** identical campaigns (same words, offer, target, market) for different clients produced wildly different results. Marketing depends on the messenger and uncontrollable factors. He doesn't take friends as clients because he can't guarantee results.
- **Honest statistics:** on aggregate clients made far more than CyberLeads did and the average client multiple times their money back, but the median client didn't. "Whenever you hear someone talk about total numbers, assume that they are hiding the average. And whenever you hear someone talk about the average, assume that they are hiding the median."
- **Principle:** "business is more like jazz." You do it your own way and jam.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Book 10 of Alex West's personal essay series, written at roughly $40k/month in year 6. It is mostly travel and life reflection, with a few durable lessons: run a boring business that funds a rich life, converge by experimenting then keeping little, cut information, and trust real feedback over echo chambers.

chunks.heading: Giving up possessions to find peace instead of clutter
chunks.text: Alex gave nearly everything away and went fully nomadic. He kept only a laptop, phone and chargers, five white and five black t-shirts, two pairs of jeans, two pairs of shorts, a haircut and beard machine, and his documents. Clutter has always given him anxiety, and having little gives him peace of mind. He remembers being happier on a carpet on the floor than on any anatomical bed. Looking at his suitcase, he smiled at how little he needed. He also decided to do the things he always wanted, even trivial or childish ones: tattoos, laser eye surgery, training martial arts again. With money, time and low stress, he re-explored subjects school ruined for him (history, ancient Greek and Latin texts, microscopes, telescopes) and wants a small museum of ancient coins, meteorites and similar pieces someday.

chunks.heading: Why he drops the "rich businessman" image and the full circle fallacy
chunks.text:
When he moved to Milan and started making good money, he adopted slicked-back hair, glasses, a briefcase, an expensive watch, business class and fancy restaurants. It never felt natural: "I always felt like a monkey dressed in clothes and clown shoes." He realized he had circled back to his high school self (buzz cut, baggy clothes, fighting, traveling).

He describes a repeated cycle: experiment with a million things, go overboard, then keep one or two that are worth keeping.
- Skincare: kept only a moisturizer and one soap.
- Biohacking: kept a sleep/heart-rate wearable and intuitive protein and calorie tracking.
- Workouts: ended at powerlifting and Muay Thai, which he already loved and which cover most bases, so he stays consistent.
- Diet: a few supplements and a few boring balanced recipes.
- Clothes: simplest clothes from one Japanese brand with good fabric.
- CyberLeads: out of everything tried over the years, the only thing added and kept was the service.

It feels like wasted time, but the circle is not perfect. He likens it to the Shotgun to Sniper strategy, applied to life.

chunks.heading: Boring business, exciting life
chunks.text:
Alex loves the setup of a boring business and an exciting life. He prefers working 2 hours a day on a boring business, making a ton of money and enjoying life, over the opposite. He knows because he has done the opposite: cool projects like Epilepsy Blocker made no money and left no free time.
- He can keep doing something forever if he can attach a mission to it and see progress over time, like adding even 1kg to the bar in powerlifting.
- His main charity is boring too: bednets against Malaria. They are the best at it, among the most cost effective charities, statistically preventing one death (usually a child's) per $5,000 spent, and have prevented millions of deaths.
- At a rooftop social event he left a table when people talked software, AI and business. After years of imagining admiring conversations about his business, he rarely talks about it now, sometimes says only that he runs a tech business and changes the subject, and wonders whether business is boring once solved.

chunks.heading: Disconnecting from the phone, news and unvetted information
chunks.text:
Alex argues most online content is fake or exaggerated: fake news, fake revenue numbers, fake fitness and business advice, fake connections.
- Learning: apps got him nowhere in Italian for months. Learning the most common 1000 words and practicing with friends and his Italian girlfriend made him fluent enough for a 2h conversation inside 3 months.
- Dating apps: he deleted them in Colombia, because they were a leading way people got kidnapped, robbed or killed. "Ironically, it was the best thing I ever did for my dating life."
- Comparison: a travel video of someone in Bangkok doing Muay Thai, dating and making friends made him feel like he was wasting his life, though he was also in Bangkok, training Muay Thai and sleeping next to a woman he was dating.
- Night runs: he used to run in silence and solve business and personal problems "like tidying my room, but for my mind." He had drifted into running with podcasts, adding thoughts instead.
- Information overload: he hired an online personal trainer (a school friend) because too much information left him unsure what to eat or how to train. He wanted someone to say "these are the only 3 things that matter." He concludes knowledge is subtractive and would rather grow up with a few shelves of vetted books than unlimited unvetted information.

What he did: threw his airpods away, stopped following the news, downgraded his phone and deleted everything except navigation, messaging and calling. "I never missed anything. And I never felt calmer." Earlier he deleted YouTube from his phone and blocked it on his computer, "the best thing I've ever done for my productivity." He also stopped stressing about capturing moments; the best moments are never on camera.

chunks.heading: AI sycophancy, echo chambers and the need for real feedback
chunks.text:
His brother's friend believed he had a mathematical theory explaining the whole universe, would not show it to a professor or forum for fear of theft, and talked only to AI that kept assuring him he was right. Alex admits he does the same: share work with AI and, depending on what he shares, he is "the second coming of Steve Jobs, Miyamoto Musashi or Fyodor Dostoevsky."

- He has seen long-term solo, online travelers become "insanely eccentric and weird" from confirming beliefs through echo chambers, sycophantic AI, superficial friends and bot-filled comments.
- It also affects people who live alone with no real friends or family to observe them, successful people surrounded by yes men, and people cut off from nature or the free market, "forces that don't care about your feelings and give you real feedback."
- He worries about this for himself.

chunks.heading: Books, old books and the limits of knowledge
chunks.text:
Alex weighs books against scrolling. Arguments for books:
- Effort is a filter: months or decades of work versus minutes.
- They are purer, because the selling is over by the time you buy.
- They are more intentional, since you pick the topic and teacher.
- Reading is less passive: you highlight, take notes and form your own realizations.
- Range: thoughts from the past 3,000 years.
- Retention: he remembers books from decades ago but almost nothing from videos, articles and tweets.
- Repetition can change a life: re-reading one idea through different examples, finger tracking the line, can engrave it deeply. "Even a single strong idea can literally change your life."

But books are not perfect or real life, and a best seller can implant a wrong idea. He trusts older books more because of the Lindy effect: if people have copied, translated and read something for hundreds or thousands of years, there is probably a reason. Terrible books existed in ancient Rome too; he and a friend keep the tradition of buying each other terrible self-help books as a prank.

His London bookstore test: he bought three books on travel that were 10, 100 and about 3,000 years old. The 10-year-old, by a life coach, was a collection of client case studies and he could not finish it. The 100-year-old, by an American explorer who died in 1939 crossing the Pacific on a raft, he loved. The third was the Odyssey.

chunks.heading: Why his own advice-writing sounded smart but aged badly
chunks.text:
While writing his books, Alex found it easy to support any argument and make it sound smart by naming frameworks, laws and philosophers (Parkinson's Law, Aristotle's Sophrosyne, Pareto, Occam's Razor, Skin in the Game, survivorship bias and so on) and drawing analogies, like comparing business scaling to physics scales or to civilization's virtues. Those takes "always aged like milk." Each time he returned to edit, they were wrong, simplistic, changed in his mind, or already said better by someone 2,000 years ago.

After writing daily for almost a decade, he concluded the only things that are true are the ones that reflect reality. So he writes the way he started: "Just say what you did. And what happened." He says real morals are actions, real intelligence is behavior, real philosophy is scars, and real teaching is leading by example; the rest is words. He is not here to teach or moralize, is sick of everyone prescribing the perfect routine, diet or business model, and thinks reading should be like hitting two rocks together until you get your own spark, not being spoon fed.

chunks.heading: What travel does: environment shapes you more than you think
chunks.text:
- Alex returned to his hometown after years abroad and within weeks was his old self: waking late, anti-social, no drive, messed-up routine. "I hadn't changed. My environment had."
- He has a baseline character, personality and happiness, and can change, but not as much as he thought.
- He is strongly influenced by weather, home, routine, people, language and body chemistry: introvert or extrovert by setting, different on acne pills, different after weeks of bad sleep and food versus working out and sleeping well.
- Most people are in the middle on most traits, so they fluctuate with their environment.
- Travel forces a different environment on you, so you explore yourself, not just the world. At home you rarely meet new people or try new things; abroad you are forced to.
- By living in many climates, cities, houses and neighborhoods, trying hobbies and dating, he knows what fits him through experience, not guesses. A place alone won't make you happy, but it is far easier in a place you love, with people you love, doing what you love, and money helps by letting you create that.
- Experiences make time feel slow in memory; routine feels fast looking back because it leaves no memories.
- Travel also teaches your own country through contrast and can produce reverse culture shock.

chunks.heading: Places, advice and "little moments"
chunks.text:
- No place is perfect. Big cities inspire him but make him feel broke; nature relaxes him but he gets bored and itches for a challenge; comfortable places change him little; culture-shock places stress him but change his perspective permanently.
- Experience of a place depends on luck, company and mood, so he avoids recommending places. He once confidently sent a friend to a Spanish city where he had great weather, friends and a great life; it went badly for the friend, then he sent him to the other side of the world, which also went badly.
- At a beach fire, a woman asked for his craziest story and he blanked. He had no robbery or arrest stories. He concluded his real travel is "a collection of tiny moments": eating alone at a restaurant, a neighbor practicing opera in Sicily, Friday pizza with flatmates in Milan, working in libraries, a stray dog at a cafe, a favorite table and route, a social circle.
- Big stories he could have told (scuba diving with sharks, sailing through a storm, sparring Muay Thai champions) sounded more dramatic than they felt.
- He tries to learn the language everywhere: it signals respect and effort, carries humor and culture, and "you are talking to the child within them."
- Seeing the world with a "kid's eye" came from a film-viewfinder camera in Vietnam; understanding how things work (why sunsets are red, how undersea cables carry the internet) makes them more magical, not less.

chunks.heading: Accepting a finite life and not maximizing everything
chunks.text:
- He cites roughly 4,000 weeks of life expectancy and the cost of traveling: watching his parents age over video calls and missing small shared moments.
- Business skill carries over: "One of the most important meta skills in business is being ok with not finishing your TODOs." Sometimes the most productive thing is to stop and go to bed, or delete half the list to focus on the few important items, because work never ends and desires never end.
- He rejects the belief that everything happened for a reason or that he is the best possible version of himself. He probably could have made $10M with a different business, had more fun, been a better fighter, spent more time with family, or had more impact via charity. The point is not to maximize everything, which is impossible.
- His target: one great career and business that lets him live comfortably, one place that feels like home, one routine that makes him a happy version of himself, and one person to share life with.
- He is not enlightened: some days he is the grasshopper enjoying life, others the ant wanting money, status and fame. He still compares himself, feels behind, and falls off the horse; his life is "Sisyphean." What matters is being proud and happy with his current life.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West reflects on making his first $1M in revenue after six years of bootstrapping. He argues advice is a treasure map that ages badly, so rely on external maps early and your own compass as you gain experience. He is candid that the milestone felt anticlimactic and that his business was free-falling after a $50k/month peak.

chunks.heading: Making the first $1M: what the numbers and milestones actually looked like
chunks.text:
- Alex hit $1,001,490 in cumulative revenue on June 1, 2024, a few days before his 30th birthday. He calls it revenue only, not profit or income, and says it technically missed his goal of $1M/year by age 30.
- He summed Gumroad, PayPal, every bank account and every Stripe account in a calculator app.
- His timeline: started bootstrapping January 1, 2018; first successful launch May 13, 2018; first dollar June 1, 2018 (two customers at $5/month each on the premium version of GitGardener); moved to Milan January 4, 2020; launched CyberLeads February 14, 2020; first blew up on Twitter April 22, 2020; surpassed his salary July 27, 2020; first day of self-employment January 6, 2021; discovered "the service" November 1, 2021; started it February 1, 2022.
- When he launched the $5/month plan, his father's reply was "Alex.. have you thought of finding a job?"
- He says it took about 20 tries to figure out something that worked, and that "you only have to figure it out once to change your life."
- He celebrates small milestones (launch dates, first dollar, hire dates) as anniversaries. His reasoning: "They mean something to you. So they are important."

chunks.heading: Why the milestone felt flat: ants, grasshoppers and "enough"
chunks.text:
- Alex asks whether a moment will matter in a day, a month, a year or a decade. Most things won't. Even though hitting $1M felt anticlimactic, he expects it to give fulfillment for a long time.
- He separates short-term happiness (exercise, swimming, food) from slow-release fulfillment (his fighting journey, his entrepreneurship journey). He wants both.
- His ant/grasshopper model: the ant works all day on one project; the grasshopper lives for the day and does the minimum. He treats them as complementary, not contradictory.
- He says he used to confuse the two. He chased fleeting pleasure and ended up unfulfilled, then chased big goals and found they didn't make him happy.
- In practice he lets life swing naturally. Recent years alternated between one "ant" year and one "grasshopper" year. The aim is to know which phase he is in and feel zero guilt about it. His line: "it's called work-life balance. Not work-day balance."
- After the milestone he says he feels "enough" for the first time. His anxieties about age and accomplishments faded, he stopped envying anyone, and he found himself celebrating other people's success. He judges people by whether they are kind, authentic and fun, and by how they treat waiters and taxi drivers, not by money or fame.
- He never did the backpacking-hostel phase. By the time he traveled at 25 he had a business and wanted a nice apartment and routine. His takeaway: "whatever you don't experience today, you might never experience. Not because the opportunity will be gone. But because you will."

chunks.heading: Why advice often fails: his friend's launch with no customers
chunks.text:
- Alex helped a friend launch a product using his full distribution:
  - Posted on Product Hunt from his personal account (tens of thousands of followers).
  - Posted on his Twitter (millions of views) and his newsletter (5,000 businesses).
  - Ran email campaigns almost identical to ones he ran for clients that made them millions.
  - Spent hours consulting on the idea, offer and product.
- Result: zero customers.
- The friend moved from excited to neutral to disappointed. Alex's only advice was to keep trying, with this or another idea, until it works.
- He says even a perfect playbook often fails because he can't know the friend's terrain, and he admits he recommends his own path to fewer and fewer people each year.
- He says it's easy to forget what starting from scratch is like without a platform, experience, network or audience: "It's fucking hard. I am very lucky."

chunks.heading: Maps versus compasses: when to follow playbooks and when to trust instinct
chunks.text:
- **Maps** are other people's explicit knowledge: frameworks, playbooks, books (his examples: "How to become a millionaire", "The 5 laws of marketing", "The 3 best business models", "The ultimate guide to hiring"). They are accurate but hard to match to your own circumstances, and the terrain keeps changing.
- **Compasses** are your own intuition and experience. They are vague and only directionally correct, but apply to many cases.
- Rule he states: the earlier you are in a domain, the more you should rely on external knowledge; the more experience you gain, the more you should trust your own intuition. Don't burn the maps and don't follow the compass blindly. "Like a real captain, you consult them both."
- Early on he distrusted himself ("full of cognitive biases") and followed mental models, decision frameworks and playbooks. Books "changed my life." As his situation got more unique, that started backfiring, and decisions based on his own experience worked better.
- His caveats on his own advice: he may misremember, confuse luck for skill (and skill for luck), and some of it is outdated.
- His example of timeless versus dated advice: "don't camp near water at night" holds, while "turn left at the oak tree" may no longer apply.
- Musashi's Book of Five Rings, as he summarizes it: "Learn the rules. Abide by the rules. Break the rules." You can't skip the sequence. You start with maps and shift to your compass over time.

chunks.heading: On business coaches and mentors
chunks.text:
- A client introduced Alex to a business coach who had run a large business. Alex took two calls.
- He found it felt like "founder therapy": questions about stress, exercise, goals, hiring and delegation. The growth ideas for CyberLeads were things he had already thought of, already tried, or found irrelevant.
- His reasoning: nobody can know his business in two hours when he has looked at it from every angle for half a decade.
- He says he does the same when helping others: "think out loud and throw shit at the wall."
- He still sees value. A conversation like this is how he discovered "the service" (November 2021). But he says it's never one person handing over a precise map; it's mostly swapping experiences.

chunks.heading: Setting a big goal, and knowing when it's costing you
chunks.text:
- Advice to his younger brother: pick any big goal and become that person. It could be getting lines on your stomach. Motives don't matter either. Alex started Muay Thai because he got beaten up, and started building businesses to prove to himself and others that he was better.
- What matters is that you start, from anywhere, and "improve over time and adjust your sails."
- Skills transfer across fields. He draws parallels between fighting, business, photography, writing and travel, and says taking anything to depth teaches you about the rest. Diving into a new subject is a good way to go deeper in an old one.
- Warning from a school friend: for five years, every time they talk, the friend is "one week away" from hitting it big. His life is on hold (no socializing, no girls, only gym and work) until it happens, and he has sometimes self-sabotaged. Alex admits he has encouraged the cycle.
- Alex's fix: write down exactly what you would do, feel and experience if your craziest dreams came true. When he did this years ago he was surprised how little he wanted. Much of it (travel, friends, a photo album, music, a film, a book, a language, love, family) may be reachable now, for example through a good remote job. "Work isn't the only place you can get fulfillment from."
- His stance: set big goals and give life everything, but be aware you may not reach them, may stop wanting them, or may waste years.

chunks.heading: The $50K/month peak and the decline
chunks.text:
- In the appendix Alex says that a few months earlier he hit a record month of $50k/month.
- He says his business "has began to die and is free falling."
- He is afraid and trying to work out what is going wrong, but doesn't "allow myself to complain too much."
- He frames it as the cost of the path he chose, alongside other fighters, entrepreneurs and artists: "The highest highs. And the lowest lows."
- He gives no cause or fix yet: "I hope I can fix this."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West recounts CyberLeads falling from $50k to $20k/month. Tracking 30+ metrics, then three big levers, backfired past a threshold. Doing the work himself and talking to clients exposed the real problems, and a feature-heavy relaunch bloated the product and diluted its core.

chunks.heading: Why Alex's metrics didn't save CyberLeads: tracking 30+ metrics and the three-input equation
chunks.text:
Alex's business plateaued at about $42k/month, then fell to $25k/month, and then to roughly $20k/month in year 7. His first response was to track more. He and Jonathan held daily multi-hour calls through 30+ metrics grouped into fulfillment, sales, marketing and business. They tried to bring every metric back to its level from when CyberLeads made $50k/month, reasoning that matching the inputs would reproduce the outputs.

- Revenue kept falling anyway. Some metrics improved 5X, some stayed flat and some declined, so he couldn't tell whether the business was dying because of the metrics that hadn't improved or because results hadn't kicked in yet.
- Historically, marketing and product work took about 3 months to show up in revenue. At this point it had been 4.
- His conclusion: "We are tracking too much. And we are working on too many things."
- His own explanation for not fighting at his best with a camp: he tried to focus on too many things at once and "fucked up". His best fights came with few variables and no camp.

chunks.heading: The equation of business: customers, retention and price
chunks.text:
After years of tracking 30+ metrics, Alex concluded that only 3 inputs mattered: how many clients he signs per month, how many months they stay, and how much they pay.

- For years he signed about 4 new clients per month, who stayed about 4 months and paid $2k/month. CyberLeads therefore plateaued at 4 x 4 x $2k = $32k/month. The newsletter sat around $10k/month, giving about $42k/month, or $500k/year.
- The plateau happened because the number of customers coming in equaled the number leaving, an equilibrium. He had assumed things would compound just by staying in business.
- Not on his list of what mattered: average onboarding time, emails sent per client per week, follow-ups to hot leads, social post counts, or even churn.

chunks.heading: Working backwards to $1M/year: the "3-4-5"
chunks.text:
Alex used the equation to reverse engineer a $1M/year target.

- The "3-4-5": clients pay $3k/month, he signs 4 new clients per month, and they stay 5 months on average. That doubles the agency side.
- He judged it realistic because he had charged $3k/month, signed 4 clients in a month, and kept clients 5 months many times before. The task was lifting the averages.
- Adding another $10k to $20k/month from the newsletter and other offers (which he had done before) would reach about $83k/month, or $1M/year.
- He found one "golden metric" per lever, and none were the obvious ones:
  - More new clients correlated most with the number of meetings with potential clients (not traffic or Twitter impressions).
  - Longer retention correlated most with the number of leads forwarded to clients (not deals closed or lower prices).
  - Price: higher prices didn't mean clients stayed less, and $3k/month appeared to maximize LTV.

chunks.heading: What he tried, and why every lever backfired
chunks.text:
Alex pushed all three golden metrics hard.

- Meetings: "book a call" links went into the free newsletter signup, the weekly email, the monthly list, cold email campaigns and welcome emails. He offered free AI demos, free introductions to other agency owners and free consultations. Meetings went up 5X.
- Leads: he built an agency network matching agencies with complementary services, and a referral network asking each new newsletter agency if it wanted to hire another agency. Leads forwarded went up 5X. He also posted 5X more on Twitter.
- Result: all of it backfired past a certain point.
  - More booked calls did not close more deals. Calls were mostly unqualified: no-shows, a prospect who only wanted a free lead first, a prospect interrogating credibility, and one who feared being burned by agencies after losing over $10k. Only one prospect closed, the one who found him on Twitter and booked on his own, and only at $2k/month. $3k/month was too expensive for everyone.
  - More leads forwarded became overwhelming. His best client cancelled after months of daily leads: "we would prefer to have 1 solid call per week than scheduling calls every day with bad fits."
  - The $3k/month price made it impossible to close anyone.
  - A free newsletter tier increased lead volume but killed paid newsletter growth.
  - Posting more on social media eventually dropped engagement and caused unfollows.
- His general lesson: optimizing a metric beyond a point backfires. He compares this to chasing "super-optimal" blood pressure, which ended with him fainting in a pool of blood.

chunks.heading: Why the dashboard lied, and going back into the work
chunks.text:
Alex says "numbers don't lie, but in my case they did." Dashboard metrics looked fine while the actual work had decayed, because he had removed himself from the business.

- He jumped in himself: tweaking campaigns that weren't generating leads, doing slow tasks, and watching recorded sales calls.
- He found mistakes in client campaigns, embarrassing emails going to clients, outdated systems followed blindly instead of common sense, extremely salesy emails to hot leads, and sales calls with no structure.
- He then held many meetings with his team to fix systems, client communication and campaign writing.
- He had told himself he could work 2 hours per day, make $500k/year and enjoy life. His honest read was that those days might be over and he needed to do the work he disliked.

chunks.heading: Asking customers for the truth: honesty and brutal feedback
chunks.text:
When Jonathan said he no longer believed in the service ("we could do so much more with AI and all these new tools, but we're still running things old school"), Alex contacted every current and past client.

- His rule: "When you don't know what to say, just tell the truth." He told them he had tried to remove himself, things slipped, he was back, and he would personally handle their campaigns.
- Clients responded well to the honesty. Some stayed, some left, a couple came back.
- He asked for brutally honest feedback and took notes through hour-long conversations. He called it painful but necessary.
- He has a no-ego rule with Jonathan: when talking business, it's about the business, not the people, so they can be honest.
- He had been skeptical of AI tools because earlier attempts only marginally improved things while adding cost and complexity. He reconsidered because it had been years.

chunks.heading: Founder mode vs. manager mode, and rebuilding the offer
chunks.text:
Alex realized he had built the perfect business for himself (minimum work, maximum money, industry-standard quality) and forgot to build the perfect service for clients. He had never aimed to be the best at what he did.

- His new view: founder mode and manager mode are cyclical. Founder mode invents, sets up and turns the business into a machine. Manager mode oversees, steps back and enjoys life. Removing yourself is not a one-way destination, and you may need to return to fix things.
- To redesign the service he imagined it at 10X the price, $20k/month. That version would include:
  - Joining clients as a co-founder, sending leads from day one, and weekly consulting on offer and business.
  - Partnerships with agencies serving Silicon Valley startups, retweets from his account (millions of views per year), showcases in his newsletter (5,000 business owners) and launches on his Product Hunt (tens of thousands of followers).
  - Introductions to VC funds, a founder community as a moat against copycats and AI, and a network for boosting each other's content.
  - Custom campaigns per client instead of only funded startups, using AI and the latest tools, "even if they only help marginally."
- Lesson he re-learned: "It's not about what you think your customers 'need'. It's about what your customers 'want'." They all want AI and to feel they are not being left behind, so give it to them.
- It took about 3 months of full-day work to rebuild. For the first 2 years CyberLeads was a monthly list, then for 3 more years a simple service on top.

chunks.heading: Bloat, the first idea, and changing one thing at a time
chunks.text:
The rebuilt CyberLeads diluted its core, and prospects got confused. A typical reaction: "we were interested in the funded startup list and the cold email campaigns. But all the rest is cool too, I guess."

- Why competitors fell away: for years he added almost nothing to CyberLeads, so positioning stayed clear. Most copycats kept adding features until they were no longer competing with him. Keeping a product extremely simple for years is hard, especially as building gets easier.
- His takeaway: "Sometimes the first idea is the best idea. And then you just destroy it over time. That's why launching fast is important." He sees the same in photography, where the first photo is usually the best.
- A painter he met in Cyprus said he knows a painting is finished when he names it, and after that he is not allowed to touch it or he destroys it. Alex wonders if he had already "christened" CyberLeads.
- Powerlifting rules he applies to business:
  - If you are progressing, change nothing.
  - If you are stuck, make one change at a time, and the smallest possible: add a rep, then a set, then a day, then an exercise.
  - Don't nuke the program and start over. Change reluctantly.
- Injury lesson: he changed too many things at once and spent half a year troubleshooting a back injury.
- Organism, not machine: after his friend (a medical student) told him the body is a complex, interconnected system that dislikes extremes, Alex suggests CyberLeads may be more organism than machine. It responds to simple levers, dislikes extremes and many simultaneous changes, is shaped by its environment, and may have a finite lifespan.

chunks.heading: Limits of control and knowing when to stop searching
chunks.text:
Alex ends unresolved, with CyberLeads dying and no fix found.

- He feels less control the older he gets. He now distrusts research studies (few people, narrow conditions) and prefers adapting his lifestyle around injuries to eliminating them.
- He uses the book "Uncle Petros and Goldbach's Conjecture" as a warning: a mathematician spends his life searching for a proof that may not exist, like looking for keys that might not be in the house.
- His fear: he has already wasted years searching for keys that may never have existed, with City Vibes, Epilepsy Blocker, and CyberLeads when it was stuck at $500k/year.
- He doesn't want to give up, but doesn't want to keep searching a room with no keys. His conclusion: "The only place left is the external."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex West recounts burning out as CyberLeads declined from about $500k/year, pivoting to a $3k consulting offer, and spending a year writing his books. He distills what he learned: businesses are sequences of S curves that eventually fall, waves shape outcomes more than models, and growth comes from shotgunning products, sniping a winner, then shotgunning again for the next lever.

chunks.heading: The collapse of CyberLeads: what Alex learned shutting down his $500k/year business
chunks.text:
Alex's agency-style business CyberLeads peaked at about $500k/year and then declined. He fell apart personally, killed the service, switched to consulting, and rebuilt on a smaller, calmer base.

- **Signal that something was wrong:** he could work 16 hours a day happily when the business was thriving, but struggled to work 10 minutes on a failing one.
- **Reaction:** "It is lack of direction, progress and results. Not hours worked. That makes me feel like I want to quit."
- **Symptoms:** pretend work, ghosting employees, skipped marketing and follow-ups, and lost passports, flights and gear.
- **Cost cutting:** he was close to breaking even for the first time ever. He cancelled unneeded software and let go of two contractors to roughly halve expenses.
- **Honest takeaway:** morals like "I would never fire anyone" "don't mean shit until they are tested in the real world."
- **Trigger for the change:** a friend asked what he would do if he retired today. His answer was to stop traveling, shut the service, keep only the newsletter and write his books.

chunks.heading: The $10k/year plan that backfired
chunks.text:
When clients stopped closing deals, Alex tried a radical annual offer.

- **Offer:** $800/month on a $10k/year plan, with no monthly billing, plus access to his calendar.
- **Logic:** with a full year, surely a referral, partnership or cold email campaign would pay the client back. His LTV would go from $6k to $10k, or $20k on renewal.
- **Result:** his calendar flooded. One client booked a weekly call, and Alex ended up doing product launches and "founder therapy".
- **Lesson:** "the more I offered and gave, the more expectations rose and they asked for."
- **Fallout:** one client said he felt Alex "didn't even care about my business". Another cut a 12-month deal at 2 months, took the refund, and still issued a chargeback.
- **Outcome:** after refunds and chargebacks he broke even that month, which helped push him to shut the service down.

chunks.heading: The consulting offer: $3k single payment, $8k/month
chunks.text:
Alex replaced the service with consulting and it worked quickly.

- **Offer:** everything he did for clients at $3k/month, sold instead as a single $3k payment through a self-checkout page with no sales calls.
- **Delivery:** calls where he walks clients through each step and says what he would do in their position.
- **Results:** $20k in the first month, all profit, then stabilizing at about $8k/month (about $100k/year).
- **Belief behind it:** "Marketing shouldn't be outsourced... It's a founder activity. It's the oxygen of the business. And no one is going to care about your business the way you will."
- **Honest expectation setting:** marketing isn't a science. He might try 3-4 experiments for a client, but they may need 30.
- **Team:** he kept two team members to run the newsletter and the new service, and parted ways with a contractor, giving another several months of salary.
- **Feeling:** consulting felt easier. "I don't feel sad like I thought I would. I feel relief."

chunks.heading: Why CyberLeads declined: waves, not a bad model
chunks.text:
Alex concluded he had mistaken success for mastery and that a pile of changes outside his control had hit him.

- **Success despite his habits:** he says he is a "terrible entrepreneur" by conventional measures (no contracts, slow replies, soft on refunds, avoids competitors). Looking back, CyberLeads had "great genetics" (channels, retention, pricing, brand, market timing).
- **The plateau:** at about $500k/year, nothing he did moved clients signed, retention or price much.
- **What changed:**
  - Tools cut the cost of leads (to $49/month) and email sending (to $99/month) by roughly 10x, removing barriers to entry.
  - Influencers promoted the model, creating thousands of competitors, fake testimonials and spam, so buyers went from "default excited" to "default suspicious".
  - Google and Microsoft anti-spam changes forced system rebuilds roughly every 6 months, and cold email stopped working.
  - Twitter's "For You" algorithm meant follower count stopped mattering. He gets fewer views at 40,000 followers than he did at 4,000.
  - AI threatens to generate his monthly funding list from one prompt.
- **Prediction error:** he was right about agencies, funded startups and email persisting, but "I was trying to predict the tiny earthquakes... while missing the invisible giant tsunamis."
- **Probability point:** 1,000 independent events that are each 99% likely all happening has only about a 0.43% chance, which is why hindsight feels obvious.

chunks.heading: Riding waves and living in the future
chunks.text:
Alex says he wrongly believed he never rode waves.

- **Waves he did ride:** the internet itself, bootstrapping/solopreneur/build-in-public, Covid (companies hiring remote agencies), post-Covid money printing (US companies hiring agencies), and paid newsletters being trendy.
- **Wrong lesson:** he ignored Crypto, NFT and AI waves because they didn't affect him, then concluded he should ignore every wave forever.
- **His view:** "The magic of entrepreneurship is deciding how to respond to each wave." That means choosing which to capitalize on, adapt to, or ignore, and when to adjust sails versus jump in the lifeboat.
- **Growth curves:** he says they are "a crazy, random squiggly line", not linear, compounding or S curve models. Every framework he made eventually broke.
- **Catching waves:** he didn't spot them; he lived in the future. "The future is already here, it's just unevenly distributed." You only need to be earlier than most. He planned a remote, hire-online, travel business in 2017 when family thought it absurd.
- **Risk:** once ideas are mainstream you lose that edge. A competing agency at $500k/year was breaking even with co-founders, a London office, about 15 staff, paid marketing and custom work. Alex ran solo at 80% margins with a niche, productized offer, organic channels, newsletter upgrades and about 90% automation.

chunks.heading: Adapt or die: ships vs fleets, and why one win isn't enough
chunks.text:
Alex's father asked how he stayed in business 40 years answered that every industry demands adaptation.

- **Father's point:** "Whoever stops adapting, ends up having the same fate as the dinosaurs." Nothing from his business in the 80s is the same except the name.
- **Ship of Theseus:** old companies are really new ones with old names.
- **Fleets:** it may be easier to navigate with multiple boats than to endlessly adapt one. Large companies often hold multiple businesses.
- **Entrepreneurial judgment:** know when to stay focused on one boat, when to adapt it, and when to add a new one.
- **Dropped belief:** he thought he only needed to reach escape velocity once and then coast. "I was wrong. Again... I will have to find another CyberLeads again. And, who knows, it might take me another 20 tries."
- **Retirement math:** plans are fragile (US dependence, 5% vs 3% inflation, war), so he reframes the goal as loving work enough to do it by choice. "Not to retire young. But to love your job and life so much that you enjoy it every day."
- **Durable assets:** some skills fade like cardio (idea generation, stress tolerance, work ethic) and some persist like motor skills (coding, design, marketing, hiring, management, audience, customer list, intuition). He also notes: "the only thing that cannot be taken away from you is your story."

chunks.heading: The updated "Shotgun to Sniper" framework
chunks.text:
Alex's one remaining framework, which he expects to break too.

- **Idea phase ("artist mode"):** shotgun many products and cut losers fast. Don't fall in love with ideas; everything has a "next day version". What worked for him was choosing the distribution channel and market first, then the idea. CyberLeads came from copying someone and adding his twist. The goal is a good product plus a good channel, and "when something works, you will know it."
- **Growth phase ("athlete mode"):** no more creativity; put in reps and ride the S curve. Height is set by "business genetics": how many people you sign, how long they stay, how much they pay.
- **Plateau:** if numbers are large, optimize. Improving signups, retention and price by 25% each doubles the business; 8x if all double. Doubling CyberLeads from $250k to $500k/year was worth it, but doubling the newsletter from $4k to $8k/month wasn't, so he looked for a new S curve.
- **Optimizing:** work back to front (fulfillment, then sales, then marketing), systematizing, productizing, delegating and automating first.
- **New S curves:** look at marketing (new channels, hardest), product (retention), and pricing (easiest, most effective). His price went from $5/month (GitGardener) to $300/month (newsletter) to $3k/month (service), a 600x rise, while revenue went from $100/month to $50,000/month, a 500x rise.
- **Loop:** shotgun products, sniper the winner to the plateau, squeeze it if worthwhile, otherwise shotgun new experiments for the next lever, and repeat. "Just do shit."

chunks.heading: Reflection: building during uncertainty
chunks.text:
Takeaways Alex draws on starting again.

- **Being lost is normal:** "For the vast majority of the past 8 years, I've been lost."
- **Reverse sabbatical:** when in doubt do the opposite of what you've been doing. He stopped traveling, worked on writing instead of business, and settled in a beach apartment with a daily routine. This restored his spark and made work feel interesting again.
- **Ownership principle (Little Prince):** he can't help everyone, but "my frog, my employees, my family" come first, which is why he tried to keep his team employed.
